## Vinaya Piṭaka
## Pārājika-kaṇḍa Commentary (Volume I)
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Introduction to the Text

To that Blessed One, the Refuge of the world of beings, who for countless aeons and for an immeasurable period performed extremely difficult deeds and reached exhaustion for the welfare and benefit of the world; to that Buddha of Great Compassion, I pay homage.

To that noble Dhamma, which was constantly practiced by the Buddha, and which the world of beings, unable to penetrate its nature, wanders through the rounds of existence; to that Dhamma which destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance (avijjā), I pay homage.

To that Noble Saṅgha, endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana); who is like a fertile field for those beings desiring merit; to that Noble Saṅgha, I pay homage with my head.

By the power of the merit, an abundant stream of goodness, which I have obtained through thus constantly paying homage to the Triple Gem, may all dangers and obstacles be destroyed.
2:
As long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains (undiminished in text and meaning among the conscientious), the Sāsana of the Buddha—who, without leaning towards the two extremes, remained well-established in the Middle Way of the Eightfold Path—remains firmly rooted (among the conscientious). Relying on the power of the ancient teachers (or the commentaries they explained), I shall explain that Vinaya Piṭaka, unmixed with views other than those of the Mahāvihāra tradition.

Indeed, the great ancient teachers—who had completely washed away the stains of defilements and taints (āsavas) with the water of the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, who possessed pure higher knowledge (vijjā) and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), who were experts in explaining the True Dhamma, who were incomparable in the practice of effacing defilements, and who were like the banners of the Mahāvihāra monastery—have truly explained this Vinaya Piṭaka through various beautiful methods and in accordance with the intention of the Exalted Buddha.

However, because that commentary was composed in the Sīhaḷa (Sinhalese) language, it does not serve any benefit to the monks in other islands (such as Jambudīpa). Therefore, well-remembering the request and encouragement of the Elder named Buddhasiri, I shall now begin this new commentary in accordance with the methods found in the Pali texts.

In beginning this commentary, I shall take the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā as the primary body, and likewise, without discarding the appropriate meanings stated in the famous commentaries such as the Mahāpaccariya and Kurundī, and including the traditions of the Elders, I shall begin this commentary appropriately and well.
3:
May the Elders, the middle-seated monks, and the newly ordained monks, who possess devout hearts and who respect and cherish the Dhamma of the Buddha—the Lamp of Dhamma—listen to this (explanation) of mine.

The Buddha taught the Dhamma and the Vinaya; the sons of the Buddha (such as Mahākassapa and other Elders) understood them exactly as they were. Because the ancient teachers, not discarding the views of those Elders, composed the commentaries in the past.

Therefore, all the words spoken in those commentaries—excluding errors of negligence in transcription—shall be the standard (measure) for wise monks in this Sāsana who have respect for the three trainings (sikkhā).

Furthermore, discarding the foreign (Sīhaḷa) language, condensing the detailed methods, including all decisions without omission, and not deviating even slightly from the order of the Pali texts.

Since this explanation (commentary), which clarifies the meaning of the words in the Sutta texts in accordance with those very Suttas, will also be a standard, it should therefore be studied with respect and consistency.
4:
## External Introduction (Bāhiranidāna-kathā)

In that context, since it was said "I shall explain that Vinaya," the Vinaya must first be defined. Therefore, it is said: "In this Sāsana, 'Vinaya' means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is intended." For the purpose of explaining that Vinaya Piṭaka, this matrix (mātikā) is set forth:

By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken;
By whom it was maintained, and by whom it was brought;
Where it was established; having stated this procedure,
I shall then perform the explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya,
Showing the meaning of the text beginning with 'Tena' in various ways.

In that matrix, the phrase "By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken" refers to such words as "At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Verañjā." These words are not the direct personal words of the Buddha himself; therefore, it must be asked: "By whom was this spoken? When was it spoken? And why was it spoken?" It was spoken by the Venerable Upāli Thera, and that was at the time of the First Great Council.

## Account of the First Great Council

Although this so-called First Great Council was described in the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka of the Cullavagga, it should also be understood here in this manner for the sake of proficiency in the introduction.

Beginning from the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta until the discipline of the wanderer Subhadda, the Blessed One performed the duties of a Buddha. Then, at Kusinārā, in the Sāla grove of the Malla kings, between the twin Sāla trees, at the time of dawn on the full moon day of the month of Visākha (Kason), the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue. When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, the head of the Saṅgha among the seven hundred thousand monks who had assembled, recalled the words spoken on the seventh day after the Buddha's Parinibbāna by Subhadda, who had gone forth in his old age: "Enough, friends, do not sorrow, do not lament; we are well-freed from that Great Ascetic. We were harassed by him saying, 'This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you!' But now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish." Recalling this, Mahākassapa thought, "It is possible that wicked monks might think the Teaching has no teacher..."
5:
(Wicked monks), holding to their own views and gaining a following, would soon cause the threefold True Dhamma to disappear. As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya remain, the Dispensation of the Teacher is not without a master. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and prescribed shall be your teacher after my passing."

"It would be well if I were to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya so that this Dispensation may endure and last for a long time. The Blessed One showed me favor by saying, 'Kassapa, will you wear my hempen pāṃsukūla robes that have been worn out?' thus allowing me to share his own robes. Furthermore, he favored me by placing me on an equal footing with himself in terms of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), including the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihārasamāpatti) and the six higher powers (abhiññā), in this manner: 'Monks, just as I, whenever I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures... enter and dwell in the first jhāna; so too, monks, does Kassapa, whenever he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures... enter and dwell in the first jhāna.' For such favor, how else could I be free from debt other than by reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya? Just as a king favors his son, who will maintain the royal lineage, by bestowing upon him his own armor and authority, so too the Blessed One, thinking, 'This Kassapa will be the one to maintain my lineage of the True Dhamma,' favored me with this extraordinary favor not shared with other disciples." Thinking thus, he encouraged the monks to strive for the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

Regarding this matter, it should be understood in detail starting from the entire Subhadda Section, which says: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks, saying: 'Friends, once I was traveling on the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a large community of monks, about five hundred in number...'"
6:
Then (the Venerable Mahākassapa) said this:

"Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Before what is not Dhamma (adhamma) shines forth and Dhamma is pushed aside; before what is not Vinaya (avinaya) shines forth and Vinaya is pushed aside; before those who speak what is not Dhamma become powerful and those who speak Dhamma become weak; before those who speak what is not Vinaya become powerful and those who speak Vinaya become weak (let us recite the Dhamma and Vinaya)."

The monks said, "If that is so, Bhante, let the Elder select the monks (for the council)." The Elder, setting aside many hundreds and thousands of worldlings (puthujjana), stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmi), non-returners (anāgāmi), and dry-insight Arahants (sukkhavipassaka) who were bearers of the ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher, selected only four hundred and ninety-nine Arahants who were bearers of the entire Tipiṭaka, who had attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), who possessed great psychic power, who were mostly designated as foremost (etadagga) by the Blessed One, and who possessed the three knowledges (tevijja) and other qualities. Referring to this selection, it is said (in the Cullavagga): "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected five hundred Arahants less one."

Why did the Elder select one less than five hundred? It was to leave a place for the Venerable Ānanda. This was because the recitation of the Dhamma could not be performed either with him or without him. Since that Venerable was then a trainee (sekkha) with tasks still to be done (to reach Arahantship), the recitation could not be done with him. However, since there was no Sutta or Geyya taught by the Ten-Powered One that the Venerable had not heard or received in the presence of the Blessed One, the recitation could not be done without him.

If it is asked, "Even though he was a trainee, since he would be of great help in the recitation, why was he not selected by the Elder?" The answer is: to avoid the criticism of others. The Venerable Mahākassapa was very intimate with the Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, he would admonish him by calling him a "youth" (kumāraka), saying, "This youth does not know his measure," even when grey hairs had appeared on Ānanda's head. Furthermore, this Venerable was born of the Sakyan clan and was the son of the Blessed One's younger paternal uncle (a cousin). In that situation, other monks might criticize, thinking the Elder was acting out of favoritism, saying, "The Elder has set aside many Arahants who have attained the analytical insights and selected Ānanda, who is only a trainee." To avoid such criticism from others, he left Ānanda out...
7:
Thinking, "The Council cannot be held (excluding Ven. Ānanda); I will select (Ven. Ānanda) only with the consent of the monks," Ven. Mahākassapa did not initially select Ven. Ānanda. Then, the monks themselves entreated the Elder on behalf of Ven. Ānanda. Regarding that entreaty, Ven. Upāli said: "Venerable Mahākassapa, although this Ven. Ānanda is a trainee (sekha), he is incapable of following the four wrong courses (agati) of favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear. This Ven. Ānanda has learned much of the Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, Venerable Elder, please select Ven. Ānanda as well." Then, Ven. Mahākassapa selected Ven. Ānanda. Thus, including Ven. Ānanda who was selected with the consent of the monks, there were five hundred Elders.

Then, the Elder monks thought: "Where shall we recite the Dhamma and Vinaya?" Then, the Elder monks thought: "Rājagaha is a place of great resort with abundant lodgings. What if we, while spending the rainy season in Rājagaha, recite the Dhamma and Vinaya, and no other monks spend the rainy season in Rājagaha?" Why did they think so? It was because: "This Council is our enduring task. We fear that some incompatible person, like Subhadda, might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and cause disruption." Then, Ven. Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha through a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiya-kammavācā). That proclamation should be understood as stated in the Saṅgītikhandhaka.

After informing the Saṅgha, when the seven days of the funeral rites and the seven days of relic worship following the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata had passed, thinking, "Half a month has passed; now only one and a half months of the summer remain, and the commencement of the rainy season is near," Ven. Mahākassapa said, "Friends, let us go to Rājagaha," and taking half of the Saṅgha, he departed by one route. Ven. Anuruddha also took half of the Saṅgha and departed by another route. Ven. Ānanda, however, taking the bowl and robes of the Blessed One and surrounded by a company of monks, went to Sāvatthī, and wishing to go to Rājagaha, he set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. Wherever Ven. Ānanda went, there was great lamentation: "Venerable Ānanda, where have you left the Teacher and come..."
8:
"...where have you left the Teacher and come?" thus they lamented loudly. When the Elder arrived at Sāvatthī in due course, there was great lamentation just like on the day the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna.

There, Ven. Ānanda consoled the multitude with a Dhamma talk related to impermanence (anicca) and other themes. He then entered the Jetavana monastery, opened the door of the Gandhakuṭi where the Possessor of the Ten Powers (Dasabala) used to reside, took out the couch and stool, dusted them, swept the Gandhakuṭi, discarded the withered flowers and rubbish, brought the couch and stool back inside, placed them in their original positions, and performed all the minor and major duties that were to be done when the Blessed One was alive.

After doing so, because the Elder had been mostly standing and sitting since the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, in order to soothe his body whose elements were disturbed, he drank a milk purgative on the second day and remained only within the monastery. Referring to that drinking of medicine, he said to the youth sent by the youth Subha: "Young man, it is not the right time today; I have taken a dose of medicine today. Perhaps we may visit tomorrow."

On the second day, taking Ven. Cetaka as his attendant monk, he was questioned by the youth Subha and preached the Subha Sutta, which is the tenth sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya.

After preaching thus, the Elder had the broken and dilapidated parts of the Jetavana monastery repaired, and as the commencement of the rainy season drew near, he went to Rājagaha. Similarly, Ven. Mahākassapa and Ven. Anuruddha also went to Rājagaha, taking the entire Saṅgha of monks with them.

At that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha. All of them were neglected, dilapidated, and cluttered with rubbish. This was because when the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, all the monks took their own bowls and robes, abandoned the monasteries and precincts, and departed. In those monasteries, the Elders thought, "Let us repair the broken and dilapidated parts in the first month," both to honor the words of the Blessed One and to avoid the criticism of the heretics (titthiya). For if they did not repair them, the heretics might say: "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while their Teacher was alive; they abandoned them when he attained Parinibbāna." It is meant that they planned this to avoid their criticism. This has also been said:
9:
Then the elder monks had this thought: "Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repair of what is broken and dilapidated. Come, friends, let us spend the first month repairing what is broken and dilapidated, and in the middle month, let us assemble and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya."

On the second day, those elders went and stood at the palace gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid homage, and asked about his duties, saying, "Venerable sirs, why have you come?" The elders informed him of the need for manpower to repair the eighteen great monasteries (Mahāvihāras). "Very well, venerable sirs," the King replied, and provided the laborers. The elders had all the monasteries repaired during the first month and then informed the King: "Great King, the repair of the monasteries is complete. Now we shall hold the collection of the Dhamma and Vinaya."

"Very well, venerable sirs, please proceed with confidence. Let mine be the wheel of authority, and yours be the wheel of Dhamma. Command me, venerable sirs, what shall I do?" the King asked. "Great King, provide a meeting place for the monks who will perform the recital," the elders replied. "Venerable sirs, where shall I build it?" the King asked. "Great King, it is appropriate to build it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra," the elders said.

"Very well, venerable sirs," King Ajātasattu replied. He then had a pavilion (maṇḍapa) constructed that was like the creation of Vissakamma, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and stairs, adorned with various floral and creeper patterns. It was as if it surpassed the splendor of a royal palace and mocked the glory of a celestial mansion; it was like the abode of beauty, a landing place where the birds—the eyes of gods and humans—flocked together, and like a collection of all the delightful essences of the world. He decorated the great pavilion with a beautiful canopy from which hung various garlands of flowers. The floor was finished with various floral offerings, appearing like a jeweled floor of precious gems. Having adorned it like a mansion of the Brahmās, he had five hundred priceless seats prepared for the five hundred monks. He placed the seat for the presiding elder on the south side facing north, and in the middle of the pavilion, he prepared a Dhamma seat (dhammāsana) worthy of the Blessed Buddha, facing east. Having placed an ivory-inlaid fan there, he sent word to the Saṅgha of monks: "Venerable sirs, my task is finished."

At that time, some monks, referring to the Venerable Ānanda, said: "In this Saṅgha of monks, there is one monk who wanders about emitting a raw smell (vissagandha)." The elder heard this and thought, "In this Saṅgha of monks, there is no other monk who wanders about emitting a raw smell..."
10:
"...there is no monk who wanders about emitting a raw smell; surely, these monks are speaking with reference to me," he thought, and was moved by a sense of urgency (saṃvega). Some monks said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, the assembly is tomorrow. You are still a trainee (sekha) who has work to do for the three higher paths. It is not proper for you to go to the assembly as a trainee; strive with diligence!"

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: "The assembly is tomorrow. It is not fitting for me to go to the assembly while still being a trainee." He spent much of the night in mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). At dawn, he came down from the walkway, entered the monastery, and thinking, "I will lie down," he inclined his body. His two feet were off the ground and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in that very interval, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging.

Although this Venerable Ānanda had spent much of the night on the walkway without attaining the special distinction, he thought: "Did not the Blessed One say to me, 'Ānanda, you have performed merit; strive repeatedly in exertion, and you will soon be free from the taints'? The words of the Buddhas cannot fail. Because my energy is too persistent, my mind is tending toward restlessness. Now, I shall balance energy and concentration." He then came down from the walkway, stood at the place for washing feet, and after washing his feet, entered the monastery and sat on the couch. Thinking, "I will rest for a moment," he inclined his body toward the couch. While his feet were off the ground and his head had not yet reached the pillow, in that interval, without clinging, his mind was liberated from the taints, and the elder attained Arahantship, free from the four postures. Therefore, in this Dispensation (Sāsana), if it is asked, "Which monk attained Arahantship without lying down, sitting, standing, or walking?" it should be said, "The Elder Ānanda."

Then, on the second day, the elder monks, having finished their meal and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma hall. The Venerable Ānanda, wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship, did not go with the other monks. The monks sat in their respective seats according to seniority, leaving a seat for the Venerable Ānanda. When some asked, "For whom is this seat?" they were told, "It is for the Venerable Ānanda." When they asked, "Where has Ānanda gone?" the elder thought, "Now is the time for me to go." Then, wishing to show his psychic power, he dived into the earth and manifested himself in his own seat. Some say he came through the air and sat down.

While the Venerable Ānanda was seated, the Venerable Mahākassapa consulted the monks: "Friends, which shall we recite first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?" The monks replied: "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the life of the Blessed One's Dispensation; as long as the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation stands. Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya first." When he consulted them again, "Friends, with whom as the leader shall we recite the Vinaya first?" the monks requested that the Venerable Upāli be made the leader.
11:
While Venerable Ānanda was seated thus, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Friends, what shall we recite first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?" The monks replied: "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the very life of the Buddha's Dispensation; as long as the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation stands. Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya first." "Whom shall we make the leader?" "The Venerable Upāli." "Is Venerable Ānanda not capable?" "It is not that he is not capable, but rather that while the Blessed One was still alive, he appointed Venerable Upāli as the foremost (Etadagga) among his monk disciples who are masters of the Vinaya, saying: 'Monks, the foremost among my monk disciples who are masters of the Vinaya is this Upāli.' Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya by questioning the Elder Upāli."

Then the Elder designated himself to question the Vinaya, and Venerable Upāli designated himself to answer. In this regard, the Pāḷi is as follows:

"Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:

'Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli regarding the Vinaya.'

Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha:

'Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer.'"

Having thus designated himself, Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat on the Dhamma-seat, holding an ivory-inlaid fan. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa sat on the Elder's seat and questioned Venerable Upāli on the Vinaya: "Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika promulgated?" "In Vesālī, venerable sir." "Concerning whom?" "Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka." "On what subject?" "On the matter of sexual intercourse."

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned Venerable Upāli regarding the basis (vatthu), the origin (nidāna), the person (puggala), the primary rule (paññatti), the secondary rule (anupaññatti), the offense (āpatti), and the non-offense (anāpatti) of the first Pārājika. Just as with the first, he questioned him regarding the basis... and the non-offense of the second, third, and fourth Pārājikas. As he was questioned, the Elder Upāli answered.
12:
Then they categorized these four Pārājikas, establishing them as "This is the Pārājika-kaṇḍa." They established the thirteen Saṅghādisesas as the "Terassaka." They established the two Aniyata rules as "These rules are the Aniyatas." They established the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules as "These rules are the Nissaggiya Pācittiyas." They established the ninety-two Pācittiya rules as "These rules are the Pācittiyas." They established the four Pāṭidesanīya rules as "These rules are the Pāṭidesanīyas." They established the seventy-five Sekhiya rules as "These rules are the Sekhiyas." They established the seven principles of Adhikaraṇasamatha as "These principles are the Adhikaraṇasamathas."

Having thus categorized the Mahāvibhaṅga, they also categorized the eight Pārājika rules in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga as "This is the Pārājika-kaṇḍa." They established the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules as the "Sattarasaka." They established the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules as "These rules are the Nissaggiya Pācittiyas." They established the one hundred and sixty-six Pācittiya rules as "These rules are the Pācittiyas." They established the eight Pāṭidesanīya rules as "These rules are the Pāṭidesanīyas." They established the seventy-five Sekhiya rules as "These rules are the Sekhiyas." They established the seven principles of Adhikaraṇasamatha as "These principles are the Adhikaraṇasamathas." Having thus categorized the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, they categorized the Khandhaka and Parivāra in the same manner. In this way, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, consisting of the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra, was brought into the communal recitation; Venerable Mahākassapa questioned, and Venerable Upāli answered. At the conclusion of the questioning and answering, the five hundred Arahants performed a group recitation in the same manner as the categorization. At the end of the Vinaya recitation, Venerable Upāli set down the ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dhamma-seat, paid homage to the senior monks, and sat in his own appropriate seat.

Having recited the Vinaya and wishing to recite the Dhamma, Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the monks: "In reciting the Dhamma, whom shall we make the leader to recite the Dhamma?" The monks said: "Let us make the Elder Ānanda the leader."

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha: "Friends, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda regarding the Dhamma."

Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I, being questioned on the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, would answer."
13: Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat on the Dhamma-seat, holding a fan inlaid with ivory. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda on the Dhamma: 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?' 'Venerable sir, it was spoken at the royal rest-house in Ambalaṭṭhikā, between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā.' 'Concerning whom was it spoken?' 'Concerning the wanderer Suppiya and the youth Brahmadatta.' 'On what subject?' 'On praise and dispraise.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda on the origin (nidāna), the persons (puggala), and the subject (vatthu) of the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'And where, friend Ānanda, was the Sāmaññaphala Sutta spoken?' 'Venerable sir, it was spoken in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove at Rājagaha.' 'With whom was it spoken?' 'With King Ajātasattu, the son of the Videhan princess.' Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda on the origin and the persons of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. In this manner, he questioned him on the five Nikāyas.  The five Nikāyas are: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among these, the Khuddaka Nikāya consists of all the remaining words of the Buddha, excluding the first four Nikāyas. In that collection, the Vinaya was answered by the Venerable Upāli, while the rest of the Khuddaka Nikāya and the four Nikāyas were answered by the Venerable Ānanda. All these words of the Buddha should be understood as: onefold by way of flavor (rasa); twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya; threefold by way of the first, middle, and last; likewise, threefold by way of Piṭaka; fivefold by way of Nikāya; ninefold by way of Anga; and eighty-four thousandfold by way of Dhamma-units (dhammakkhandha).  How is it onefold by way of flavor? From the time the Blessed One attained the peerless supreme enlightenment until he attained parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder—during these forty-five years, all that he spoke, whether in admonishing devas, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and others, or in reflection, has only one flavor: the flavor of liberation (vimuttirasa). Thus, it is onefold by way of flavor.  How is it twofold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? All these words of the Buddha are classified as Dhamma and Vinaya. Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya, and the remaining words of the Buddha are the Dhamma. Therefore, it was said: 'Friends, let us chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya.'
14: 'I shall question Upāli on the Vinaya and Ānanda on the Dhamma.' Because of this statement, there are two divisions by way of Dhamma and Vinaya.  How is it threefold by way of the first, middle, and last? All these words of the Buddha have three divisions: the first words of the Buddha, the middle words of the Buddha, and the last words of the Buddha. Therein:  'Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house (craving). Sorrowful is birth again and again. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no house (body) again. All your rafters (defilements) are broken, and the ridge-pole (ignorance) is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned (Nibbāna); it has attained the destruction of craving.' These are the first words of the Buddha.  Some elders who were reciters of the Khandhakas say that the Udāna verse in the Khandhaka beginning with 'Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā' is the first words of the Buddha. However, that Udāna verse should be understood as having arisen when the Buddha, having attained omniscience on the first day of the waning moon of Kason (Vesākha), was reflecting on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with knowledge accompanied by joy.  The words spoken near the time of parinibbāna: 'Now, monks, I exhort you: all conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence'—these are the last words of the Buddha.  Whatever was spoken between these two is the middle words of the Buddha. Thus, it is threefold by way of the first, middle, and last.  How is it threefold by way of Piṭaka? All these words of the Buddha are only of three kinds: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein, all the words chanted in the First Council, when combined, consisting of the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras, are called the Vinaya Piṭaka.  The Dīgha Nikāya, which is a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta; the Majjhima Nikāya, which is a collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta; the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which is a collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta; the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which is a collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta; and the Khuddaka Nikāya, which has fifteen divisions, namely: Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—these are called the Suttanta Piṭaka.  Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—these are called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
15: The Khuddaka Nikāya, which consists of fifteen divisions by way of the Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka, is called the Suttanta Piṭaka. Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—this is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among those Piṭakas— ## Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ, ## Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto. In this Vinaya, there are various methods such as the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the seven classes of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga. There are also methods of supplementary regulations (anupaññatti) which are distinct from the original regulations and serve the purpose of strengthening or relaxing the training rules. This Vinaya disciplines the body and speech by prohibiting transgressions of body and speech. Therefore, because it contains various methods, special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, it is called 'Vinaya'. Thus, for the sake of proficiency in the meaning of the word, it is said: ## Vividhavisesanayattā, vinayanato ceva kāyavācānaṃ, ## Vinayatthavidūhi ayaṃ, vinayo vinayoti akkhāto. As for the other, the Sutta— ## Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato, ## Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhātaṃ. That Sutta indicates various meanings such as one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and so forth. Because they are taught according to the inclinations of those to be led (veneyya), the meanings are well-spoken. Just as a crop produces fruit, it produces benefits. Just as a cow lets down milk, it pours forth benefits. It also protects the benefits well. Just as a string (sutta) is a measure for carpenters, so is this Sutta for the wise. Just as flowers strung together with a thread do not get scattered by the wind, so the meanings encompassed by this Sutta do not perish. Thus, for the sake of proficiency in the meaning of the word, it is said: ## Atthānaṃ sūcanato, suvuttato savanatotha sūdanato, ## Suttāṇā suttasabhāgato ca, suttanti akkhātaṃ.
16:
Another [teacher/commentator] says: Because it teaches doctrines that are augmented, distinguished by their own characteristics, revered, defined, and excellent, for that reason it is called 'Abhidhamma'.

Indeed, this word 'Abhi' is seen in the senses of augmentation, characteristic, revered, defined, and excellent. To explain: in such passages as "Friend, my painful feelings are greatly increasing (abhikkamanti), not subsiding," it occurs in the sense of augmentation (vuḍḍhi). In such passages as "Those nights which are well-known and marked (abhilakkhitā) [by the full moon, etc.]," it occurs in the sense of characteristic (lakkhaṇa). In such passages as "The king of kings (rājābhirājā), the lord of men," it occurs in the sense of revered (pūjita). In such passages as "He is capable of training in Abhidhamma and Abhivinaya," it occurs in the sense of defined (paricchinna). It means the Dhamma and Vinaya without mutual confusion. In such passages as "With exceeding (abhikkantena) splendor," it occurs in the sense of excellent (adhika).

And in this Abhidhamma, doctrines that are augmented are taught by such methods as "He develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere" and "He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness." Doctrines distinguished by their own characteristics are also taught because they are characterized by objects such as visible forms or sounds. Doctrines that are revered are also taught by such methods as "The doctrines of the trainee (sekha), the doctrines of the non-trainee (asekha), and the supramundane doctrines," meaning they are worthy of reverence. Doctrines that are defined are also taught because they are defined by their nature (sabhāva) through such methods as "Contact occurs, feeling occurs." Doctrines that are excellent are also taught by such methods as "The great (mahaggata) doctrines, the immeasurable (appamāṇa) doctrines, and the unsurpassed (anuttara) doctrines." Therefore, for the sake of proficiency in the meaning of the word of this Abhidhamma, it is said—

"Because it teaches doctrines that are augmented, distinguished by their own characteristics, revered, defined, and excellent, for that reason it is called Abhidhamma."

As for the term 'Piṭaka' which is common [to all three], those who know the meaning of Piṭaka say it is so called because of the sense of scriptural learning (pariyatti) and the sense of a vessel (bhājana). By combining [the specific names] with that word 'Piṭaka', the three—Vinaya and so on—should be known.
17:
The learned Pāḷi (pariyatti) is also called 'Piṭaka' in such passages as 'mā piṭakasampadānena' (do not go by the authority of the basket). In passages such as 'atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakaṃ ādāya' (then a man might come taking a hoe and a basket), any kind of container (or basket) is also called 'Piṭaka'. Therefore, scholars who know the meaning of Piṭaka call it 'Piṭaka' because of the meaning of the learned Pāḷi and the meaning of a container.

Now, by combining with that word 'Piṭaka', the three—Vinaya and so forth—should be understood. Thus, by forming a compound with the word 'Piṭaka' which has two meanings, it is called the 'Vinaya Piṭaka' because it is the learned Pāḷi and because it is the container of various meanings. In the same manner, it is called the 'Suttanta Piṭaka' because it is both Suttanta and a Piṭaka, and the 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka' because it is both Abhidhamma and a Piṭaka. In this way, these three—Vinaya and so forth—should be understood.

Having understood this, again, for the sake of proficiency in these Piṭakas through various methods—

One should point out the distinctions of Desanā (Exposition), Sāsana (Instruction), and Kathā (Discourse) in those Piṭakas;
And the Sikkhā (Training), Pahāna (Abandoning), and the nature of depth (Gambhīra) as they appropriately apply.

In whichever Piṭaka, in whatever manner, the distinctions of learning are found,
And to whatever fulfillment or failure a monk arrives, all that should be clearly explained.

In those verses, what follows is the detailed explanation and clear demonstration. These three Piṭakas are respectively called Āṇā-desanā (Teaching of Command), Vohāra-desanā (Teaching of Convention), and Paramattha-desanā (Teaching of Ultimate Reality); Yathāparādha-sāsana (Instruction according to offense), Yathānuloma-sāsana (Instruction according to inclination), and Yathādhamma-sāsana (Instruction according to Dhamma); and Saṃvarāsaṃvara-kathā (Discourse on restraint and non-restraint), Diṭṭhiviniveṭhana-kathā (Discourse on disentangling views), and Nāmarūpapariccheda-kathā (Discourse on the delimitation of mind and matter).

Among these, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Āṇā-desanā because it was taught mostly through commands by the Blessed One who is worthy of issuing commands. The Suttanta Piṭaka is called Vohāra-desanā because it was taught mostly through conventional terms by the Blessed One who is skilled in convention (vohāra). The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called Paramattha-desanā because it was taught mostly through ultimate terms by the Blessed One who is skilled in ultimate reality (paramattha).

Similarly, in the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, it is called Yathāparādha-sāsana because beings who have many offenses are instructed according to their offenses. In the second, the Suttanta Piṭaka, it is called Yathānuloma-sāsana because beings who have various dispositions, latent tendencies, characters, and inclinations are instructed according to their inclinations. In the third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, it is called Yathādhamma-sāsana because beings who perceive 'I' and 'mine' in a mere heap of phenomena (mind and matter) are instructed according to the nature of the Dhamma.
18:
Likewise, in the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, it is called 'Saṃvarāsaṃvara-kathā' because restraint and non-restraint (saṃvara, asaṃvara), which are the opposites of transgressing in conduct by body and speech, are taught here. In the second, the Suttanta Piṭaka, it is called 'Diṭṭhiviniveṭhana-kathā' because the disentangling of wrong views (diṭṭhiviniveṭhana), which is the opposite of the sixty-two types of wrong views, is taught here. In the third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, it is called 'Nāmarūpapariccheda-kathā' because the delimitation of mind and matter (nāmarūpapariccheda), which is the opposite of lust and so forth, is taught here.

In these three Piṭakas, the three trainings (sikkhā), the three abandonings (pahāna), and the fourfold nature of depth (gambhīra-bhāva) should also be understood. To speak in detail—in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is especially taught; in the Suttanta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā); and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of transgression (vītikkama-pahāna) of the defilements is taught, because virtue (sīla) is the opposite of transgression. In the Suttanta Piṭaka, the abandoning of obsession or outbreak (pariyuṭṭhāna-pahāna) of the defilements is taught, because concentration (samādhi) is the opposite of obsession. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the abandoning of latent tendencies (anusaya-pahāna) of the defilements is taught, because wisdom (paññā) is the opposite of latent tendencies.

In the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of defilements by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) is taught; in the other two Piṭakas, abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) and abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) are taught. In the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṅkilesa) is taught; in the other two Piṭakas, the abandoning of the defilements of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) is taught.

In each of these Piṭakas, the fourfold depth of Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha should be understood. Among these four, 'Dhamma' means the Pāḷi text. 'Attha' means the meaning of that Pāḷi text. 'Desanā' means the oral teaching of that Pāḷi text as it has been defined by the mind. 'Paṭivedha' means the penetration and realization of the Pāḷi text and its meaning as they truly are. In these three Piṭakas, these four—Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha—are deep because they are difficult for persons of little wisdom to plunge into and find a footing, just as the great ocean is for animals like rabbits. Thus, the fourfold nature of depth should be understood in each of these Piṭakas.

In another way—'Dhamma' means cause (hetu). For it is said: 'Knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).' 'Attha' means the result of the cause (hetu-phala). For it is said: 'Knowledge of the result of the cause is the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).' 'Desanā' means designation (paññatti), meaning the exposition of the Dhamma according to its nature. 'Paṭivedha' means penetration or realization (abhisamaya); that realization is of two kinds, mundane and supramundane, and it is the understanding of meanings within the Dhammas, of Dhammas within the meanings, and of designations within the paths of designation, according to their nature, through objective focus and non-delusion.

Now, in these Piṭakas, whatever causal nature (dhamma-jāta) or resultant nature (attha-jāta) there may be, and whatever meaning is to be made known that comes before the knowledge of the listeners, the exposition (desanā) that illuminates that specific meaning, and which...
19:
In this Dispensation, there is also penetration (paṭivedha), which is defined as the unerring realization. All these four (dhamma, attha, desanā, and paṭivedha) are profound because, for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit and lack wisdom, they are difficult to plunge into and offer no footing, just as the great ocean is to hares and such animals. Thus, in each of these three Pitakas, the fourfold state of profundity should be understood.

To this extent—

"One should explain the divisions of desanā, sāsanā, and kathā, as well as the states of sikkhā, pahāna, and gambhīra in those [Pitakas] as appropriate." This verse has the meaning already stated.

"One should also clarify the divisions of pariyatti, and how and where a bhikkhu reaches success (sampatti) and failure (vipatti)." I shall now state the meaning of this verse.

In these three Pitakas, the threefold division of pariyatti (scriptural study) should be noted. There are three kinds of pariyatti: the simile of the water-snake (alagaddūpamā), that for the purpose of deliverance (nissaraṇattha), and the treasurer-like (bhaṇḍāgārika) pariyatti.

Among these, that which is wrongly grasped and studied for the sake of criticizing others and so on is the water-snake simile pariyatti. With reference to such wrong grasping, it was said (in the Alagaddūpama Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya): "Monks, suppose a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake, should see a large water-snake. He would grasp it by its coils or by its tail. That water-snake would turn back and bite him on his hand, his arm, or some other limb. On that account, he would suffer death or deadly pain. Why is that? Because, monks, of the water-snake being wrongly grasped. Even so, monks, here some worthless men (moghapurisa) study the Dhamma—sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla. Having studied that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. Not examining the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not gain their reflective acceptance. They study the Dhamma only for the sake of criticizing others and for the sake of rebutting others' arguments. They do not experience the goal for which they study the Dhamma. Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that? Because, monks, of the teachings being wrongly grasped."
20:
But that pariyatti which is well-grasped, studied by one desiring only the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so on, and not for the sake of criticizing others, is the pariyatti for the purpose of deliverance (nissaraṇattha). With reference to this, it was said: "Monks, those teachings, being well-grasped by them, lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time. Why is that? Because, monks, of the teachings being well-grasped."

Furthermore, that pariyatti which an Arahant—one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakable [attainment], realized cessation, and destroyed the taints—studies merely for the sake of preserving the tradition and protecting the lineage, is the treasurer-like (bhaṇḍāgārika) pariyatti.

A bhikkhu who practices well (suppaṭipanna) in the Vinaya reaches the threefold knowledge (vijjā) by depending on the perfection of virtue; for the divisions of those knowledges are taught in that very Vinaya. A bhikkhu who practices well in the Sutta reaches the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) by depending on the perfection of concentration; for the divisions of those direct knowledges are taught in that very Sutta. A bhikkhu who practices well in the Abhidhamma reaches the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) by depending on the perfection of wisdom; for the divisions of those analytical knowledges are taught in that very Abhidhamma. Thus, one who practices well in these Pitakas reaches this success (sampatti) consisting of the threefold knowledge, the six direct knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges in due order.

However, a bhikkhu who practices poorly (duppaṭipanna) in the Vinaya, because of the similarity between the touch of allowed comfortable rugs, robes, etc., and the touch of forbidden things like a woman's touch, tends to perceive no fault in those forbidden touches. Thus it is said: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be obstructions for one who indulges in them." From there, he reaches the state of immorality (dussīla). A bhikkhu who practices poorly in the Sutta, not knowing the intention in such passages as "Monks, these four persons are found existing," grasps it wrongly. With reference to such wrong grasping, it was said: "By his own wrong grasp, he misrepresents us, digs himself up, and produces much demerit." From there, he reaches the state of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). A bhikkhu who practices poorly in the Abhidhamma, overreaching in his reflection on the nature of things, thinks about the unthinkable (acinteyya); from there, he reaches mental distraction (cittakkhepa). For it was said: "Monks, these four unthinkables are not to be thought about; one who thinks about them would reap madness and frustration." Thus, one who practices poorly in these Pitakas reaches this failure (vipatti) consisting of immorality, wrong view, and mental distraction in due order.
21:
By this sequence of words also—
“The varieties of learning (pariyatti), its success and failure, wherever and however a monk attains them—all these should be clearly explained.”
This verse also has the meaning already stated. Having known the Piṭakas in various ways, the Buddha’s words (Buddhavacana) should be understood as being threefold by way of those Piṭakas.

How is it fivefold by way of Nikāya (Collection)? All these Buddha’s words are of five divisions: Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya. Among these, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? It consists of thirty-four suttas, such as the Brahmajāla Sutta, collected into three groups (vaggas) such as the Sīlakkhandhavagga.

There are exactly thirty-four suttas,
Collected into three groups;
This collection, the first and most appropriate,
Is called the Dīgha Nikāya.

Why is this called the Dīgha Nikāya? It is so called because it is a collection (samūha) and an abode (nivāsa) of suttas of long (dīgha) extent. Indeed, a collection and an abode are called 'Nikāya'. “Monks, I do not see any other single group (nikāya) so diverse as these animals. The Poṇika group, the Cikkhallika group”—such words from both the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the world are evidence in this matter. In this way, the etymological meaning of the remaining Nikāyas as 'collections' should also be understood.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? It consists of one hundred and fifty-two suttas of middle (majjhima) extent, such as the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, collected into fifteen groups (vaggas).

There are one hundred and fifty suttas,
And two more suttas therein;
That collection, comprising fifteen groups,
Is known as the Majjhima Nikāya.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? It consists of seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two suttas, such as the Oghataraṇa Sutta, arranged by way of the Devatāsaṃyutta and so on.

Seven thousand suttas,
And seven hundred suttas,
And sixty-two suttas as well;
This is the Saṃyutta collection.
22:
What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? It consists of nine thousand, five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, such as the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, arranged by way of increasing factors (aṅga) one by one.

Nine thousand, five hundred,
And fifty-seven suttas;
This is the count in the Aṅguttara.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? Excluding the four Nikāyas such as the Dīgha Nikāya, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions previously mentioned such as the Khuddakapāṭha, the remaining Buddha’s words are called the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Excluding these four,
Nikāyas beginning with the Dīgha,
The rest of the Buddha’s words,
Are known as the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Thus, it is fivefold by way of Nikāya.

How is it ninefold by way of Aṅga (Limb)? All these Buddha’s words have nine divisions: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. Among these, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, Parivāra, and the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta, and other words of the Tathāgata bearing the name 'Sutta' should be known as Sutta. All suttas containing verses should be known as Geyya. Specifically, the entire Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other Buddha’s words not included in the other eight limbs should be known as Veyyākaraṇa. The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and those pure verses in the Suttanipāta not bearing the name 'Sutta' should be known as Gāthā. Eighty-two suttas connected with verses consisting of joy and wisdom should be known as Udāna. One hundred and ten suttas occurring in the manner beginning with “Thus it was said by the Blessed One” should be known as Itivuttaka. The five hundred and more birth stories beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka should be known as Jātaka. All suttas connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, occurring in the manner beginning with “Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in Ānanda,” should be known as Abbhutadhamma. All suttas asked and answered after having gained wisdom and satisfaction, such as the Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Sammādiṭṭhi, Sakkapañha, Saṅkhārabhājaniya, and Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, should be known as Vedalla. Thus, it is ninefold by way of Aṅga.
23:
How are there eighty-four thousand divisions by way of the Dhamma-aggregates (Dhammakkhandha)? All these words of the Buddha are indeed thus:

'I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; these eighty-four thousand teachings are those which I have mastered.' (Spoken by the Venerable Ānanda).

In this way, there are eighty-four thousand divisions by way of the Dhamma-aggregates as shown. Among those collections of teachings, a Sutta with a single connection (anusaandhi) is one Dhamma-aggregate. In a Sutta with multiple connections, the count of Dhamma-aggregates is according to the connections. In verse compositions, a question is one Dhamma-aggregate, and the answer is one. In the Abhidhamma, each analysis of a triad (tika) or a dyad (duka), and each analysis of a section on consciousness (cittavāra), is one Dhamma-aggregate. In the Vinaya, there are the basis (vatthu), the matrix (mātikā), the word-analysis (padabhājanīya), the intermediate offense (antarāpatti), the offense (āpatti), the non-offense (anāpatti), and the determination (pariccheda); therein, each part should be known as one Dhamma-aggregate. Thus, there are eighty-four thousand divisions by way of the Dhamma-aggregates.

Thus, this word of the Buddha—which is of one kind by way of its flavor (rasa) being without division, and of two or more kinds by way of the divisions of Dhamma, Vinaya, and so forth—was rehearsed by the assembly of masters led by the Venerable Mahākassapa, having defined the divisions thus: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the last word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya... [etc.]... this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine factors (aṅga) such as Sutta; these are the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-aggregates.' Not only this much, but they also rehearsed it for seven months, having defined the various types of collections found in the three Piṭakas, such as the summary collection (uddāna-saṅgaha), the group collection (vagga-saṅgaha), the repetitive collection (peyyāla-saṅgaha), the collections of the numerical divisions such as the Book of Ones (Ekaka-nipāta) and the Book of Twos (Duka-nipāta), the connected collection (saṃyutta-saṅgaha), and the collection of fifty (paṇṇāsa-saṅgaha).

At the conclusion of the rehearsal, as if shouting 'Sādhu' in great joy, saying, 'The Elder Mahākassapa has made the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One capable of lasting for a period of five thousand years,' this great earth, down to its water-limit, shook, trembled, and quaked in various ways, and many wonders appeared. This is known as the First Great Council (Paṭhama Mahāsaṅgīti). In the world, it is called:

'Pañcasatika' because it was performed by five hundred Arahants, and
'Therika' because it was performed only by the Elders.
24:
While this First Great Council was proceeding, the Venerable Mahākassapa, questioning the Vinaya, asked: 'Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika promulgated?' At the end of such words, it is said: 'He asked about the basis (vatthu), he asked about the origin (nidāna), and he asked about the person (puggala).' In that context, when the origin was asked, the Venerable Upāli, wishing to explain everything from the beginning in detail—by whom it was promulgated and for what reason—said: 'At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Verañjā,' and so forth. Thus, these words were spoken by the Venerable Upāli, and it should be understood that they were 'spoken at the time of the First Great Council.' By this much, the meaning of the terms 'By whom was this word spoken?' and 'When was it spoken?' has been clarified.

Now, regarding the question 'Why was it spoken?', the answer is given: Because the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the origin, therefore he spoke in order to detail that origin from the beginning. Thus, although these words were spoken by the Venerable Upāli at the time of the First Great Council, it should be understood that they were spoken for this reason. By this much, the meaning of the introductory terms (mātikā-pada) 'By whom, when, and why' has been clarified.

Now, in order to clarify the meaning of the terms 'Who mastered it, who brought it down, and where is it established?', this is said: By whom was this Vinaya Piṭaka—which has its origin adorned with such words as 'At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Verañjā'—mastered by heart, by whom was it brought down in succession, and where is it established? It is said: First of all, this was mastered by the Venerable Upāli in the presence of the Blessed One. From his presence, it was mastered by many thousands of monks, such as those with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā), before the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna; and after the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, it was mastered by the Elders who were the rehearsers of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka), led by Mahākassapa. As for 'By whom was it brought down?': In the island of Jambudīpa, it was brought down by the lineage of teachers starting with the Elder Upāli until the Third Council. Herein is the lineage of teachers:

Upāli, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava,
And Tissa Moggaliputta—these five conquerors,
Brought the Vinaya in succession in the island named the glorious Jambu,
Without interruption, until the Third Council.
25:
The Venerable Upāli, having learned this Vinaya lineage, this Vinaya tradition, and this Vinaya succession from the presence of the Blessed One, established it in the hearts of many monks. Among those who learned the Vinaya lineage from the presence of the Venerable Upāli and attained mastery in the Vinaya, the worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners were beyond the range of counting; there were one thousand Arahants.

The Elder Dāsaka was also a co-resident pupil of that Venerable Upāli; that Elder Dāsaka, having learned from the presence of the Venerable Upāli, taught the Vinaya in the same manner. Among those worldlings and others who learned from the presence of that Venerable Dāsaka and attained mastery in the Vinaya, they were beyond the range of counting; there were exactly one thousand Arahants.

The Elder Soṇaka was also a co-resident pupil of the Elder Dāsaka; that Elder Soṇaka also, having learned from the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka, taught the Vinaya in the same manner. Among those worldlings and others who learned from the presence of that Venerable Soṇaka and attained mastery in the Vinaya, they were beyond the range of counting; there were exactly one thousand Arahants.

The Elder Siggava was also a co-resident pupil of the Elder Soṇaka; that Elder Siggava also, having learned the Vinaya from the presence of his preceptor, the Elder Soṇaka, became the leader of a thousand Arahants. Among those worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners, as well as Arahants, who learned from the presence of that Venerable Siggava and attained mastery in the Vinaya, they were so numerous that they could not be defined as being so many hundreds or so many thousands.

At that time, it is said that there was a very large assembly of monks in Jambudīpa. The prowess of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa will become manifest in the Third Council. Thus, it should be understood that this Vinaya Piṭaka was brought to Jambudīpa by this lineage of teachers until the Third Council.

## The Account of the First Great Council is Finished.

## The Account of the Second Council

For the purpose of understanding the Second Council, this sequence should be known. At that time—

Having chanted the True Dhamma and having made it shine everywhere,
Those five hundred (elders such as Mahākassapa), remaining until the end of their lives—
26: The Arahants, possessed of the light of wisdom, the elders beginning with Kassapa, Attained peace without any attachment, like lamps whose oil is exhausted. After those great elders had attained peace, as days and nights passed in succession, one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Vajjiputtaka monks residing in Vesālī displayed these ten points in Vesālī: "Carrying salt in a horn is allowable; eating when the sun is two finger-breadths past noon is allowable; going to another village and eating again without performing the 'not-left-over' (atittavinaya) rite is allowable; performing the Uposatha separately in monasteries within the same boundary is allowable; performing a legal act and obtaining the consent of absent monks later is allowable; following the practice of one's preceptor is allowable; drinking milk that is no longer milk but not yet curd even after one has finished eating is allowable; drinking unfermented palm wine is allowable; a sitting cloth without a border is allowable; accepting gold and silver is allowable." King Kālāsoka, the son of Susunāga, took their side. At that time, the Venerable Yasa, the son of Kākaṇḍaka the Brahmin, while wandering in the Vajjī country, heard that "the Vajjiputtaka monks in Vesālī are displaying ten points in Vesālī." Hearing this, he thought, "It is not proper for me to remain indifferent while hearing of the decline of the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers. Let me suppress those who speak against the Dhamma and display the Dhamma." Thinking thus, he arrived at Vesālī. There, the Venerable Yasa, the son of Kākaṇḍaka, stayed at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) in Vesālī. At that time, the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī, on that Uposatha day, filled a bronze bowl with water and placed it in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, saying to the lay devotees of Vesālī who came: "Friends, give to the Saṅgha even a kahāpaṇa, or a half-kahāpaṇa, or a pāda, or a māsakarūpa; there will be business for the Saṅgha to do with these requisites." Everything should be told up to the words: "In this Vinaya recital, there were exactly seven hundred monks, neither more nor less; therefore, this Second Council is called 'The Seven Hundred' (Sattasatikā)." Thus, in that assembly, one million two hundred thousand monks gathered, encouraged by the Venerable Yasa. In the midst of those monks, the Elder Sabbakāmī, being questioned by the Venerable Revata, settled those ten points by explaining the Vinaya, and the legal issue was stilled. After that settlement, the elders, thinking, "We shall chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya again," selected seven hundred monks who were masters of the Three Piṭakas and had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)...
27:
Having gathered at the Vālikārāma monastery in the city of Vesālī, they purified the Sasana of all stains, just as the Elder Mahākassapa had done. They then recited the entire Dhamma and Vinaya according to the divisions of the Piṭakas, Nikāyas, Aṅgas, and Dhammakkhandhas. This council was completed in eight months. In the world, it is known as the 'Sattasatika' (Council of the Seven Hundred) because it was performed by seven hundred monks, and it is called the 'Second Council' in reference to the first council performed previously.

## Regarding that council—
Among the Elders who performed the recitation, the Elders Sabbakāmī, Sāḷha, Revata, Khujjasobhita, Yasa, and Sāṇasambhūta were well-known and famous. These Elders were the co-residents (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Ānanda and had personally seen the Tathāgata.

The Elders Sumana and Vāsabhagāmī should be known as the co-residents of the Elder Anuruddha; they too had personally seen the Tathāgata.

All those Elders who performed the second recitation were those who had laid down the burden (of the aggregates), had completed what was to be done, and were taintless Arahants.

This is the Second Council.

After performing this Second Council, the great Elders, while considering whether such a calamity (abbuda) would arise in the Sasana in the future, saw this matter: 'One hundred and eighteen years from now, a king named Dhammāsoka will arise in the city of Pāṭaliputta and rule over the entire island of Jambudīpa. That king will have faith in the Buddha's Sasana and will provide great gain and honor. At that time, heretics (titthiyas), desiring gain and honor, will ordain in the Sasana and propagate their own views. Thus, a great calamity will arise in the Sasana.' Then, the thought occurred to those Elders: 'When that calamity arises, will we be present or not?' All those Elders then realized that they would not be present at that time. Thinking, 'Who will be able to settle that legal issue (adhikaraṇa)?', they looked through the entire human world and the six deva worlds of the sense sphere but saw no one. Then, they saw the Great Brahma named Tissa in the Brahma world.
28:
They saw the Great Brahma named Tissa, who had a short lifespan and had developed the path (meditative absorptions) for rebirth in a higher Brahma realm. Upon seeing him, the Elders thought: 'If we strive to have this Brahma reborn in the human world, he will surely take conception in the house of the Brahmin Moggali. Thereafter, being enticed by the mantras (of the Buddha), he will leave the household life and ordain. Having ordained in this way, he will master the entire word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana), attain the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), crush the heretics, settle that legal issue, and support the Sasana.'

The Elders went to the Brahma world and said this to Tissa Mahābrahmā: 'O Brahma, one hundred and eighteen years from now, a great calamity will arise in the Sasana. While looking through the entire human world and the six deva worlds of the sense sphere, we saw no one capable of supporting the Sasana, but in searching the Brahma world, we saw you. O virtuous one, please give your promise to be reborn in the human world to support the Sasana of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala).'

When this was said, the Great Brahma, being exceedingly joyful and delighted, thinking, 'It is said that I shall be able to purify the calamity that has arisen in the Sasana and support the Sasana,' consented and gave his promise. The Elders, having completed that task in the Brahma world, returned.

At that time, the two Elders Siggava and Caṇḍavajjī were junior monks, yet they were masters of the Tipiṭaka, had attained the analytical insights, and were Arahants; however, they did not participate in that legal issue. The Elders said to them: 'Friends, you did not become our companions in this legal issue. Therefore, let this be your punishment: The Brahma named Tissa will take conception in the house of the Brahmin Moggali; one of you must bring him out and ordain him, and one must teach him the word of the Buddha.' Having said this, all the Elders remained for the duration of their lifespans and then—

Those Elders, headed by Sabbakāmī, who possessed great psychic power,
Having shone like great masses of fire in the world, attained Parinibbāna.
Having performed the second recitation and purified the Sasana,
They established the cause for the purity of the True Dhamma in the future.
29:
Those elders, whose taints were exhausted, who had attained mastery, and who possessed the analytical knowledges, have also come under the power of impermanence. Thus, knowing this wretched impermanence which is difficult to overcome, the wise person should strive to reach that Nibbāna, which is permanent and deathless.

## Thus, the explanation of the Second Council in all its aspects is finished.

## The Account of the Second Council is Finished.

## The Account of the Third Council

The Mahābrahmā named Tissa, having passed away from the Brahma world, took rebirth in the house of the Brahmin Moggali. From the time of that child's conception, the Elder Siggava entered that Brahmin's house for alms for seven years. Not even for a single day did he receive a ladleful of rice gruel or a ladleful of alms-food. After the lapse of seven years, one day he received only the words, "Please move on, Venerable Sir."

On that very day, the Brahmin, returning after performing some business outside, saw the Elder on the way and asked, "O ascetic, did you go to our house?" "Yes, Brahmin, I went," he replied. "Did you receive anything?" he asked. "Yes, Brahmin, I received [something]," he replied. When the Brahmin reached home, he asked, "Did you give anything to that ascetic?" "We did not give anything at all," they said.

On the second day, the Brahmin sat at the door of the house, thinking, "Today I will refute the ascetic with [the charge of] lying." On the second day, the Elder arrived at the door of the Brahmin's house. As soon as the Brahmin saw the Elder, he said, "Yesterday, you said 'I received [something]' even though you received nothing at all in our house. Is lying proper for you?"

The Elder said, "Brahmin, for seven years in your house, we did not receive even the words 'Please move on,' but only yesterday did we receive the words 'Please move on.' It was in reference to that courtesy that I spoke thus."

The Brahmin thought, "These ascetics praise even the receipt of mere courtesy by saying 'I received [something]'; why would they not praise if they received other food and edibles?" Having gained faith, he had a ladleful of alms-food and suitable curry from the food prepared for himself offered [to the Elder] and said, "You shall receive this alms-food at all times."
30:
From the following day onwards, seeing the Elder's calm composure as he arrived, the Brahmin became even more inspired and requested the Elder to always take his meals at his house. The Elder accepted, and every day after finishing his meal, he would preach a little of the Buddha's word before leaving. That young man (Tissa), by the age of sixteen, had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. As he was a pure being who had come from the Brahma realm, no one else sat or slept on his seat or bed. When the young man went to his teacher's house, the household members would cover his couch with a white cloth and keep it suspended.

The Elder thought, "Now is the time to ordain this young man. Although I have been coming to this house for a long time, not a single conversation has occurred with him. Now, by this means, a conversation will arise because of the couch." He then went to the house and made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) such that no other seat besides the young man's couch could be seen in that house. When the Brahmin's household saw the Elder and found no other seat, they spread out the young man's couch and offered it to the Elder. The Elder sat upon the couch.

At that very moment, the young man returned from his teacher's house and, seeing the recluse sitting on his couch, became angry and displeased, asking, "Who spread my couch for this recluse?"

After the Elder had finished his meal and the young man's anger had subsided, the Elder asked, "Young man, do you know any mantras?" The young man replied, "O recluse, if one such as I does not know the mantras, who else would know them?" and then asked the Elder, "Do you, however, know the mantras?" "Ask, young man; only by asking can it be known," the Elder replied.

Then the young man questioned the Elder on difficult and profound points in the three Vedas—including the Nighaṇḍu, Keṭubha, Akkharappabheda, and Itihāsa as the fifth—which neither he nor his teacher understood. The Elder, having already mastered the three Vedas and now possessing the analytical insights, found no difficulty in answering those questions and replied to them immediately. Then he said to the young man, "Young man, you have asked me much. Now I shall ask you one question; will you answer me?" "Yes, O recluse, ask; I shall answer," the young man replied. The Elder then asked this question from the Citta-yamaka:
31:
"Venerable monk, now you too ask a question. I shall answer your question," said the young man. The Elder asked this question from the Citta Yamaka: "To whom the mind is arising but not ceasing, will the mind of that person cease but not arise? Or else, to whom the mind will cease but not arise, is the mind of that person arising but not ceasing?"

The young man, being unable to ponder the question from top to bottom, asked, "Venerable monk, what is this called?" "Young man, this is called the Buddha-manta (the Buddha's lore)," he replied. "Venerable monk, is it possible to give this Buddha-manta to me as well?" he asked again. "Young man, it is possible to give this Buddha-manta to one who takes ordination in our presence," the Elder replied. After that, the young man approached his parents and said, "Mother, Father, this monk knows what is called the Buddha-manta, but he does not give it to one who is not ordained under him. I will ordain under this monk and learn that lore."

Then his parents, thinking, "Let our son learn the lore even by ordaining; having learned it, he will return to us," gave their permission, saying, "Dear son, go and learn the lore by ordaining under this monk." The Elder gave the boy the novice ordination and first taught him the meditation on mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati) consisting of the thirty-two parts, such as hair and so on. While that novice was practicing meditation on those thirty-two parts repeatedly, before long, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

After he was so established, the Elder thought, "This novice is established in the fruit of Stream-entry; now he is incapable of turning away from the Dispensation. If I were to teach him to develop meditation further, the novice might reach the fruit of Arahantship. If he reaches the fruit of Arahantship, he might become indifferent to learning the Buddha-vacana (the Tipitaka). Now is the time to send this novice to the presence of the Elder Caṇḍavajji." Having thought so, he instructed, "Novice, come, go to the presence of the Elder and learn the Buddha-vacana. In my name, ask after the Elder's health. Say, 'Venerable sir, my preceptor (upajjhāya) has sent me to your presence.' If he asks, 'What is your preceptor's name?', say, 'Venerable sir, his name is Elder Siggava.' If he asks, 'What is my name?', say, 'Venerable sir, my preceptor knows your name.'"

"Very well, venerable sir," Tissa the novice replied, and having respectfully prostrated before the Elder and circumambulated him, he went in due course to the presence of the Elder Caṇḍavajji. Having prostrated, he stood in a suitable place. The Elder asked the novice, "Where have you come from?" "Venerable sir, my preceptor has sent me to your presence," he replied. "What is your preceptor's name?" "Venerable sir, his name is Elder Siggava." "What is my name?" "Venerable sir, my preceptor knows your name." "Now, set aside the bowl and robes," the Elder said. "Very well, venerable sir," the novice replied, and having set aside the bowl and robes, on the following day, he swept the monastery grounds and prepared the water for washing the face and the tooth-sticks. The Elder swept again the place that the novice had swept.
32:
The Elder swept that place again. He poured out that water and brought other water. He removed that tooth-stick and took another tooth-stick. Having done this for seven days, on the seventh day, he questioned him again. The novice replied exactly as he had before. The Elder, realizing, "This is indeed that Great Brahma," asked, "For what purpose have you come?" "Venerable sir, I have come to learn the Buddha-vacana," he replied. The Elder said, "Novice, learn now," and from the next day, he began teaching the Buddha-vacana. While still a novice, Tissa learned all the Buddha-vacana along with the commentaries, except for the Vinaya Piṭaka. By the time he reached full ordination, even before he had completed a single vassa, he became a Tipitaka-dhara (a bearer of the Three Baskets). The teacher and the preceptor, having established the entire Buddha-vacana in the hands of the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa, lived out their life spans and attained Parinibbāna. The Elder Moggaliputta Tissa also later developed meditation, attained the fruit of Arahantship, and taught the Dhamma-Vinaya to many monks.

At that time, King Bindusāra had one hundred and one sons. Prince Asoka killed all of them, except for Prince Tissa, who was born of the same mother as himself. Having killed them, he ruled for four years without being anointed. After four years had passed, two hundred and eighteen years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, he received the consecration as the sole emperor of the entire Jambudīpa. Due to the power of his consecration, these royal psychic powers came to him: his authority extended one yojana beneath the great earth, and likewise upwards into the sky. Deities brought sixteen pots of water from Lake Anotatta daily using eight carrying-poles. Out of devotion to the Dispensation, he offered eight pots to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, two pots to sixty monks who were Tipitaka-dharas, two pots to the Chief Queen Asandhimittā, and used four pots himself. Deities also brought daily from the Himalayas tooth-sticks called nāgalatā, which were smooth, soft, and flavorful. With those tooth-sticks, the daily requirement for the King, the Queen, sixteen thousand dancing women, and sixty thousand monks was fulfilled. Daily, the deities also brought him medicinal emblic myrobalan, medicinal yellow myrobalan, and ripe mangoes of golden hue, endowed with fragrance and flavor. Likewise, they brought from Lake Chaddanta garments of five colors, yellow hand-towels, and divine drinks. Furthermore, daily to that King...
33:
The Nāga kings brought from the Nāga realm bathing perfumes, anointing perfumes, jasmine-cloth not made of thread for wearing, and very precious collyrium. Parrots daily brought nine thousand loads of self-grown hill-paddy from Lake Chaddanta. Mice removed the husks and bran so that not even a single grain was broken; the King consumed only this hill-paddy throughout his realm. Honey-bees made honey. In the smithies, bears struck with hammers. Karavīka birds came and sang with sweet voices, performing service for the King.
