At that time, the beings in Ojadīpa were perishing from a severe fever. When the Blessed Kakusandha surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, he saw those beings perishing. Seeing this, he came surrounded by forty thousand monks. By the power of the Buddha, the fever was immediately pacified. After the disease was cured, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, and eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One gave his water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa) and departed. They built a stupa at Paṭiyārāma, enshrining that water-strainer within it. The Elder Mahādeva remained, instructing the island.

In the time of the Blessed Koṇāgamana, this island was named Varadīpa, the king was named Sameṇḍီ, the city was named Vaḍḍhamāna, and the mountain was named Suvaṇṇakူဋ. At that time, there was a drought and famine in Varadīpa, and beings were perishing from the affliction of hunger. The Blessed Koṇāgamana surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw those beings perishing, so he came surrounded by thirty thousand monks. By the power of the Buddha, the rain fell properly and abundance returned. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma, and eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One left the Elder Mahāsumana with a thousand monks on the island, gave his waist-band (kāyabandhana), and departed. They built a stupa, enshrining that waist-band.

In the time of the Blessed Kassapa, this island was named Maṇ္ဍဒီပ, the king was named Jayanta, the city was named Visāla, and the mountain was Subhakūṭa...
65:
At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa had appeared in the world. At that time, a great dispute occurred on the island of Maṇḍadīpa. Many beings, engaged in quarrels and strife, were falling into ruin and disaster. The Blessed One Kassapa, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw those beings falling into ruin and disaster. Having seen them, he arrived surrounded by twenty thousand monks, settled the dispute, and preached the Dhamma. Eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma. The Blessed One established the Elder named Sabbananda, who was surrounded by a thousand monks, on that island, gave him his bathing robe, and departed. They placed that bathing robe inside and built a cetiya. Thus, the cetiyas of the three previous Buddhas were established at Thūpārāma. Those cetiyas vanished due to the disappearance of the Dispensations; only the sites remained. Therefore, it is said: 'At that time, at Thūpārāma, there was the site of the use-relic cetiya (paribhogacetiya) of the three previous Samma-sambuddhas.' This very site of the use-relic cetiya, when the cetiyas had perished, remained surrounded by various thickets with thorny branches through the power of deities, as if saying, 'Let no one defile this place with leftovers, excrement, impurities, or rubbish.'

Then, the king's men, going ahead of the elephant, cut down all the bushes, cleared the ground, and made it as level as the palm of a hand. The noble elephant went and, keeping that site in front, stood to the west of it at the site where the Bodhi tree would be. Then they began to take down the relic from the elephant's head. The elephant did not allow it to be taken down. The king asked the Elder: 'Venerable Sir, why does the elephant not allow the relic to be taken down?' 'Great King, it is not proper to take down the relic that has been mounted,' he replied. At that time, the water in the Abhayavāpi tank was exhausted. The surrounding ground was cracked, and lumps of fine clay were easy to extract. From there, many people quickly brought the fine clay and made a platform the size of the elephant's frontal globe. At that very moment, they began to make bricks for the purpose of building the stupa. Until the bricks were finished, the noble elephant stayed in the elephant stable at the site of the Bodhi tree during the day, and at night, he circumambulated the ground where the stupa was to be established. Then, having had the platform built, the king asked the Elder: 'Venerable Sir, what shape should the stupa be made?' 'Great King, it should be made like a heap of paddy,' he replied.

'Very well, Venerable Sir,' the king agreed, and having had a stupa built to the height of a knee, he had a great offering prepared for the purpose of enshrining the relic. The people of the whole city and the countryside assembled to witness the great relic festival. When that great multitude of people had assembled—
66:
The relic of the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, rose from the elephant's frontal globe into the air to the height of seven palm trees and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya). From various parts of the relic, streams of water and masses of fire of six colors issued forth. The miracle was just like the one shown by the Blessed One at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree in Sāvatthī. And that miracle occurred neither by the power of the Elders nor by the power of the deities, but indeed by the power of the Buddha alone. For the Blessed One, while still alive, had resolved: 'When I have attained Parinibbāna, on the day my right collarbone relic is established at the site of the use-relic cetiya of the three previous Buddhas, to the south of the city of Anurādhapura on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, let there be a Twin Miracle.'

## 'Thus, the Buddhas are unthinkable, and the Dhamma (attributes) of the Buddhas are unthinkable; for those who have faith in the unthinkable, the result is unthinkable.'

The Samma-sambuddha had also come to this island three times during his lifetime. First, he came alone for the purpose of taming the Yakkhas, and having tamed them, he thought, 'After my Parinibbāna, the Dispensation will be established on this island,' and while providing protection for the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he circumambulated the island three times. The second time, he came alone for the purpose of taming the Naga kings, who were uncle and nephew, and having tamed them, he departed. The third time, he came surrounded by five hundred monks and sat entering the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) at the site of the Mahācetiya, the site of the Thūpārāma Cetiya, the site where the Mahābodhi is established, the site of the Mahiyangana Cetiya, the site of the Mutiyangana Cetiya, the site of the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, and the site of the Kalyāṇī Cetiya. This was his fourth arrival by means of his bodily relic.

Moreover, there was no place on the entire surface of Tambapaṇṇi that was not touched by the drops of water issuing from that bodily relic. Thus, that bodily relic, having quelled the heat of the surface of Tambapaṇṇi with the drops of water and having shown the miracle to the great multitude, descended from the sky and rested upon the head of the king. The king, thinking that his attainment of human life was fruitful, made a great offering and enshrined the relic. Simultaneously with the enshrinement of the relic, a great earthquake occurred. Having gained confidence in that miracle of the relic, the king's brother, a prince named Abhaya, went forth into homelessness together with a thousand men. Five hundred youths from the village of Cetiyagāma ordained; likewise, five hundred youths each, having come out from small villages such as Dvāramaṇဍala, ordained.
67:
The total number of monks who went forth from both inside and outside the city, including groups of five hundred boys each, amounted to thirty thousand. When the stupa was completed, the King, along with the princes and queens, made individual offerings that were marvelous even to the devas, nāgas, and yakkhas. After the conclusion of the relic-offering ceremony and the enshrining of the noble collarbone relic, Mahinda Thera went to the Meghavana Park and resided there.

At that time, Queen Anulā, desiring to go forth, informed the King. Upon hearing the Queen's words, the King said to the Elder: "Venerable Sir, Queen Anulā wishes to go forth; please ordain her." The Elder replied: "Great King, it is not proper for us to ordain women. However, in the city of Pāṭaliputta, there is a Theri named Saṅghamittā, who is my sister; have her summoned. Great King, in this island of Sīhaḷa, the Bodhi trees of the three previous Buddhas were established. The Bodhi tree of our Blessed One, which emits a net of rays from its body, must also be established on this island. Therefore, send a message so that Theri Saṅghamittā may come, bringing the Bodhi tree with her."

"Very well, Venerable Sir," the King replied, accepting the Elder's words. After consulting with his ministers, he asked his nephew named Ariṭṭha: "Dear son, are you able to go to the city of Pāṭaliputta and bring the Theri Saṅghamittā along with the Mahābodhi?" Ariṭṭha replied: "Great King, I am able, provided you grant me permission to go forth as a monk." The King said: "Go, dear son; after bringing the Theri, you may go forth." Taking the messages of the King and the Elder, Ariṭṭha reached the port of Jambukola in a single day through the power of the Elder's resolution. He boarded a ship, crossed the ocean, and arrived at Pāṭaliputta.

Queen Anulā, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the palace, undertook the ten precepts, wore saffron-dyed robes, and resided in a nunnery built in a certain part of the city. On that very day, Ariṭṭha delivered the message to King Asoka, saying: "Great King, your son Mahinda Thera says: 'It is said that Queen Anulā, the wife of the brother of your friend King Devānampiyatissa, wishes to go forth. To ordain her, please send the Theri Saṅghamittā, and along with the Theri, send the Mahābodhi tree.'" After conveying the Elder's message to the King, he approached Theri Saṅghamittā and said: "Noble Lady, your brother Mahinda Thera has sent me to you. Queen Anulā, the wife of King Devānampiyatissa's brother..."
68:
...together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the palace, wishes to go forth. It is said that you should come and ordain her." Immediately, she went in haste to the King and said: "Great King, my brother Mahinda Thera has sent this message: 'It is said that Queen Anulā, the wife of the King's brother, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the palace, wishes to go forth and is awaiting my arrival.' Great King, I shall go to Tambapaṇṇidīpa."

The King said: "Dear daughter, my son Mahinda Thera and my grandson Sumana Sāmaṇera have already gone to Tambapaṇṇidīpa, leaving me like a man with severed hands. The grief that has arisen in me from not seeing them is only appeased when I see your face. Enough, dear daughter, do not go." She replied: "Great King, my brother's word is very weighty for me. Princess Anulā, surrounded by a thousand women, is also looking forward to going forth and is awaiting me. Great King, please let me go." The King said: "If that is so, daughter, take the Mahābodhi and go."

From where did the King obtain the Mahābodhi? Even before Ariṭṭha arrived and before Sumana Sāmaṇera came to fetch the relics, the King had the desire to send the Mahābodhi to the island of Sīhaḷa. "How shall I send the Mahābodhi, which should not be struck with a weapon?" Not finding a way, he asked a minister named Mahādeva. The minister replied: "Great King, there are many wise monks." Hearing this, the King prepared a meal for the Saṅgha, and after the meal, he asked the Saṅgha: "Venerable Sirs, should the Mahābodhi of the Blessed One go to the island of Sīhaḷa?" The Saṅgha entrusted the responsibility to Moggaliputtatissa Thera.

The Elder said: "Great King, the Mahābodhi should go to the island of Sīhaḷa," and he related the five great resolutions of the Blessed One. What are the five? It is said that while the Blessed One was lying on his deathbed at the time of his Great Parinibbāna, for the sake of establishing the Mahābodhi on the island of Sīhaḷa, he resolved: "When King Asoka the Great comes to take the Mahābodhi, let the southern branch of the Mahābodhi detach itself and settle in a golden vase." This is the first resolution.

And at the time of its settling in that golden vase, he resolved: "Let the Mahābodhi enter into a snowy cloud and settle." This is the second resolution.
69:
“On the seventh day, descending from within the mist-cloud and staying in the golden vessel, may the six-colored rays be emitted from the leaves and the fruits.” He made this resolution—this was the third resolution.

“On the day the right collarbone relic is enshrined in the stupa at the Thūpārāma monastery, may it perform the twin miracle.” He made this resolution—this was the fourth resolution.

“In the island of Laṅkā itself, when a doṇa-measure of my relics is to be established in the Mahācetiya, may they take the form of the Buddha, rise into the air, and perform the twin miracle.” He made this resolution—this was the fifth resolution.

Having heard these five great resolutions, the King, with a heart full of faith, had the road from the city of Pāṭaliputta to the Great Bodhi Tree prepared, and he brought out a great amount of gold for the purpose of making a golden vessel. At that very moment, knowing the King’s intention, the divine son Vissakamma created the appearance of a goldsmith and stood before him. Seeing him, the King said, “Dear man, take this gold and make a vessel.” When asked, “Great King, do you know the dimensions?” the King replied, “Dear man, you yourself should know and make it.” Saying, “Very well, Great King, I shall do so,” he took the gold, and by his own psychic power, he kneaded it with his hands and created a golden vessel that was nine cubits in circumference, five cubits in height, three cubits in diameter, and eight finger-breadths in thickness, with a rim the size of an elephant’s trunk.

Then the King, accompanied by a great army seven yojanas in length and three yojanas in width, and having invited the Noble Saṅgha, went to the vicinity of the Great Bodhi Tree. The army surrounded the Great Bodhi Tree, which was adorned with raised banners and flags, made beautiful with various jewels, decorated with many ornaments, strewn with various kinds of flowers, and resounded with the music of many instruments. The King invited about a thousand leading Great Elders of the community, and together with a thousand kings who had been consecrated throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he caused himself and the Great Bodhi Tree to be surrounded. Standing at the foot of the Great Bodhi Tree, he gazed up at it. Except for the trunk of the Great Bodhi Tree and a four-cubit portion of the great southern branch, the remaining parts became invisible.

Seeing that miracle, the King was filled with joy and rapture, and addressing the community of monks, he said, “Venerable sirs, having seen this miracle and being delighted, I offer the Great Bodhi Tree the sovereignty of the whole of Jambudīpa,” and he performed the ceremony of consecration. Then, after making offerings of flowers, perfumes, and so on, and circumambulating it three times, he paid homage at eight places, and then rising, with palms joined...
70:
...lifting them up and standing, desiring to receive the Great Bodhi by an act of truth, he had the golden vessel placed upon a throne made of all kinds of jewels, which was set at a height reaching up to the southern branch of the Great Bodhi Tree from the ground. Ascending the jeweled throne and taking a golden brush, he made a mark with red arsenic and performed an act of truth, saying: “If the Great Bodhi is to be established in the island of Laṅkā, and if I am one who is without doubt in the Dispensation of the Buddha, let the Great Bodhi itself descend and be established in this golden vessel.” Simultaneously with the act of truth, the Bodhi branch severed itself at the place marked with the red arsenic and settled above the golden vessel filled with fragrant mud. The trunk of that Bodhi tree was ten cubits in height; there were five great branches, each four cubits in length, adorned with only five fruits; and there were a thousand small branches. 

Then the King made another mark three finger-breadths above the original mark at the base. At that very moment, nodules appeared and ten great roots came forth. Again, he made nine other marks at intervals of three finger-breadths higher and higher. From those marks also, ten nodules appeared at each, and ninety roots came forth. The first ten great roots grew to about four finger-breadths. The other roots also came forth, intertwining with each other like a lattice window. Standing on the jeweled throne and seeing such a miracle, the King raised his joined palms and uttered a great shout. Many thousands of monks shouted “Sādhu.” The entire royal army resounded with cheers. Hundreds of thousands of robes were tossed into the air. From the earth-dwelling devas up to the Akanittha Brahmas, all uttered cries of “Sādhu.” 

While the King stood with joined palms, his body pervaded with continuous joy as he witnessed this miracle, the Great Bodhi Tree established itself in the golden vessel with its hundred roots. The ten great roots reached and stayed at the bottom of the golden vessel. The remaining ninety small roots, growing in succession, descended and stayed in the fragrant mud.

As soon as the Great Bodhi was thus established in the golden vessel, the great earth quaked. In the sky, the divine drums of the devas thundered. With the dancing of the mountains, the “Sādhu” cries of the devas, the roars of the Yakkhas, the praises of the Asuras, the clapping of the Brahmas, the thundering of the clouds, the cries of the four-footed beasts, and the warbling of the birds...
71:
Due to the playing of all the musicians, each according to their own skill, a tumultuous sound echoed simultaneously from the surface of the earth up to the Brahma world. Six-colored rays issued forth from each and every fruit on the five branches, spreading up to the Brahma world, making the entire universe appear as if entwined with jeweled rafters. From that moment, for seven days, the Great Bodhi tree entered and remained within a mass of snowy clouds. No one could see the Great Bodhi tree. The King descended from his jeweled throne and had the worship of the Great Bodhi tree performed for seven days. On the seventh day, the snow and the six-colored rays from all directions returned and entered the Great Bodhi tree itself. When the snowy clouds cleared and the interior of the universe became exceptionally bright, the Great Bodhi tree appeared, complete with its trunk, branches, and twigs, adorned with five fruits, and established within the golden vessel. Seeing the Great Bodhi tree and being filled with joy and rapture due to such miracles, the King thought, "I shall worship the young Great Bodhi tree with the sovereignty of the entire Jambudīpa," and after performing the consecration, he remained at the site of the Great Bodhi tree for seven days.

The Great Bodhi tree first became established in the golden vessel on the evening of the Pavāraṇā day, the full moon of the early Kattika. After passing the seven days within the snowy clouds and the seven days of the consecration ceremony, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, the King entered the city of Pāṭaliputta in a single day. On the first day of the waxing fortnight of Kattika, he placed the Great Bodhi tree near the great Sāla tree in the east. On the seventeenth day from the day it was established in the golden vessel, new shoots appeared on the Great Bodhi tree. Seeing those shoots, the King, being further inspired with faith, again offered the consecration of the entire Jambudīpa, wishing to worship the Great Bodhi tree with his kingship. At that time, the novice Sumana Sāmaṇera, while going to fetch the relics on the full moon day of Kattika, witnessed the Kattika festival worship of the Great Bodhi tree. Referring to the Great Bodhi tree brought from the Mahābodhi-maṇḍa and placed in Pāṭaliputta in this manner, the King said, "In that case, dear daughter, take the Great Bodhi tree and go." The Theri Saṅghamittā accepted, saying, "Very well."

To protect the Great Bodhi tree, the King provided eighteen families of devas, eight families of ministers, eight families of brahmins, eight families of householders, eight families of cowherds, eight families of Taraccha clans, and eight families of Kaliṅga clans. For the purpose of pouring water, he provided eight golden pots and eight silver pots, and with this retinue—
72:
—having placed the Great Bodhi tree on a boat in the Ganges, the King himself departed from the city, crossed through the Viñjhā forest, and in due course reached the port of Tāmalitti in seven days. Along the way, devas, nagas, and humans performed a grand worship of the Great Bodhi tree. The King also kept the Great Bodhi tree at the shore of the ocean for seven days and offered the sovereignty of the entire great Jambudīpa. This was his third offering of the kingdom of Jambudīpa to the Great Bodhi tree.

Having worshipped with the great kingship in this manner, on the first day of the waxing moon of Maggasira, King Asoka the Righteous lifted the Great Bodhi tree, waded into the water up to his neck, and established it on the boat. He then had the Theri Saṅghamittā and her retinue board the boat and said to the minister Ariṭṭha: "Dear son, I have worshipped the Great Bodhi tree three times with the sovereignty of the entire Jambudīpa and, wading into the water up to my neck, have sent it to my friend. Let that friend also worship the Great Bodhi tree in this same manner." Having thus given the message for his friend, the King worshipped, saying, "Alas, the Great Bodhi tree, which emits the net of rays like those of the Buddha (Dasabala), is departing!" and stood there with joined palms, shedding tears. While the Great King was watching, the boat carrying the Great Bodhi tree sped out into the surface of the great ocean.

In the great ocean, for a distance of one yojana all around, the waves became calm; lotuses of five colors bloomed; divine musical instruments resounded in the sky; and an exceptionally grand worship was performed by the deities residing in the sky, the water, the land, and the trees. The Theri Saṅghamittā also terrified the Naga clans in the great ocean by assuming the form of a Garuḍa. Those terrified Nagas came and, seeing that splendor, entreated the Theri and took the Great Bodhi tree to the Naga realm. After worshipping it with the luxury of the Naga kingdom for seven days, they placed it back on the boat. On that very day, the boat reached the port of Jambukola. King Asoka, distressed by the separation from the Great Bodhi tree, lamented and wept, watching until it was out of sight before turning back.

King Devānampiyatissa, according to the words of Sumana Sāmaṇera, had the road cleared and decorated from the North Gate to the port of Jambukola starting from the first day of the waxing moon of Maggasira. On the day of departure from the city, while standing at the Samuddasālā (Sea-hall) near the North Gate, he saw the Great Bodhi tree coming across the great ocean with such splendor—
73:
Seeing the power of the Great Elder, the King was filled with joy and delight. Leaving his palace, he ordered five-colored flowers to be scattered along the entire route and flower altars to be placed at intervals. In a single day, he reached the port of Jambukola. Surrounded by all kinds of musical ensembles and making offerings of flowers, incense, perfumes, and ointments, he waded into the water up to his neck and exclaimed with a devoted heart, 'O friends, the Great Bodhi Tree, which emits the net of rays of the Lord Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, has indeed arrived!' He then lifted the Great Bodhi Tree and placed it upon his head, the noblest part of the body. Accompanied by the sixteen noble clans who had come escorting the Great Bodhi Tree, he emerged from the sea. Placing the Great Bodhi Tree on the shore, he honored it with the sovereignty of the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi for three days, entrusting the kingdom to those sixteen noble clans.

Then, on the fourth day, taking the Great Bodhi Tree and performing grand offerings, he reached the city of Anuradhapura in due course. In Anuradhapura as well, after making great offerings and honors, on the fourteenth day of the waxing moon of the month of Kattika, when the shadows were lengthening near sunset, he brought the Great Bodhi Tree in through the North Gate. Carrying it along the central road of the city, he exited through the South Gate. At a place about five hundred bow-lengths from the South Gate—where our Fully Enlightened Buddha had sat after entering the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); where the three previous Fully Enlightened Buddhas had also sat after entering their respective attainments; where the Mahāsirīsa Bodhi of the Blessed Kakusandha, the Udumbara Bodhi of the Blessed Koṇāgamana, and the Nigrodha Bodhi of the Fully Enlightened Kassapa had stood; which is like the frontal ornament (tilaka) of the Mahāmeghavana Park; and where the ground had been prepared beforehand according to the words of the novice Sumana—at the site of the entrance gate of the royal residence, he established the Great Bodhi Tree.

How was it established? It is said that those sixteen noble clans who came escorting the Great Bodhi Tree assumed the appearance of kings. The Great King himself assumed the appearance of a gatekeeper. Those sixteen clans lifted the Great Bodhi Tree and set it down. As soon as the Great Bodhi Tree was released from their hands, it rose eighty cubits into the air and emitted the six-colored rays. These rays spread throughout the entire island and reached up to the Brahma realm. Seeing this miracle of the Great Bodhi Tree, ten thousand people, filled with faith, developed insight (vipassanā) in due order, attained Arahantship, and entered the monkhood. The Great Bodhi Tree remained in the sky until sunset. When the sun set, it settled upon the earth under the Rohiṇī constellation. Simultaneously with the establishment of the Bodhi Tree, the great earth shook as far as the water's edge. After being established, the Great Bodhi Tree remained within a mass of mist for seven days, becoming invisible to the people.
74:
On the seventh day, the sky became clear and free of clouds. The six-colored rays shone brightly and spread in all directions. The trunk, branches, and leaves of the Great Bodhi Tree, along with five fruits, became clearly visible. Mahinda Thera, Saṅghamittā Therī, and the King, along with their retinues, went to the place where the Great Bodhi Tree stood. Most of the inhabitants of the island also gathered there. While they were watching, a fruit from the northern branch ripened and fell from the branch. The Elder held out his hand, and the fruit landed in it. The Elder gave it to the King, saying, 'Great King, plant this.' The King took the fruit, poured sweet soil into a golden vessel, filled it with fragrant mud, planted the fruit, and placed it near the Great Bodhi Tree. While everyone was watching, eight young Bodhi saplings, about four cubits in height, sprang up. Seeing this wonder, the King honored the eight young Bodhi saplings with a white parasol and performed a consecration (abhiseka) ceremony.

Furthermore, among those young Bodhi saplings, one was planted at the port of Jambukola, the place where the Great Bodhi Tree first landed. One was planted near the village gate of the Brahmin Tavakka, one at Thūpārāma, one at Issaranimmāna Vihāra (Vassagiri Monastery), one at the site of the Paṭhama Cetiya, one on the Cetiyapabbata mountain, one at the village of Kājaragāma in the province of Rohaṇa, and one at the village of Candanagāma, also in the province of Rohaṇa. The thirty-two young Bodhi saplings that grew from the seeds of the remaining four fruits were established in monasteries within a radius of one league (yojana) around Anuradhapura.

Thus, while the Great Bodhi Tree, which serves as the banner of the Dhamma of the Possessor of Ten Powers, remained established for the welfare and happiness of the island's inhabitants through successive generations of descendants, Queen Anulā, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred ladies of the court—a total of one thousand women—ordained in the presence of Saṅghamittā Therī and soon attained Arahantship along with her retinue. Prince Ariṭṭha, the King's nephew, also ordained in the presence of the Elder along with five hundred men and soon attained Arahantship along with his retinue.

After the Great Bodhi Tree was established, one day the King, after paying homage to the Great Bodhi, went to Thūpārāma with the Elder. When they reached the site where the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace) was to be built, people brought flowers. The King offered those flowers to the Elder. The Elder honored the site of the Lohapāsāda with the flowers. As soon as the flowers touched the ground, a great earthquake occurred. The King asked, 'Venerable Sir, why did the earth shake?' The Elder replied, 'Great King, in this place, there will be an Uposatha hall for the Saṅgha in the future; this earthquake is the omen of that Uposatha hall.'
75:
The King, proceeding again with the Elder, arrived at the place called Ambangaṇa. There, a ripe mango fruit, endowed with color and fragrance and of extremely sweet taste, was brought to him. The King offered that mango to the Elder for his consumption. Having consumed it right there, the Elder said, "Plant this mango stone in this very spot." The King took the mango stone, planted it in that very place, and poured water over it. Simultaneously with the planting of the mango seed, the earth quaked. The King asked, "Venerable Sir, why did the earth quake?" "Great King, in this place, in the future, there will be an assembly hall for the Saṅgha called 'Ambangaṇa'; this is the preceding sign of that."

The King scattered eight handfuls of flowers there, paid homage, and proceeding again with the Elder, arrived at the site of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya). There, men brought campaka flowers. The King offered those flowers to the Elder. The Elder honored the site of the Great Stupa with the flowers and paid homage. At that very moment, the great earth quaked violently. The King asked, "Venerable Sir, why did the earth quake?" "Great King, in this place, in the future, there will be an incomparable Great Stupa of the Blessed Buddha; this is the preceding sign of that." "I myself will build it, Venerable Sir," the King said. "Enough, Great King, you have many other tasks; however, your grandson named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya will build it," the Elder replied. Then the King said, "Venerable Sir, if my grandson will build it, it is as if I have built it myself." He had a stone pillar twelve cubits long brought and had these words inscribed: "Let the grandson of King Devānampiyatissa, named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya, build a stupa in this place." Having erected it and paid homage, he asked the Elder, "Venerable Sir, is the Sāsana established in the island of Tambapaṇṇi?" "Great King, the Sāsana is indeed established, but its roots have not yet descended (taken firm hold)." "Venerable Sir, when will the roots be said to have descended?" "Great King, when a youth born in the island of Tambapaṇṇi to parents who are inhabitants of the island of Tambapaṇṇi, having gone forth in the island of Tambapaṇṇi itself, learns the Vinaya in the island of Tambapaṇṇi and teaches it in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, then the roots of the Sāsana will be said to have descended." "Venerable Sir, is there such a monk?" "Great King, there is the monk named Mahā-Ariṭṭha who is capable of this task." "Venerable Sir, what should I do in this matter?" "Great King, it is proper to build a pavilion (maṇḍapa)." "Very well, Venerable Sir," the King agreed. In the precinct of the minister Meghavaṇṇābhaya, he had a pavilion built with royal majesty, similar to the pavilion built by the Great King Ajātasattu at the time of the Great Council. Having engaged all the musicians to play according to their respective skills, [he thought], "The roots of the Sāsana...
76:
"...I shall see the roots of the Sāsana descending," thinking thus, he arrived at Thūpārāma surrounded by many thousands of people.

At that time, sixty-eight thousand monks were assembled in the Thūpārāma monastery. A seat for the Venerable Mahā-Mahinda was prepared facing South. A Dhamma-seat for the Venerable Mahā-Ariṭṭha was prepared facing North. Then, the Venerable Mahā-Ariṭṭha, requested by the Venerable Mahinda, sat upon the Dhamma-seat in the appropriate order. Sixty-eight Great Elders, headed by the Venerable Mahinda, sat surrounding the Dhamma-seat. The King's younger brother, the Venerable Mattābhaya, thinking, "I will learn the Vinaya by taking the lead," sat surrounding the Dhamma-seat of the Venerable Mahā-Ariṭṭha together with five hundred monks. The remaining monks and the assembly headed by the King also sat in their respective appropriate seats.

Then the Venerable Mahā-Ariṭṭha recited the Vinaya Nidāna (Introduction to the Vinaya): "At one time, the Blessed Buddha was staying at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naḷeru-pucimanda neem tree." When the Venerable Ariṭṭha recited the Vinaya Nidāna, great sounds thundered in the sky. Out-of-season flashes of lightning appeared. Devas and Brahmas shouted "Sādhu" in approval. The great earth quaked violently as far as the water's edge.

While many such miracles were occurring, the Venerable Ariṭṭha—surrounded by the sixty-eight Great Elders who were Arahants (khīṇāsava) and leaders of their respective groups, headed by Mahā-Mahinda, and by other sixty-eight thousand monks—expounded the Vinaya Piṭaka in the midst of the Thūpārāma monastery on the first Kattika Pavāraṇā day. This Vinaya Piṭaka demonstrates the Buddha's quality of compassion and disciplines the wavering bodily and verbal actions of those who follow the Blessed One's instructions. Having thus expounded and taught it, he remained for the duration of his life, teaching many and establishing it in the hearts of many, and then attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). The Elders who participated in that assembly, headed by Mahā-Mahinda:

"Sixty-eight Great Elders, the leaders, assembled;
All were heads of their respective groups, disciples of the King of Dhamma.

Arahants who had attained mastery, possessing the three knowledges and skilled in psychic powers,
Having realized the supreme goal, they exhorted the kings.

Having shown the light and illuminated this earth,
Shining like great masses of fire, those Great Sages have passed away into Nibbāna."
77:
After the parinibbāna of those elders headed by Mahā-Mahinda, at a later time, their disciples such as Tissadatta, Kāḷasumana, and Dīghasumana, as well as the disciples and grand-disciples of the elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha—this lineage of teachers as previously mentioned—have brought this Vinaya Piṭaka down to the present day. Therefore, it is said: "After the Third Council, this was brought to this island of Sīhaḷa by Mahinda and others; having learned it from Mahinda, it was brought for some time by Ariṭṭha and others; from then until today, it has been brought by the lineage of teachers who are the succession of their disciples."

Where does the Vinaya Piṭaka stand? It should be known that it stands in those persons who possess it without deficiency in both text (Pāḷi) and meaning (attha), where it does not leak out even a little, like lion's oil placed in a jeweled jar; in such persons who possess superior mindfulness, understanding, perseverance, and wisdom, who are conscientious (lajjī), scrupulous (kukkuccaka), and desirous of training (sikkhākāma). Therefore, for the sake of the establishment of the Vinaya, a monk who desires training should learn the Vinaya, having well noted the benefits of the study of the Vinaya.

Herein are the benefits of the study of the Vinaya: A person skilled in the Vinaya scriptures (Vinaya-pariyatti) is like a father and mother to the sons of good family who have gained faith in the Dispensation (Sāsana). This is because their going forth (pabbajjā), higher ordination (upasampadā), performance of major and minor duties, and skill in conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara) depend on him. Furthermore, by depending on the study of the Vinaya, his own aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is well-guarded and well-protected. He becomes a refuge for monks who are troubled by remorse (kukkucca). He speaks confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha. He well-refutes opponents with Dhamma-based reasons. He practices for the longevity of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these five benefits in a person who is a bearer of the Vinaya: his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected... he practices for the longevity of the True Dhamma." (Pari. 325).

A person who bears the Vinaya is also the heir to the wholesome states (kusala dhamma) rooted in restraint (saṃvara) taught by the Blessed One. This is because those states are rooted in the Vinaya. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Vinaya is for the sake of restraint, restraint is for the sake of non-remorse, non-remorse is for the sake of joy, joy is for the sake of rapture, rapture is for the sake of tranquility, tranquility is for the sake of happiness, happiness is for the sake of concentration, concentration is for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they really are, knowledge and vision of things as they really are is for the sake of disenchantment, disenchantment is for the sake of dispassion, dispassion is..."
79:
## Commentary on the Verañja Section

Now, since it has been stated in the verse beginning with "Tena-ti-ādi-pāṭhassa" that the explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya will be presented through various methods, I shall provide the explanation of the passages beginning with "Tena samayena Buddho Bhagavā."

The explanation is as follows: The word "tena" is an indefinite demonstrative. Although "tena" is not explicitly defined in its own form, it is subsequently referred back to by the word "yena" which is established by the sense. This is because the thought of the Venerable Sāriputta, which was the cause for the request to prescribe the Vinaya rules, later became manifest. Therefore, the connection should be understood here as: "At which time that thought arose, at that time the Blessed One was dwelling in Verañjā." This is the appropriate method throughout the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. How so? Wherever "tena" is mentioned, it should be referred back to by the word "yena" which is established by the sense, whether occurring before or after.

This is a brief illustration: "Monks, for which reason Sudinna engaged in sexual intercourse, for that reason I shall prescribe a training rule for the monks." This is the intended meaning. Thus, it is appropriate to refer back with the word "yena" established by the sense beforehand. "At which time Dhaniya, the potter's son, took the King's wood without it being given, at that time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha." Thus, it is also appropriate to refer back with the word "yena" established by the sense afterwards. This is the meaning of the word "tena."

Regarding the word "samayena," the word "samaya" is found in the senses of:
Coincidence, opportunity, time, assembly, cause, view,
Acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.

Accordingly—in such passages as "Perhaps we might approach tomorrow, depending on the time and the coincidence (samavāya)," coincidence is the meaning. In such passages as "Monks, there is only one moment (khaṇa) and occasion for living the holy life," opportunity is the meaning.
80:
"The hot time, the sweltering time," etc., it means time (kāla). "There is a great assembly (samūha) in the forest," etc., it means assembly. "Bhaddāli, the cause (hetu) was not penetrated by you: 'The Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī; the Blessed One will know me—the monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher's Dispensation.' Bhaddāli, this cause was also not penetrated by you," etc., it means cause. "At that time, the wanderer Uggahamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was staying in Queen Mallikā’s park, which was surrounded by Tinduka trees and had a single hall, where views (diṭṭhi) were debated," etc., it means view.

"Because of the acquisition (paṭilābha) of the welfare in the present life and the welfare in the life to come, the steadfast one is called a wise man," etc., it means acquisition. "Through the proper abandonment (pahāna) of conceit, he has made an end of suffering," etc., it means abandonment. "The sense of oppression of suffering, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, the sense of penetration (paṭivedha)," etc., it means penetration. In this Vinaya, however, the meaning of this word "samaya" is time (kāla). Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as "at that time"—the time when the thought arose in the Venerable Sāriputta, which was the cause for the request to prescribe the Vinaya rules.

Here it is asked: "Why is it that in the Sutta it is designated by the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) as 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', and in the Abhidhamma by the locative case (bhumma-vacana) as 'yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ', but here in the Vinaya, it is designated by the instrumental case (karaṇa-vacana) as 'tena samayena'?"

It is because in those (Sutta and Abhidhamma) it is so, and in this (Vinaya) it is otherwise, due to the possible meanings. How? In the Sutta, first of all, the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga) is possible. This is because as long as the Blessed One was teaching the Suttas such as the Brahmajāla Sutta, He was dwelling continuously in the abiding of compassion (karuṇā-vihāra). Therefore, to illustrate that meaning, the accusative designation was used there. In the Abhidhamma, the sense of basis (adhikaraṇa) and the sense of marking a state by another state (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa) are possible. For "samaya" in the sense of time and assembly is the basis. By the presence of the "samaya"—defined as the coincidence of the moment and the cause for the states such as contact (phassa) mentioned in that Abhidhamma—the presence of those states is marked. Therefore, to illustrate that meaning, the locative designation was used there. In this Vinaya, however, the sense of cause (hetu) and the sense of means (karaṇa) are possible.
81:
For the occasion of the promulgation of the training rules, which is difficult to understand even for great elders such as Sāriputta, is both the root cause and the instrument (of the promulgation). Therefore, the Blessed One, being mindful of the reason for the promulgation of those training rules, dwelt in various places (such as Vesālī). Thus, it should be understood that in this Vinaya, the reference is made using the third case (instrumental case, karaṇavacana) to clarify that meaning.

In this regard, there is this verse:

"In texts other than the Vinaya, depending on the respective meaning,
The word samaya is expressed in the accusative or locative case.
But here in the Vinaya, depending on the meaning of cause or instrument,
That word samaya is expressed only in the instrumental case."

However, the ancient commentators (Porāṇā) explain: "The expressions 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' (accusative), 'yasmiṃ samaye' (locative), or 'tena samayena' (instrumental) differ only in phrasing (sadda); in all instances, the meaning is that of the locative case (bhumma)." Therefore, according to their view, even though it is said "tena samayena," the meaning should be understood as "tasmiṃ samaye" (at that time).

We shall explain the meaning of the words "Buddho Bhagavā" later. In the phrase "Verañjāyaṃ viharati," "Verañjā" is the name of a certain city. The locative case in "Verañjāyaṃ" is used in the sense of proximity (samīpattha). "Viharati" (dwells) is a general term indicating that the Blessed One is endowed with one of the modes of dwelling, such as the dwelling in postures (iriyāpatha-vihāra), the divine dwelling (dibba-vihāra), the sublime dwelling (brahma-vihāra), or the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra). In this context, however, it indicates being engaged in one of the four postures: standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, it should be understood that the Blessed One "dwells" (viharati). This is because the Blessed One carries on and maintains the physical body (attabhāva) without letting it fall, by interrupting the fatigue caused by one posture with another posture; thus, it is said "viharati."

In the phrase "naḷerupucimandamūle," "Naḷeru" is the name of a yakkha. "Pucimanda" refers to a neem tree. "Mūla" means proximity (samīpa). This word "mūla" is seen in the sense of a physical root (mūlamūla) in passages such as "He should pull up the roots, even down to the fibers of the usīra grass." It is seen in the sense of an uncommon cause (asādhāraṇa-hetu) in passages such as "Greed is the root (mūla) of the unwholesome." It is seen in the sense of proximity (samīpa) in passages such as "The area where the shadow falls at noon and where leaves fall when the wind is still is the root (mūla) of the tree." In this context, the sense of proximity (samīpa) is intended. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "near the neem tree presided over by the yakkha Naḷeru." That neem tree was said to be delightful, pleasing, and stood like a sovereign over many other trees in a place easy to reach, not far from that city.
82:
Then the Blessed One, having gone to the city of Verañjā and staying in a suitable place, dwelt at the foot and in the vicinity of that neem tree. Because of this dwelling, it is said: "He dwells at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree."

In this regard, there might be an objection: If the Blessed One dwells in the city of Verañjā, it should not be said "at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree"; if He dwells at the foot of that neem tree, it should not be said "in Verañjā." For it is impossible to dwell in both places at the same time without one being before or after the other. However, it should not be viewed in this way. Did we not say that "the locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle wandering near the Ganges or Yamuna rivers are said to be "wandering in the Ganges" or "wandering in the Yamuna," so too here, the Blessed One, while dwelling at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree near Verañjā, is said to be "dwelling at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree." Indeed, the mention of "Verañjā" is to indicate the village for alms-resort, while the mention of "at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree" is to indicate a dwelling place suitable for a renunciant.

Among those words, the Elder Upāli, by mentioning "Verañjā," shows the Blessed One's favor toward householders; by mentioning "at the foot of the Naḷeru neem tree," he shows favor toward renunciants. Likewise, by the former, he shows the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification through the acceptance of the four requisites; by the latter, he shows the means of avoiding devotion to sensual pleasures through the abandonment of the objects of desire. By the former, he shows the commitment to preaching the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination toward seclusion. By the former, the approach through compassion; by the latter, the withdrawal through wisdom. By the former, the desire to fulfill the welfare and happiness of beings; by the latter, the absence of defilement while performing the welfare of others. By the former, a comfortable dwelling (phāsuvihāra) based on not renouncing the happiness obtained in accordance with the Dhamma; by the latter, a dwelling based on the practice of the states beyond those of ordinary humans (uttarimanussadhamma). By the former, the great benefit to humans; by the latter, to the deities. By the former, the fact of being born and raised in the world; by the latter, being undefiled by the things of the world. By the former, he shows the fulfillment of the purpose for which the Blessed One arose, in accordance with the statement: "Monks, there is one person who, when born into the world, is born for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Who is that one person? The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One." By the latter, he shows a dwelling suitable for the place of His arising. Indeed, the Blessed One was born first in the Lumbinī grove and attained enlightenment secondly at the Bodhimaṇḍa; thus, in both mundane and supramundane arisings, He arose only in the forest. Therefore, it shows His dwelling only in the forest. In this way and others, the connection of the meaning in this context should be understood.
83:
In the phrase "mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ," the word "mahatā" (great) refers to greatness due to both excellence of qualities and largeness of number. That community of monks was indeed great in qualities because even the lowest monk among them was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). It was also great in number because it consisted of five hundred. "Bhikkhusaṅghena" means with the community of monks; it refers to a group of recluses united by the commonality of view and virtue. "Saddhiṃ" means together. In the phrase "pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi," they are called "pañcamatta" because they have a measure of five. "Mattā" refers to measure (quantity). Therefore, just as in the phrase "bhojane mattaññū" (knowing the measure in food), it means knowing the measure or quantity in food, so too here, it should be understood that those hundreds of monks have a measure of five (a quantity of five hundred). Hundreds of monks are called "bhikkhusatāni." It means together with that group of five hundred monks. By this phrase "pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi," the greatness in number of that great community of monks mentioned in "mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ" is shown. Later, however, their greatness in qualities will become manifest through the words: "Sāriputta, the community of monks is free from strife, free from danger, free from stain, pure, and established in the essence. Sāriputta, even the lowest monk among these five hundred is a stream-enterer."

In the phrase "assosi kho Verañjo brāhmaṇo," "assosi" means he heard, he received, or he understood according to the sound of the words reaching the door of the ear. "Kho" is a particle used either as a mere filler or in the sense of emphasis. Among these, if taken in the sense of emphasis, it should be understood as "he indeed heard; there was no obstacle to his hearing." As a filler, it is merely for the smoothness of the syllables. He is called "Verañja" because he was born in Verañjā, originated in Verañjā, or because Verañjā was his residence. By the name given by his parents, this Brahmin is called "Udaya." He is called "brāhmaṇa" because he recites the Vedas (brahma); it means he chants the mantras. This is the etymological definition (nirutti) for Brahmins by birth. Noble ones (ariyas), however, are called "brāhmaṇas" because they have discarded evil.

Now, wishing to reveal the matter that the Brahmin of Verañjā heard, he said: "The recluse Gotama, sirs..." and so on. Therein, he should be known as "samaṇa" because he has stilled evil. For it has been said: "Because he has discarded evil, he is called a brāhmaṇa" (Dhammapada 388).
84:
"Because he has stilled evil, he is called a samaṇa (recluse)" (Dhammapada 265). The Blessed One has also stilled evil through the unsurpassed Noble Path; therefore, because of that state of having stilled evil, this name "Samaṇa" is a name acquired in accordance with his actual qualities. "Khalu" is a particle in the sense of hearsay. "Bho" is merely a form of address common to the Brahmin caste by birth. For it has been said: "He is called a 'bho-sayer' if he still has defilements" (Dhammapada 396, Sutta Nipāta 625). By the word "Gotama," he praises the Blessed One by way of his clan. Therefore, in the phrase "samaṇo khalu bho gotamo," the meaning should be understood as: "Sirs, it is said that the recluse of the Gotama clan is staying." "Sakyaputto" (Son of the Sakyans) is a declaration of the Blessed One's high birth. "Sakyakulā pabbajito" (Gone forth from the Sakyan family) is a declaration of his state of having gone forth out of faith. It means that he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that family while it was still undiminished and not overcome by any loss. The words mentioned after that have the same meaning as already stated. "Taṃ kho pana" is an accusative case in the sense of relating an account of that Venerable Gotama. "Kalyāṇo" means endowed with good qualities, meaning excellent. "Kittisaddo" means fame or the sound of praise.

In the phrases "iti pi so bhagavā" etc., the grammatical connection (yojanā) is: "That Blessed One is an Arahant for this reason, he is a Sammāsambuddha for this reason, he is a Vijjācaraṇasampanno for this reason, he is a Sugato for this reason, he is a Lokavidū for this reason, he is an Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi for this reason, he is a Satthā Devamanussānaṃ for this reason, he is a Buddho for this reason, and he is a Bhagavā for this reason."

Now, for the sake of the Vinaya-bearers' proficiency in the Sutta method, and to gladden the mind with a Dhamma talk related to the Buddha's qualities at the beginning of the Vinaya commentary, I shall provide a detailed explanation of these terms. Therefore, in the words "so bhagavā iti pi arahaṃ" etc., the Blessed One should be known as "Arahaṃ" for these reasons: because of being remote (āraka), because of having killed the enemies (ari), because of having destroyed the spokes (ara), because of being worthy (arahatta) of requisites etc., and because of the absence of secrecy (raha) in doing evil. He is "Arahaṃ" because of being remote, for he stands very far away from all defilements, having destroyed the defilements along with their residual impressions (vāsanā) by means of the Path. He is also "Arahaṃ" because of having killed the enemies, for those enemies that are defilements were killed by him through the Path. Furthermore, the wheel of saṃsāra, which has been revolving since time immemorial, having ignorance and craving for existence as its hub, having formations such as meritorious formations as its spokes, having aging and death as its rim, and being pierced by the axle made of the origin of taints and joined to the chariot of the three worlds—all the spokes of this wheel...
85:
Because He stands on the ground of virtue (sīla) with the feet of energy (vīriya) near the Bodhi tree, and holding the axe of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa)—which brings an end to kamma—with the hand of faith (saddhā), He has destroyed all the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; thus He is called 'Arahaṃ' (the Worthy One). 

Alternatively, the beginningless round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) is called the wheel of saṃsāra (saṃsāracakka). In this wheel of saṃsāra, ignorance (avijjā) is called the hub (nābhi) because it is the root. Aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) are called the rim (nemi) because they are the end. The remaining ten factors are called the spokes (ara) because they have ignorance as their root and aging and death as their end. 

In that wheel of saṃsāra, lack of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering (dukkha), is called ignorance (avijjā). In the sensual realm (kāmabhava), ignorance is a condition for the formations (saṅkhāra) in the sensual realm. In the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), ignorance is a condition for the formations in the fine-material realm. In the immaterial realm (arūpabhava), ignorance is a condition for the formations in the immaterial realm. In the sensual realm, formations are conditions for the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) in the sensual realm. This method applies to the other realms as well. 

In the sensual realm, rebirth-linking consciousness is a condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in the sensual realm; it is the same in the fine-material realm. In the immaterial realm, however, it is a condition for name (nāma) only. In the sensual realm, name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) in the sensual realm. In the fine-material realm, name-and-form is a condition for three sense bases in the fine-material realm. In the immaterial realm, name is a condition for one sense base in the immaterial realm. 

In the sensual realm, the six sense bases are conditions for the six kinds of contact (phassa) in the sensual realm. In the fine-material realm, the three sense bases are conditions for the three kinds of contact, and in the immaterial realm, the one sense base is a condition for the one kind of contact in the immaterial realm. In the sensual realm, the six kinds of contact are conditions for the six kinds of feeling (vedanā) in the sensual realm. In the fine-material realm, the three kinds of contact are conditions for the three kinds of feeling in that very realm, and in the immaterial realm, the one kind of contact is a condition for the one kind of feeling in that very realm. 

In the sensual realm, the six kinds of feeling are conditions for the six groups of craving (taṇhā) in the sensual realm. In the fine-material realm, the three kinds of feeling are conditions for the three groups of craving in that very realm, and in the immaterial realm, the one kind of feeling is a condition for the one group of craving in the immaterial realm. In each respective realm, each respective craving is a condition for each respective clinging (upādāna). Clinging and the subsequent factors are conditions for becoming (bhava) and so forth. 

How? In this world, a certain person, thinking, 'I shall enjoy sensual pleasures,' practices bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct due to the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). Due to the fulfillment of misconduct, he is reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth in those states of deprivation is called kamma-process becoming (kammabhava). The aggregates produced by kamma are called rebirth-process becoming (upapattibhava). The manifestation of the aggregates is birth (jāti), their ripening is aging (jarā), and their breaking up is death (maraṇa).
86:
Another person thinks, 'I shall enjoy the bliss of the heavenly realm,' and likewise practices good conduct (sucarita). Due to the fulfillment of good conduct, he is reborn in heaven. The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth in that heaven is called kamma-process becoming (kammabhava). The method is the same. 

Another person, however, thinking, 'I shall enjoy the bliss of the Brahma world,' practices loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), or equanimity (upekkhā) solely due to the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). Due to the fulfillment of meditation (bhāvanā), he is reborn in the Brahma world. The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth in that Brahma world is called kamma-process becoming (kammabhava). The method is the same. 

Another person thinks, 'I shall enjoy the bliss of the immaterial realm (arūpabhava),' and likewise develops attainments such as the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Due to the fulfillment of meditation, he is reborn in that immaterial realm. The kamma that is the cause of his rebirth in that immaterial realm is called kamma-process becoming (kammabhava). The aggregates produced by kamma are called rebirth-process becoming (upapattibhava). The manifestation of the aggregates is birth (jāti), their ripening is aging (jarā), and their breaking up is death (maraṇa). This method is also the same for the applications (yojanā) rooted in the remaining types of clinging. 

Thus, the wisdom that discerns the causes, thinking, 'This ignorance is the cause, formations are produced by the cause, both of these are produced by causes,' is called the Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa). In the same way, the wisdom that discerns the causes in the past and in the future, thinking, 'Ignorance is the cause, formations are produced by the cause, both of these are produced by causes,' is called the Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma. By this method, all the terms should be expanded. 

Among those factors, ignorance and formations are one group (saṅkhepa); consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are one group; craving, clinging, and becoming are one group; and birth, aging, and death are one group. Among these groups, the first group belongs to the past period (addhā), the two middle groups belong to the present period, and birth, aging, and death belong to the future period. 

By taking ignorance and formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included; therefore, these five factors are the kamma-round (kammavaṭṭa) in the past life. The five factors starting with consciousness are the resultant-round (vipākavaṭṭa) at present. By taking craving, clinging, and becoming, ignorance and formations are also included; therefore, these five factors are the kamma-round at present. Since consciousness and the others are indicated by the terms birth, aging, and death, these five factors are the resultant-round in the future life. 

They consist of twenty modes (ākāra). Between formations and consciousness, there is one connection (sandhi); between feeling and craving, there is one connection; and between becoming and birth, there is one connection. 

In this way, the Blessed One knows, sees, understands, and penetrates Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in all its aspects—with its four groups, three periods, twenty modes, and three connections. It is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing, and 'wisdom' (pajānana) in the sense of understanding. Therefore, it is said: 'The wisdom that discerns the causes is the Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma.' With this Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma, the Blessed One, having known those things as they really are...
87:
Having become weary of, detached from, and liberated from those states such as ignorance and so forth, he has destroyed, specifically destroyed, and demolished the spokes of this wheel of Saṃsāra of the aforementioned nature. Thus, because he has destroyed the spokes (ara), he is called Arahaṃ. Furthermore, because he is worthy of the highest offerings, he deserves to receive requisites such as robes and so forth, as well as special veneration. Precisely because he is worthy of such special veneration, when the Tathāgata appears, those deities and humans of great power do not offer veneration to anyone else. To elaborate on this: Sahampati Brahma venerated the Tathāgata with a garland of jewels as large as Mount Sineru; other deities and humans, such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala, also offered veneration according to their ability. Even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, King Asoka the Great, intending to honor the Blessed One, spent ninety-six crores of wealth and established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. What need is there to mention other special offerings? Thus, because he is worthy of requisites and so forth, he is called Arahaṃ. Just as in the world some fools who consider themselves wise commit evil in secret for fear of ill repute, the Blessed One never does so; because he has no secret place for committing evil, he is called Arahaṃ. In this context, there is this verse: 

'Because he is remote, because he has killed the enemies which are defilements, because he, the Sage, has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, because he is worthy of requisites and so forth, and because he does not commit evil in secret, he is therefore called Arahaṃ.'

Because he has known all things rightly and by himself, he is called Sammāsambuddho. Indeed, he has known all things rightly and by himself: he has known things to be known by higher knowledge through higher knowledge, things to be fully understood through full understanding, things to be abandoned through abandoning, things to be realized through realization, and things to be developed through development. Therefore, he said: 

'O Brahmin, that which should be known by higher knowledge has been known by me; that which should be developed has been developed; that which should be abandoned has been abandoned; therefore, I am the Buddha.'

In another way, the eye is the Truth of Suffering; the prior craving that originates it as its root cause is the Truth of the Origin; the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation; the practice that is the knowledge of cessation is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by extracting each individual group, he has known all things rightly and by himself. This method should also be understood for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By this same method, the six internal bases such as the eye and so forth, the six groups of consciousness such as eye-consciousness and so forth, the six groups of contact such as eye-contact and so forth, the six groups of feeling born of eye-contact and so forth, the six groups of perception such as perception of forms and so forth, the six groups of volition such as volition regarding forms and so forth, craving for forms and so forth...
88:
...the six groups of craving, the six groups of thought such as thought regarding forms and so forth, the six groups of examination such as examination regarding forms and so forth, the five aggregates such as the aggregate of form and so forth, the ten kasinas, the ten recollections, the ten perceptions by way of the perception of a bloated corpse and so forth, the thirty-two parts of the body such as hair and so forth, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the nine types of existence such as the sense-sphere existence and so forth, the four jhānas such as the first jhāna and so forth, the four immeasurables such as the development of loving-kindness and so forth, the four immaterial attainments, and the factors of Dependent Origination such as aging and death in reverse order and ignorance and so forth in forward order should be applied.

In this context, this is the application of a single group: 'Aging and death are the Truth of Suffering, birth is the Truth of the Origin, the escape from both (Nibbāna) is the Truth of Cessation, the knowledge of cessation is the Truth of the Path.' Thus, by extracting each individual term, the Blessed One has known all things rightly and by himself, has known them in accordance with the truth, and has penetrated them. Therefore, it is said: 'Because he has known all things rightly and by himself, he is called Sammāsambuddho.'

Because he is endowed with knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa), he is called Vijjācaraṇasampanno. Therein, 'knowledge' refers to the three knowledges or the eight knowledges. The three knowledges should be understood as taught in the Bhayabherava Sutta, and the eight knowledges as taught in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the eight knowledges are stated by including insight-knowledge and mind-made power along with the six supernormal knowledges. 'Conduct' (caraṇa) refers to these fifteen states: restraint of virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven qualities of a good person, and the four fine-material jhānas. These fifteen states are called 'conduct' because by means of them the noble disciple walks (carati) or goes to the deathless region (Nibbāna). As it is said: 'Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is virtuous,' and so on in detail. The Blessed One is endowed with these knowledges and this conduct; therefore, he is called Vijjācaraṇasampanno. Therein, the endowment of knowledge stands fulfilling the Blessed One's omniscience, and the endowment of conduct stands fulfilling his great compassion. Through omniscience, he knows the welfare and harm of all beings, and through great compassion, he causes them to avoid harm and directs them toward welfare. Thus, he is one endowed with knowledge and conduct. Therefore, his disciples are those who practice well, not those who practice wrongly. For the disciples of teachers who lack knowledge and conduct practice wrongly, like those who torment themselves.

Because he has a beautiful going, because he has gone to a sublime place, because he has gone rightly, and because he has spoken rightly, he is called Sugato. 'Going' is also called 'gata', and that going of the Blessed One is beautiful, pure, and faultless. What is that beautiful going? It is the Noble Path. Why is that going known as the Noble Path? Because by that going, which is the Noble Path, the Blessed One (has reached) the secure region of Nibbāna without any attachment to existences.
89:
That going is pure and faultless. What is it? It is the Noble Path. Because he has gone to the region of Nibbāna, the place of safety, without clinging to existence through that going which is the Noble Path, he is called 'Sugata' (Well-Gone) due to the excellence of his going. He is also called 'Sugata' because he has gone to the appropriate place, which is the deathless Nibbāna. He has gone well, not returning again to the defilements abandoned by the various paths. Thus it is said: "Those defilements which are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), to those defilements he does not go again, does not return, does not come back; therefore he is Sugata... Those defilements which are abandoned by the path of arahantship (Arahatta-magga), to those defilements he does not go again, does not return, does not come back; therefore he is Sugata" (Mahāniddesa). Alternatively, from the time at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-maṇḍa), he practiced the thirty perfections (pāramīs) with right conduct, acting only for the welfare and happiness of the entire world of beings. He came rightly, without approaching the extremes of eternalism (sassata), nihilism (uccheda), devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga), or devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga); thus he is called 'Sugata' because of his right coming. He is also called 'Sugata' because he speaks rightly, uttering only appropriate words at the appropriate time. 

In this regard, the supporting discourse is as follows: "Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be false, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is also disliked and disagreeable to others, that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct but unbeneficial, and which is also disliked and disagreeable to others, that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disliked and disagreeable to others, in that case, the Tathāgata knows the right time to explain that speech. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be false, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but which is liked and agreeable to others, that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct but unbeneficial, but which is liked and agreeable to others, that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is liked and agreeable to others, in that case, the Tathāgata knows the right time to explain that speech" (Majjhima Nikāya). Thus, he should be known as 'Sugata' because he speaks rightly. 

He is called 'Lokavidū' (Knower of the World) because he has known the world in every way. For that Blessed One has known, understood, and penetrated the world in every way—by its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the means to its cessation. As he said: "Friend, that place where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn, I do not say that the end of the world can be [reached] by going..."
90:
...known, seen, or reached by going. Friend, I do not say that without reaching the end of the world, one can make an end of suffering (liberation from the round of rebirth). Friend, rather, it is in this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, that I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the practice leading to the cessation of the world.

"The end of the world can never be reached by going,
Yet without reaching the end of the world, there is no release from suffering.

"Therefore, indeed, the wise one, the knower of the world,
The reacher of the world's end, who has lived the holy life,
Having known the end of the world through tranquility,
Does not long for this world or the next."

Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka), the world of beings (satta-loka), and the world of space (okāsa-loka). Among these, in the context where it is said, "One world: all beings subsist on nutriment" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.112), it should be understood as the world of formations. In the context where it is said, "The world is eternal, or the world is not eternal" (Dīgha Nikāya 1.421), it refers to the world of beings.

"As far as the moon and sun revolve,
Illuminating the quarters with their radiance,
So far does the world extend a thousandfold;
Therein your power prevails."

In this context, it should be understood as the world of space, and the Blessed One has known that world in every way. For he [knows]: One world: all beings subsist on nutriment. Two worlds: mind and matter (nāma and rūpa). Three worlds: the three types of feeling (vedanā). Four worlds: the four nutriments (āhāra). Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). Six worlds: the six internal sense bases (āyatana). Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Ten worlds: the ten sense bases (āyatana). Twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases (āyatana). Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements (dhātu). In this way, he has known this world of formations in every way.
91:
Because the Blessed One knows the inclinations (āsaya), the underlying tendencies (anusaya), the temperaments (carita), and the dispositions (adhimutti) of all beings. He knows beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those difficult to teach, and those who are capable (bhabba) and those who are incapable (abhabba). Therefore, the world of beings (sattaloka) is fully known to Him in every aspect. Just as the world of beings is known, so too is the world of locations (okāsaloka).

One such world-system (Cakkavāḷa) is one million, two hundred and three thousand, four hundred and fifty (1,203,450) yojanas in length and breadth. In circumference:
The entire circumference is
three million, six hundred and ten thousand,
three hundred and fifty (3,610,350) yojanas.

## Therein –
This earth is said to be
two hundred and forty thousand (240,000) yojanas in thickness.

## Its support –
The body of water resting on the wind, which supports that earth,
is four hundred and eighty thousand (480,000) yojanas in thickness.

## Its support as well –
The body of air (wind) that supports that water
rises into the sky for nine hundred and sixty thousand (960,000) yojanas.
This is the stability of the world.

## In this world thus established –
In this world-system thus established, Mount Sineru, the highest of mountains,
is submerged eighty-four thousand (84,000) yojanas in the great ocean,
and rises above it to the same extent.

Following that, with half the size of each preceding one in order,
submerged and rising, divine,
and adorned with various jewels,
are the seven great mountains: Yugandhara, Isadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, and Assakaṇṇa.
These seven great mountains stand around Mount Sineru,
serving as the abodes of the Great Kings and frequented by devas and yakkhas.
92:
Mount Himavā is five hundred yojanas high.
It is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
It is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks.
The Jambu tree, so-called, has a trunk fifteen yojanas in circumference.
The length of its branches all around is fifty yojanas each.
It is one hundred yojanas in breadth and also one hundred yojanas in height.
By the power of that Jambu tree, the island is known as Jambudīpa.
The Cakkavāḷa mountain is submerged eighty-two thousand yojanas in the ocean,
and rises above it to the same extent.
That Cakkavāḷa mountain stands encircling the entire world-element (lokadhātu).

In that world-system, the moon mansion (Candamaṇḍala) is 49 yojanas, the sun mansion (Suriyamaṇḍala) is 50 yojanas, and the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is ten thousand yojanas. Likewise, the Asura realm, the Avīci great hell, and Jambudīpa are each ten thousand yojanas. The island of Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas, and Pubbavideha is also seven thousand yojanas. The island of Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas. Herein, each great island is surrounded by five hundred small islands. All of that constitutes one world-system, one world-element. In the spaces between these world-systems lie the Lokantarika hells. Thus, the Blessed One, with His infinite Buddha-knowledge, has known, realized, and penetrated the infinite world-systems and infinite world-elements. In this way, the world of locations (okāsaloka) is also fully known to Him in every aspect. Because He knows the world in every aspect, He is called 'Lokavidū' (Knower of the Worlds).

Because there is no one superior to Him in His own qualities, and because there is no one higher than this Blessed One, He is called 'Anuttaro' (Unsurpassed). Indeed, He surpasses the entire world through the quality of virtue (sīla). He also surpasses the entire world through the qualities of concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). In the quality of virtue, He is peerless (asama), equal to the unequaled (asamasama), incomparable (appaṭima), matchless (appaṭibhāga), and without a counterpart (appaṭipuggala)... and He is the same in the quality of the knowledge and vision of liberation. As He said: 'Monks, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... in this generation with its devas and humans, I do not see anyone more perfect in virtue than myself.' This should be understood in detail.
93:
In this way, the Aggappasāda Sutta and others, as well as the verses beginning with "I have no teacher," should be expanded upon. He is called 'Purisadammasārathi' because he tames men who are fit to be tamed. This means he tames them and makes them disciplined. In this context, 'purisadamma' refers to those who are not yet disciplined but are suitable for taming, including animal-men, human-men, and non-human-men. Indeed, the Blessed One tamed animal-men such as the Nāga king Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, and the elephant Dhanapālaka, making them free from venom and establishing them in the refuges and the precepts. He also tamed human-men such as Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta, the youth Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others.
