Furthermore, he tamed and disciplined non-human-men such as the yakkhas Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, Kharaloma, and Sakka, the king of devas, using various methods of discipline. In this regard, the sutta stating, "Kesi, I discipline a man to be tamed by a gentle method, by a harsh method, and by both gentle and harsh methods," should be expanded upon. Alternatively, by teaching the first jhāna and so forth to those of pure virtue, and the practice of the higher paths to those such as stream-enterers, he also tames those who are already disciplined.

Alternatively, 'Anuttaro purisadammasārathi' is a single compound term. The Blessed One tames men to be tamed in such a way that, while sitting in a single posture, they can run (attain) through the eight directions without attachment. Therefore, he is called 'Anuttaro purisadammasārathi' (the Incomparable Charioteer of men to be tamed). In this regard, the sutta stating, "Monks, an elephant to be tamed, when tamed by an elephant trainer, runs in only one direction," should be expanded upon. He is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he instructs according to the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (Nibbāna). Furthermore, he is called 'Satthā' because he is like a caravan leader; the Blessed One is a caravan leader. The meaning here should be understood according to the method of the Niddesa: "Just as a caravan leader guides a caravan across a wilderness, across a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness of wild beasts, a wilderness of famine, and a wilderness of waterlessness, and brings them to safety; in the same way, the Blessed One, the Teacher and Caravan Leader, guides beings across the wilderness of saṃsāra and the wilderness of rebirth."
94:
The words 'devamanussānaṃ' (of gods and humans) are said in terms of the distinction of the highest beings among gods and humans, and in terms of the distinction of capable individuals (bhabba-puggala). However, the Blessed One is a teacher (Satthā) even to animals by giving them instruction. For they too, by hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One, attain the sufficiency of supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti), and by that very sufficiency, they become partakers of the paths and fruits in their second or third existence.

The frog-deity (Maṇḍūka Devaputta) and others are examples in this matter. It is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the people of Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lake, a frog took the voice of the Blessed One as an object (nimitta). A cowherd, standing while leaning on a staff, accidentally stepped on the frog's head and remained there. The frog died at that very moment and was reborn in a golden mansion twelve yojanas in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Like one waking from sleep, seeing himself surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, he reflected, 'How did I come to be born here?' and saw no other deed than taking the voice of the Blessed One as an object. That son of a deva immediately came with his mansion and paid homage to the Blessed One's feet with his head. The Blessed One, though knowing, asked:

'Who is it that pays homage to my feet,
Shining with psychic power and glory,
With an exceeding beauty of complexion,
Illuminating all directions?'

'I was a frog in the past,
Moving in the waters;
While listening to your Dhamma,
A cowherd killed me.'

The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to that son of a deva. At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the Dhamma. The son of a deva, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), departed with a smile.

Because he knows all that is to be known (ñeyya-dhamma), and because he knows by means of the knowledge ending in liberation (omniscience), he is called 'Buddha.' Or, because he himself realized the Four Truths and made other beings realize them, for these reasons also he is called 'Buddha.' To make this meaning known, the entire method of the Mahāniddesa and Paṭisambhidāmagga which states, 'He is the Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is the Buddha because he awakens the generation,' should be expanded upon.

'Bhagavā' is a term of respect and reverence for the Exalted One, the most excellent of beings, distinguished by his qualities. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
95:
The word "Bhagavā" signifies an excellent meaning; the word "Bhagavā" signifies a supreme meaning. He is called "Bhagavā" because He is revered and is endowed with reverence.

Names are of four kinds: (1) Āvatthika (functional/situational), (2) Liṅgika (characteristic), (3) Nemittika (qualitative/causal), and (4) Adhiccasamuppanna (arbitrary/coincidental). An arbitrary name (adhiccasamuppanna) means a name given according to one's wish (yadicchaka) in worldly usage. Among these, "calf, steer, bull," etc., are functional names. "Staff-bearer, umbrella-bearer, crested, elephant (possessor of a trunk)," etc., are characteristic names. "Possessor of the triple knowledge, possessor of the six supernormal powers," etc., are qualitative names. "Sirivaḍḍhaka, Dhanavaḍḍhaka," etc., are arbitrary names given without regard to the meaning of the words.

This name "Bhagavā" is a qualitative name (nemittika). It was not given by His mother Mahāmāyā, nor by His father King Suddhodana, nor by His eighty thousand relatives. Nor was it given by special deities such as Sakka or Santusita. Regarding this, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said: "The name Bhagavā was not given by His mother... it is a realized designation (sacchikāpaññatti) of the Blessed Buddhas, attained at the foot of the Bodhi tree along with the acquisition of omniscience; that is, the name Bhagavā."

This name is a qualitative name arising from certain attributes. To show those attributes, the ancient teachers spoke this verse:
"Because He has fortune (bhagī), associates with the Dhamma (bhajī), possesses shares (bhāgī), is a divider (vibhattavā),
has broken [defilements] (akāsi bhagga), is revered (garū), is fortunate (bhāgyavā),
has well-developed Himself through many methods,
and has gone to the end of existences (bhavantago), He is called 'Bhagavā'."

The meaning of those various terms should be understood according to the method taught in the Mahāniddesa.

This is another method:
"Because He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken [defilements] (bhaggavā), is endowed [with qualities] (yutto),
is a divider of shares (bhagehi ca vibhattavā),
is associated [with the Dhamma] (bhattavā), and has gone beyond existences having vomited [craving] (vantagamano),
He is therefore called 'Bhagavā' in existences."

In that verse, it should be understood according to the rules of grammar such as vaṇṇāgama (augmentation of letters) and vaṇṇavipariyaya (transposition of letters) found in the Nirutti texts, or by taking the method of pisodarādi found in the grammar texts. Since He possesses fortune (bhāgya)—namely, the perfections such as generosity and virtue that produce mundane and supramundane happiness—He should be called "Bhāgyavā", but it should be known that He is called "Bhagavā" by changing the letters.

Because He [has destroyed] greed, hatred, delusion, perverted attention, lack of shame (ahirika), lack of fear (anottappa), anger, enmity, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, hypocrisy, stubbornness, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence...
96:
...craving, ignorance, the three unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, uneven perceptions, thoughts, proliferation (papañca), the four perversions, taints (āsava), ties (gantha), floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), wrong courses (agati), the arising of craving, grasping (upādāna), the five mental barrennesses (cetokhīla), shackles (vinibandha), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), delight (abhinandana), the six roots of contention (vivādamūla), the body of craving, the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya), the eight wrongnesses (micchatta), the nine roots of craving, the ten unwholesome courses of action, views, the 108 varieties of craving, and all hundreds of thousands of defilements that cause distress and fever; or in brief, He has broken the five Maras: Kilesamāra, Abhisaṅkhāramāra, Khandhamāra, Maccumāra, and Devaputtamāra. Because He has thus broken these dangers (parissaya), He should be called "Bhaggavā", but He is called "Bhagavā". In this sense, it is said:

"He has broken lust, broken hatred, broken delusion, and is taintless.
Evil states have been broken by that Blessed One; therefore He is called 'Bhagavā'."

By His being fortunate (bhāgyavantatā), the perfection of His form-body (rūpakāya-sampatti), endowed with the major and minor marks produced by the momentum of merit, is indicated. By His having broken faults (bhaggadosatā), the perfection of His Dhamma-body (dhammakāya-sampatti) is indicated. Likewise, it indicates His being highly esteemed by the wise of the world, His being approachable by humans, devas, and Brahmas, His ability to remove the physical and mental suffering of those who approach Him, His being a benefactor through the gifts of material things and the Dhamma, and His ability to connect [beings] with mundane and supramundane happiness.

In the world, the word "Bhaga" is applied to six things: lordship (issariya), Dhamma, fame (yasa), splendor (sirī), success of wishes (kāma), and effort (payatta). The Blessed One possesses supreme lordship over His own mind, and the mundane supernormal powers such as aṇimā (minuteness) and laghimā (lightness) in their complete form. Likewise, He has the supramundane Dhamma; fame that pervades the three worlds, is attained through true qualities, and is exceedingly pure; the splendor of all major and minor limbs, capable of producing clarity of the eyes in those who look upon His form-body; the success of wishes (kāma) in that whatever He desired or longed for, whether for His own benefit or the benefit of others, was accomplished exactly so; and the effort (payatta) known as right effort (sammāvāyāma), which is the cause of His being revered by the whole world. Because He is endowed with these "Bhaga" qualities, He is called "Bhagavā" in the sense that these glories belong to Him.

Furthermore, [He is called "Bhagavā" because He has analyzed] all phenomena by their divisions such as wholesome, etc.; or wholesome and other phenomena by their divisions such as aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, and dependent origination; or the Noble Truth of Suffering by the meanings of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changing; or the Truth of Origin by the meanings of accumulation, source, bond, and obstacle...
97:
The Blessed One has analyzed, opened up, and taught the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) in the sense of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless; and the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) in the sense of leading out, cause, seeing, and predominance. Therefore, where 'Vibhattavā' (the analyzer) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Furthermore, that Blessed One associated with, resorted to, and frequently practiced the divine abidings (divvavihāra), the Brahma abidings (brahmavihāra), and the noble abidings (ariyavihāra); the seclusion of body (kāyaviveka), the seclusion of mind (cittaviveka), and the seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhiviveka); the void (suññata), the desireless (appaṇihita), and the signless (animitta) liberations (vimokkha); and other mundane and supramundane states of the superior man (uttarimanussadhamma). Therefore, where 'Bhattavā' (the possessor/associator) should be said, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Furthermore, because he has vomited out the 'going' known as craving (taṇhā) in the three realms of existence by means of the Noble Path, where 'Bhavesu vantagamano' (one who has vomited the going in existences) should be said, the letter 'Bha' is taken from the word 'Bhava', 'Ga' from 'Gamana', and 'Va' from 'Vanta', and by lengthening the 'Va', he is called 'Bhagavā'. Just as in the world, where 'Mehanassa khassa mālā' should be said, it is called 'Mekhalā' (girdle).

'So imaṃ lokaṃ' means that Blessed One [teaches] this world. Now he points out the world to be mentioned. 'Sadevakaṃ' means the world together with devas; likewise, 'Samārakaṃ' with Māra, 'Sabrahmakaṃ' with Brahmā, 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ' with recluses and brahmins. 'Pajā' refers to the world of beings, so called because they are born (pajātattā); 'that generation' (taṃ pajaṃ). 'Sadevamanussaṃ' means with devas and humans. Therein, by the word 'Sadevaka', the devas of the five sensual realms are to be understood. By 'Samāraka', the deva of the sixth sensual realm (Vasavatti Māra) is to be understood. By 'Sabrahmaka', the Brahmās such as those of the Brahma-kāyika realm are to be understood. By 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ', the recluses and brahmins who are opponents and enemies of the Dispensation are to be understood, as well as those recluses and brahmins who have stilled and removed evil. By 'Pajā', the world of beings (sattaloka) is to be understood. By 'Sadevamanussaṃ', the devas by convention (sammutideva) and the remaining humans are to be understood. Thus, it should be understood that here, the world of locations (okāsaloka) is taken by three terms, and the world of beings (sattaloka) is taken by two terms by way of generation (pajā).

Another method: By taking 'Sadevaka', the formless deva world (arūpāvacara) is taken. By 'Samāraka', the six sensual deva worlds are taken. By 'Sabrahmaka', the fine-material Brahma world (rūpībrahmaloka) is taken. By 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa' etc., the human world together with devas by convention is taken by way of the four assemblies, or all the remaining world of beings.
98:
Moreover, among these words starting with 'Sadevakaṃ', by the word 'Sadevaka', the Blessed One's fame spread abroad, establishing the fact that he has directly realized the entire world by way of the highest limit. After that fame had spread, there might be some who think: 'Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sensual deva realms, a ruler (vasavatti); has he also been realized by this Blessed One?' Dispelling their doubt, the fame spread that he realized the world 'together with Māra' (Samārakaṃ). Then there might be some who think: 'Mahābrahmā is of great power, he can pervade a thousand world systems with light with one finger, with two... up to ten fingers he can pervade ten thousand world systems with light, and he experiences the incomparable bliss of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti); has he also been realized by this Blessed One?' Dispelling their doubt, the fame spread that he realized the world 'together with Brahmā' (Sabrahmakaṃ). Furthermore, there might be some who think: 'There are many recluses and brahmins who are opponents of the Dispensation; have they also been realized by this Blessed One?' Dispelling their doubt, the fame spread that he realized 'the generation together with recluses and brahmins' (Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ). Thus, having shown the realization of the most eminent individuals, he then included the devas by convention (sammutideva) and the remaining humans, showing the realization of the rest of the world of beings by way of the highest limit, and the fame spread that he realized the world 'together with devas and humans' (Sadevamanussaṃ). This is the sequence of connection (anusandhi) here.

In the words 'Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti': 'Sayaṃ' means by himself (not being led by another). 'Abhiññā' means having known with higher knowledge. 'Sacchikatvā' means having made manifest (realized for himself); by this, knowledge through inference (anumāna) and so on is excluded. 'Pavedeti' means he makes known, informs, declares.

'That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning... good in the end' means that the Blessed One, out of compassion (karuṇā) for beings, teaches the Dhamma even after relinquishing the incomparable bliss of seclusion (the bliss of the attainment of fruition). And when he teaches that Dhamma, whether a little or much, he teaches it only in such a way that it is good in the beginning and so forth.

How? Even a single verse is good in the beginning with the first line, good in the middle with the second and third lines, and good in the end with the last line, because of the Dhamma's goodness in all respects. A sutta with a single sequence of connection is good in the beginning with the introduction (nidāna), good in the end with the conclusion (nigamana), and good in the middle with the rest. A sutta with various sequences of connection is good in the beginning with the first sequence, good in the end with the last sequence, and good in the middle with the remaining sequences. The entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is also good in the beginning with virtue (sīla) which is its benefit, good in the middle with calm (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala), and good in the end with Nibbāna. Or, it is good in the beginning with virtue and concentration (samādhi), good in the middle with insight and the path, and good in the end with the fruit and Nibbāna...
99:
...is good in the end. Alternatively, it is good in the beginning because of the excellence of the Blessed One's Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship or His Omniscience; it is good in the middle because of the excellence of the Dhamma known as the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna; and it is good in the end because of the Sangha's excellent practice.

For one who, having heard that Dhamma, practices to reach the state of truth, it is good in the beginning because of the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi); it is good in the middle because of Paccekabodhi; and it is good in the end because of Sāvakabodhi.

In another way, this Dhamma of the Dispensation brings benefit even by mere hearing, as it can dispel the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) when heard; thus, it is good in the beginning. When practiced, it brings benefit through practice because it brings the happiness of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā); thus, it is good in the middle. When the fruit of practice is completed after such training, it brings benefit through the fruit of practice because it brings the state of steadfastness (tādibhāva) which is unshaken by worldly conditions; thus, it is good in the end.

In another way, this Dhamma of the Dispensation is good in the beginning through the purity of its origin, as it originates from the Buddha; it is good in the middle through the purity of its benefit; and it is good in the end through the purity of its function. Therefore, it should be understood that when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, whether briefly or extensively, He teaches only that which is good in the beginning and so forth.

Regarding the terms 'sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ' (with meaning and phrasing) and so forth: because He makes known the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path through various methods when teaching this Dhamma, that holy life is called 'sāttha' because of the perfection of its meaning (attha) as appropriate, and 'sabyañjana' because of the perfection of its phrasing (byañjana). It is called 'sāttha' because it is well-connected with the meanings of summarizing, elaborating, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and designating. It is called 'sabyañjana' because of the perfection of syllables, words, sentences, modes, linguistics (nirutti), and descriptions (niddesa). It is 'sāttha' because of the profundity of meaning and the profundity of penetration. It is 'sabyañjana' because of the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching. It is 'sāttha' because it is the object of the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) and the discrimination of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā). It is 'sabyañjana' because it is the object of the discrimination of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā) and the discrimination of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā). It is 'sāttha' because it inspires the confidence of the investigative people, as it is to be known by the wise. It is 'sabyañjana' because it inspires the confidence of worldly people, as it is worthy of faith. It is 'sāttha' because of its profound intention. It is 'sabyañjana' because of its clear phrasing. It is 'kevalaparipuṇṇa' (wholly complete) in the sense of being entirely full because there is nothing to be added. It is 'parisuddha' (pure) in the sense of being faultless because there is nothing to be removed. It is called 'brahmacariya' (holy life) because it is encompassed by the three trainings (sikkhā), because it should be practiced by the noble ones such as the Buddhas, and because it is the conduct of those noble ones. Therefore, it is said: 'He makes known the holy life... with meaning and phrasing...'

Furthermore, it is good in the beginning because He teaches it with its origin and background story. It is good in the middle because it is suitable for those to be led (veneyya), because the meaning is unerring, and because it is endowed with reasons and examples. It is good in the end because of the listeners' attainment of faith...
100:
With the conclusion, He also teaches the Dhamma that is good in its end. In teaching thus, He proclaims the holy life (brahmacariya). That holy life is said to be 'with meaning' (sāttha) because of the manifestation of the attainment of the path and fruit through practice; 'with phrasing' (sabyañjana) because of the manifestation of the scriptures through learning (pariyatti); 'entirely complete' (kevalaparipuṇṇa) because it is endowed with the five aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla), etc.; and 'pure' (parisuddha) because it is free from defilements, exists for the purpose of crossing over from the round of suffering, and is independent of worldly gains. It is called 'brahmacariya' because of its noble meaning and because it is the practice of those who have become noble—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, 'That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... and proclaims the holy life.'

'Sādhu kho pana' means it is truly excellent, bringing welfare and bringing happiness. 'Tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ' refers to those like the Venerable Gotama, who are known as Arahants in the world due to their attainment of true virtues. 'Dassanaṃ hoti' means that after opening the clear and serene eyes and forming the intention, 'Even the mere sight is good,' the Brahmin Verañja approached where the Blessed One was.

'Yena' is an instrumental case used in the sense of the locative. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as, 'Where the Blessed One was, there he approached.' Or, it should be understood as, 'For the reason that the Blessed One should be approached by gods and humans, for that reason he approached.' And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? He should be approached with the desire to attain various special qualities, just as a flock of birds approaches a great tree that is always laden with fruit, desiring to enjoy the sweet fruit. 'Upasaṅkami' means he went. 'Upasaṅkamitvā' indicates the completion of the approach. Or, it means that after going in this way, he went to a place even closer, known as the presence of the Blessed One.

He exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One. Just as the Blessed One asked him whether he was enduring (khamanīya) and so on, so too did he share in the joy with the Blessed One; it was like cold water mixing with hot water to become one. Because it generates joy known as rapture and gladness, and because it is suitable for rejoicing, it is called 'sammodanīya' (pleasant). Because it is worthy of being maintained and continued for a very long time due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, and because it is worthy of being remembered, it is called 'sāraṇīya' (memorable). Or, it is called 'sammodanīya' because it is pleasant to hear.
101:
It is called 'sāraṇīya' (memorable) because it is worthy of being remembered repeatedly with happiness. Likewise, it is called 'sammodanīya' because of the purity of phrasing (byañjana), and 'sāraṇīya' because of the purity of meaning (attha). Having thus exchanged these pleasant and memorable words in many ways, having concluded and finished them, he sat down at one side (ekamantaṃ), desiring to ask about the matter for which he had come.

The word 'ekamantaṃ' is a neuter usage (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa) modifying the act of sitting, as in the phrase 'the moon and sun revolve unevenly (vissamaṃ).' Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: he sat in such a way that his sitting was 'at one side.' Alternatively, this is an accusative case used in the sense of the locative. 'Nisīdi' means he sat down nearby. Indeed, wise men, having approached a person worthy of respect, sit at one side due to their skill in seating. This Brahmin was also one of them; therefore, he sat at one side.

How does one sit so that it is called sitting 'at one side'? It is by avoiding the six faults of sitting. They are: too far, too near, upwind, on a high place, directly in front, and directly behind. For if one sits too far, one must speak with a loud voice if one wishes to speak. If one sits too near, one causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one disturbs with body odor. If one sits on a high place, it shows a lack of respect. If one sits directly in front, one must look eye-to-eye if one wishes to see. If one sits directly behind, one must stretch the neck to see. Therefore, this Brahmin also sat avoiding these six faults of sitting. Thus it is said, 'He sat down at one side.'

In the phrase 'Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho verañjo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca,' the word 'etaṃ' indicates the meaning now to be spoken. The letter 'da' is a euphonic particle (padasandhikara). 'Avoca' means he said. 'Sutaṃ me taṃ' is 'sutaṃ me etaṃ,' meaning 'This has been heard by me,' and it shows the meaning now to be spoken. With the words 'Bho Gotama,' he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.

Now, desiring to show what he had heard, he said 'Na samaṇo gotamo' and so on. In that passage, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: 'Brāhmaṇe' refers to those who are Brahmins by birth. 'Jiṇṇe' refers to those who are decayed, having reached the state of broken teeth and so on due to old age. 'Vuḍḍhe' refers to those who have reached the limit of growth of their limbs. 'Mahallake' refers to those who are elderly by birth, meaning those who have been born for a long time. 'Addhagate' means those who have reached a long period...
102:
"Addhagato" means having reached a long period of time; specifically, it means having reached a time after two or three generations of kings have passed. "Vayoanuppatto" means having well reached the final stage of life. The final stage (pacchima-vaya) refers to the last third of a hundred-year lifespan.

Alternatively, "jiṇṇo" means one who is ancient, following a lineage that has existed for a long time. "Vuḍḍho" refers to one who is endowed with growth in virtues such as morality (sīla) and conduct. "Mahallako" refers to one who is endowed with greatness of wealth and possessions, having much property and many enjoyments. "Addhagato" refers to one who has reached the path, meaning one who lives without transgressing the boundaries of the Brahmins' practices and conduct. "Vayoanuppatto" refers to one who has successively reached the state of being aged after birth, or the final stage of life; thus should the connection of meaning be understood here.

Now, the terms such as "abhivādeti" (salutes) should be understood in connection with the word "na" (not), as mentioned in the context of "na samaṇo gotamo" (the ascetic Gotama does not...), meaning: "He does not salute, nor does he rise from his seat to welcome, nor does he invite with a seat, saying, 'Let the venerable ones sit here.'" For here, the word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of clarification (vibhāvana), as in "Is form permanent or (vā) impermanent?" and so on. Having said this, seeing the Blessed One not performing salutation and so on towards him, he said: "Master Gotama, that is indeed so." What I have heard is exactly as it is; what I heard and what I now see coincide and agree; they are one in meaning. Concluding what he had heard with what he saw, and wishing to criticize, he said: "Master Gotama, this [behavior] is indeed not perfect." That not performing salutation and so on is indeed improper.

Then the Blessed One, without falling into the fault of self-exaltation or disparaging others, with a heart cooled by compassion, wishing to dispel that Brahmin's ignorance (moha) and show the propriety of his own non-action, said: "Brahmin, I... his head would also split." The summary meaning of those words is: "Brahmin, even when I look with the unobstructed eye of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), I do not see anyone in this world with its devas and so on, whom I should salute, or rise for, or invite with a seat. It is not surprising that I, having now attained omniscience, do not see such a person worthy of humble respect. Indeed, even when I was just born and walked seven steps facing north and surveyed the ten thousand world systems, even then I did not see such a person in this world with its devas and so on..."
103:
"...whom I should salute, or rise for, or invite with a seat. At that time, even the Great Brahma, a liberated one (khīṇāsava) with a lifespan of sixteen thousand aeons, with palms joined in reverence, worshipped me, saying: 'You are the Great Man in the world; you are the foremost, the eldest, and the best in the world with its devas; there is no one superior to you,' and he was filled with joy. At that time too, seeing no one superior to myself, I uttered these bold words: 'I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world.' Thus, even for me as a newborn, there was no person worthy of receiving my salutation and so on; how then, having now attained omniscience, should I salute, or rise for, or invite anyone with a seat? Therefore, Brahmin, do not expect such humble respect from the Tathāgata. For, Brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to salute, or rise for, or invite any person with a seat, that person's head would split from the neck and fall instantly to the ground at the end of the night, like a palm fruit whose stalk has loosened and detached."

Even when this was said, the Brahmin, due to his lack of wisdom, failed to recognize the Tathāgata's status as the eldest in the world. Unable to bear those words, he said: "Master Gotama is 'arasarūpa' (tasteless/lacking essence)." This was his intention: In the world, the acts of saluting, rising, joining palms, and showing respect are called "sāmaggirasa" (the essence of harmony). Since these are not found in Master Gotama, therefore Master Gotama is "arasarūpa" (tasteless), "arasajātika" (of a tasteless nature), and "arasasabhāva" (of a tasteless character). Then the Blessed One, in order to soften the Brahmin's mind and avoiding direct confrontation, wishing to show the meaning of those words in another way in relation to himself, said: "Brahmin, there is indeed a reason (pariyāya) why one might say so," and so on.

In that context, "pariyāya" means reason (kāraṇa). This word "pariyāya" is used in the senses of teaching (desanā), turn (vāra), and reason (kāraṇa). In passages such as "Remember this as the Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya," it is used in the sense of teaching. In passages such as "Ānanda, whose turn (pariyāya) is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?" it is used in the sense of turn (vāra). In passages such as "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One state another reason (pariyāya) so that this Saṅgha of bhikkhus may remain established in the knowledge," it is used in the sense of reason (kāraṇa). Here, it is used in the sense of reason. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: "Brahmin, there is indeed this reason by which [one might say of] me..."
104:
## 
“A person who says, ‘The Venerable Gotama is devoid of taste,’ would be speaking rightly; he would be one who could be counted as speaking the truth. What is the reason for this? Brahmin, the relish for forms... the relish for tangibles, which arise in worldlings, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata.

What is meant by this? Brahmin, worldlings who are considered noble by birth, such as royalty, or by rebirth among the devas, experience relish for forms and so forth. This relish, known as the enjoyment of sensual happiness, arises from enjoying with weak craving, delighting with strong craving, and being attached with powerful lust to objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. These relishes pull one toward various existences as if binding the neck of this world of beings and dragging it along. Because they arise from the harmony of the base, such as the eye, and the object, such as form, they are also called ‘relish of harmony’ (sāmaggirasa). All these relishes have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Even though it should be said, ‘I have abandoned them,’ the Buddha teaches the Dhamma without exalting himself by using the term ‘mine.’ Or rather, this is the elegance of the Blessed One’s teaching (desanāvilāsa).

In this context, ‘pahīnā’ means departed from the mental continuum or abandoned. In this sense, the possessive case should be understood as having the sense of the instrumental. Because they have their roots, consisting of craving and ignorance, cut by the sword of the Noble Path, they are ‘uprooted’ (ucchinnamūla). Because their basis is made like that of a palm tree, they are ‘made like a palm-tree stump’ (tālāvatthukata). Just as a palm tree uprooted with its roots cannot grow again, so too the relish for forms and so forth, uprooted with their roots by the sword of the Noble Path, remain only as a basis in the mental continuum because they had arisen before; thus they are called ‘tālāvatthukata.’ Or, because they are of a nature not to grow again, like a palm tree with its head cut off, they are ‘tālāvatthukata.’ Since they have been made like a palm-tree stump, they have reached the state of non-existence. Therefore, he said, ‘made non-existent’ (anabhāvaṅkata). The word analysis here is ‘anu + abhāvaṃ + katā’. There is also a variant reading ‘anabhāvaṃ gatā,’ meaning ‘reached the state of non-existence.’ ‘Āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā’ means having the nature of not arising again in the future. For how can those relishes that have reached non-existence arise again? Therefore, he said, ‘made non-existent, not subject to future arising.’

Brahmin, this is the reason why one speaking rightly could say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is devoid of taste.’ But it is not for the reason you intended (such as not showing respect). Why did the Blessed One speak thus? If the Blessed One spoke in this way, would it not mean he is admitting that the absence of the relish of harmony (such as showing respect), which the Brahmin mentioned, exists in him?
105:
Regarding the ‘relish of harmony’ (sāmaggirasa) mentioned by the Brahmin (such as bowing, welcoming, etc.), when the Blessed One said, ‘But it is not for the reason you intended,’ one might ask: Is he admitting that this relish of harmony exists in him? It is not so. For if a person who is capable of performing that relish of harmony does not do so, he should be called ‘devoid of taste’ (arasarūpa) due to that absence. However, the Blessed One is no longer capable of doing so. Therefore, to show his inability to do so, he said, ‘But it is not for the reason you intended.’ The reason for which you call me ‘devoid of taste’ is not applicable to us.

Thus, the Brahmin, unable to attribute his intended meaning of ‘devoid of taste’ to the Blessed One, spoke again in another way: ‘The Venerable Gotama is devoid of enjoyment’ (nibbhoga), and so forth. In all these methods, the sequence of connection should be understood as previously explained, and the intended meaning of the speech should be known thus: The Brahmin considers the acts of bowing to elders and so forth in the world as the ‘enjoyment of harmony’ (sāmaggipribhoga), and because of the absence of these acts, he calls the Blessed One ‘nibbhoga.’ The Blessed One, however, seeing in himself the absence of the enjoyment of craving and lust (chandarāgapribhoga) for forms and so forth, admits to this in another sense.

Again, the Brahmin, seeing that the Blessed One does not perform the customary acts of bowing to elders as people do in the world, calls the Blessed One a ‘teacher of non-action’ (akiriyavāda). The Blessed One, because he teaches the non-doing of bodily misconduct and so forth, seeing that ‘non-action’ in himself, admits to it in another sense. In this context, bodily misconduct should be understood as the intentions of killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. Verbal misconduct should be understood as the intentions of false speech, slandering speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. Mental misconduct should be understood as covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view. Setting aside these states, the remaining unwholesome states should be understood as ‘various evil, unwholesome states.’

Again, the Brahmin, not seeing those acts of bowing and so forth in the Blessed One, thinks, ‘Because of this Venerable Gotama, the continuity of the world is cut off,’ and calls the Blessed One a ‘teacher of annihilation’ (ucchedavāda). The Blessed One, however, teaches the annihilation (uccheda) of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure in the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed, and the annihilation of hatred arising in the two unwholesome consciousnesses, by means of the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). He teaches the annihilation of delusion, the root of all unwholesome states, without remainder, by means of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Setting aside these three, the remaining evil, unwholesome states are annihilated by the four paths accordingly...
106:
## 
(The Blessed One) teaches the cutting off (of unwholesome states) by means of the four paths. Therefore, seeing that annihilationism (the teaching of cutting off) within himself, he acknowledges it through another sense as well.

Furthermore, the Brahmin, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama seems to be disgusted by this social conduct of paying respect to those senior in age; it is because of such disgust that he does not perform it," addressed the Blessed One as "Jegucchī" (one who is disgusted). The Blessed One is indeed disgusted by bodily misconduct and so forth. What does this mean? Just as a man who desires to be adorned is disgusted by and ashamed of excrement, the Blessed One is disgusted by and ashamed of the three types of bodily misconduct, the four types of verbal misconduct, the three types of mental misconduct, and—excluding those misconducts—all the remaining unwholesome (akusala) states which are called 'evil' (pāpaka) due to their inferior nature and 'unwholesome' because they arise from lack of skill (moha), including their attainment, possession, and presence. Therefore, seeing that state of being disgusted (jegucchita) within himself, he acknowledges it through another sense as well. In that statement, the instrumental case in "kāyaduccaritena" should be understood in the sense of the accusative (as the object).

Again, the Brahmin, not seeing the act of paying respect and so forth in the Blessed One, thought, "This ascetic Gotama destroys this practice performed for the elders in the world," or else, "Because he does not perform this act of respect, he deserves to be disciplined (restrained)." Thus, he addressed the Blessed One as "Venayika." The meaning of the word "Venayika" is: because he destroys, it is "vinaya"; it means he destroys. "Vinaya" itself is called "Venayika." Alternatively, because he deserves discipline (vinaya), he is "Venayika"; it means he deserves restraint. However, the Blessed One is called "Venayika" because he teaches the Dhamma for the destruction and subsiding of lust and so forth. This alone is the meaning of the word in this context. Because he teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of destruction, he is called "Venayika." The formation of derivative (taddhita) suffixes is indeed diverse! The Blessed One, seeing that state of being a "Venayika" within himself, acknowledges it through another sense as well.

Furthermore, the Brahmin thought that those who perform acts of respect such as bowing make the elders pleased and joyful, whereas those who do not perform them cause them to be tormented, harassed, and dejected. Since the Blessed One does not perform those acts of respect, the Brahmin thought, "This person torments the elders," or, because he is devoid of the conduct of virtuous men, he thought, "This is a wretched man (kapaṇapurisa)," and thus addressed the Blessed One as "Tapassī." The meaning of the word "Tapassī" is: because he torments, it is "tapa"; it means he provokes or harasses. That name "tapa" is a name for the non-performance of respectful conduct. Because he has that "tapa," he is "Tapassī." In the second alternative meaning, without considering the literal grammar, a wretched man in the world is called "Tapassī." As for the Blessed One, because those unwholesome states torment the world...
107:
## 
...they are called "tapaniya" (tormenting). Because he has abandoned those unwholesome states, he is known as "Tapassī." Therefore, seeing that state of being a "Tapassī" within himself, he acknowledges it through another sense as well. The meaning of the word here is: because they torment, they are "tapa"; this is a designation for unwholesome states. Indeed, it has been said: "He torments here, he torments hereafter." Thus, because he has destroyed, abandoned, and crushed those torments (tapa), he is a "Tapassī."

Furthermore, the Brahmin, thinking that the act of paying respect and so forth leads to the attainment of a womb in the deva world and the obtaining of rebirth in the deva world, and seeing the absence of such acts in the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as "Apagabbha" (one who is free from the womb). Or, out of anger, wishing to point out a fault in the Blessed One's taking of rebirth in a mother's womb, he spoke thus. The meaning of the word here is: because he is departed from the womb, he is "Apagabbha"; the intention is that he is one who is incapable of reaching birth in the deva world. Or, because he has a low birth, he is "Apagabbha"; the intention is that because he is outside of birth in the deva world, he will be a partaker of a low birth in the future, or that his stay in the mother's womb was low. However, for the Blessed One, because lying in a womb in the future has been removed, he, seeing that state of being "Apagabbha" within himself, acknowledges it through another sense. In this context, the meaning of the words, "Brahmin, for whomsoever lying in a womb and re-existence in a future birth have been abandoned," should be understood thus: Brahmin, for whichever person lying in a womb in the future and re-existence in a new birth have been abandoned because their causes have been destroyed by the unsurpassed Path. Here, by the term "gabbhaseyya" (lying in a womb), the viviparous (jalābuja) mode of birth is taken. By the term "punabbhavābhinibbatti" (re-existence in a new birth), the other three modes of birth are also included.

Alternatively, "gabbhaseyya" means the lying of the embryo (gabbha). "Punabbhavābhinibbatti" means re-existence itself being a new birth; thus should the meaning be understood. Just as when "viññāṇaṭṭhiti" (station of consciousness) is mentioned, there is no station other than consciousness itself, so too here, it should be understood that there is no "lying" other than the "womb" itself. As for "new birth" (abhinibbatti), there is both re-existence in a future birth and non-existence in a future birth. Here, however, only re-existence in a future birth is intended. Therefore, it is said: "Re-existence itself being a new birth is punabbhavābhinibbatti."

In this way, although the Brahmin had been insulting him from the moment he arrived with the eight grounds of abuse, such as "arasarūpatā" (tastelessness) and so forth, the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma...
108:
The Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata, who has come along with the previous Buddhas such as Vipassī and others, looking with a cool eye of compassion upon beings, has attained the elegance of teaching by realizing the remainderless Dhamma-element. Because of his perfect realization of that Dhamma-element, like the full moon rising in a cloudless sky or like the sun shining in the autumn season, he dispels the darkness of the heart of the Brahmin, showing those very grounds for abuse in various ways as something else.

Once again, wishing to manifest the pervasion of his compassion, the quality of 'Tādi' (equanimity) obtained through being unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a mind like the earth, and the nature of being free from anger, he thought: 'This Brahmin recognizes his old age only by his grey hair, broken teeth, and wrinkled skin. He does not know himself as followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by disease, struck down by death, being like a stump in the cycle of rebirth, and that having died today, he will tomorrow reach the state of an infant lying on his back. Indeed, he has come to me with great effort; let his coming be fruitful.' Thus, wishing to show his own peerless state of being the first-born in this world, he expanded the Dhamma teaching to the Brahmin in the manner beginning with 'Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇa.'

In that phrase 'Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇa,' 'seyyathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison or simile. 'Pi' is a particle in the sense of praising the first-hatched chick. By both, he shows the meaning: 'Brahmin, just as that first-hatched chick is called the eldest.' In the passage 'eight or ten or twelve eggs of a hen,' it should be understood that although a hen's eggs may be fewer or more than the stated number, it is said thus for the sake of smooth speech. Only when said thus is there smoothness of speech in the world. 'Tānassu' means 'those eggs should be.' 'Well sat upon by the hen' means well sat upon by that mother hen spreading her wings over those eggs. 'Well warmed' (pariseditāni) means well-steamed all around by letting them receive the proper temperature from time to time. 'Well seasoned' (paribhāvitāni) means well-infused all around from time to time, meaning they are made to take the scent of the hen.

Now, because those eggs are protected by the hen in these three ways, they do not become rotten. The moist moisture in them also becomes exhausted. The shell becomes thin. The tips of the claws and the beak become hard. The chicks reach maturity. Because the shell is thin, the light from outside appears within. Then those chicks...
109:
'For a long time indeed we have lain in a cramped place with cramped hands and feet; and this light from outside is seen; now we shall live happily in this place.' Thus, desiring to come out, they kick the shell with their feet and stretch their necks. Due to that kicking and stretching, the eggshell breaks into two. The chicks, flapping their wings and chirping according to that moment, come out. Among those chicks coming out in this way, whichever one comes out first is called the 'eldest' (jeṭṭha). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to establish his own state of being the eldest by that simile, asked the Brahmin: 'Among those chicks... what should he be called?' In that passage, 'kukkuṭacchāpakānaṃ' means the chicks. 'Kinti svassa vacanīyo' means what should that chick be called—should he be called the eldest (jeṭṭha) or the youngest (kaniṭṭha)? The remaining words have clear meanings.

Then the Brahmin said: 'He should be called the eldest, Master Gotama.' 'Master Gotama, he should be called the eldest. Why? Because he is the eldest among them; therefore, he is the most senior among them.' Then the Blessed One, applying the simile, said: 'Even so, Brahmin, I...' and so on. Just as that chick arrives at the designation of 'eldest,' even so, I among the generation fallen into ignorance (are the eldest). 'Avijjāgatāya' means among those who have reached non-knowledge (aññāṇa) called ignorance. 'Pajāya' is a designation for beings. Therefore, here the meaning should be understood as: among beings who have entered inside the eggshell of ignorance. 'Aṇဍဘူတာယ' (aṇḍabhūtāya) means born in the egg, well-produced. Just as some beings born in an egg are called 'egg-born' (aṇḍabhūta), even so, this entire generation is called 'egg-born' because they are produced in the eggshell of ignorance. 'Pariyonaddhāya' means enveloped, bound, or wrapped all around by that eggshell of ignorance. 'Avijjāṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā' means having broken that eggshell made of ignorance. 'Eko va loke' means in the entire world of beings, I alone am without a second (adutiya). In the phrase 'anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho,' 'anuttaraṃ' means unsurpassed, the most excellent. 'Sammāsambodhiṃ' means the Bodhi-knowledge realized rightly by oneself, or the praised and beautiful Bodhi-knowledge. The word 'Bodhi' refers to the tree, the path, the knowledge of omniscience, and Nirvana. In passages such as 'first enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree' and 'between Gayā and the Bodhi,' Bodhi refers to the tree.
110:
“Bodhi means the knowledge occurring in the four paths,” as found in the Cūḷaniddesa and Khaggavisāṇasutta-niddesa; in such contexts, Bodhi refers to the Path. “The prince, possessed of wisdom as vast as the noble earth, shall reach Bodhi,” as found in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta; in that context, Bodhi refers to Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). “Having reached Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,” in that context, Bodhi refers to Nibbāna. In this specific context, however, the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One is intended. Some teachers say Omniscience is also intended.

Does the Path of Arahatship of disciples or Paccekabuddhas other than the Blessed One constitute unexcelled enlightenment (anuttara-bodhi)? It does not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. Among them, the Path of Arahatship of some disciples bestows only the Fruit of Arahatship; for some, the three knowledges (vijjā); for some, the six supernormal powers (abhiññā); for some, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); and for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). For Paccekabuddhas, it bestows only the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. For Buddhas, however, it bestows the fulfillment of all qualities, just as a king's consecration bestows sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, for anyone other than the Blessed One, there is no unexcelled enlightenment. 'Abhisambuddho' means he has known, he has penetrated, he has attained, he has acquired [it] within his own continuity.

Now, the comparison spoken by the Blessed One starting with “Even so, Brahmin, I...” should be understood by correlating it with the following meaning. Just as that hen performs the three types of actions such as sitting on her eggs, even so, the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta seated on the throne of enlightenment (bodhi-pallaṅka) should be understood as performing the three types of contemplation—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—within his own mental continuity. Just as the eggs do not rot because the hen fulfills the three actions, even so, the non-decline of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) through the Blessed One's fulfillment of the three contemplations should be understood. Just as the moisture in the eggs dries up through the hen's three actions, even so, the drying up of the moisture of craving (taṇhā) that follows the three realms of existence through the Blessed One's fulfillment of the three contemplations is intended. Just as the eggshells become thin through the hen's three actions, even so, the thinning of the eggshell of ignorance (avijjā) through the Blessed One's fulfillment of the three contemplations should be understood. Just as the tips of the claws and the beaks of the chicks become hard and sharp through the hen's three actions, even so, the sharpness, keenness, clarity, and courage of insight knowledge through the Blessed One's fulfillment of the three contemplations should be understood. Just as the time of maturity for the chicks through the hen's three actions, even so, the time of maturity of insight knowledge, the time of its growth, and the time of 'taking the womb' of the Path knowledge through the Blessed One's fulfillment of the three contemplations should be understood.
111:
Then, just as the time when the chick, through the hen's performance of the three actions, breaks the eggshell with the tip of its claws or its beak, flaps its wings, and emerges safely and well, even so, the time when the Blessed One as a Bodhisatta, having 'taken the womb' of insight knowledge through the fulfillment of the three contemplations, breaks the eggshell of ignorance with the Path of Arahatship attained in due order, flaps the wings of the supernormal powers (abhiññā), and safely realizes all the Buddha-qualities should be understood.

“Brahmin, I am the eldest and the best in the world” means: Brahmin, just as among those chicks, the one that first breaks the eggshell and emerges is the eldest, even so, among the generation of beings immersed in ignorance, having broken that eggshell of ignorance and being born first into the noble birth (ariya-jāti), I have reached the designation of being the eldest and the most senior. Because I am unequaled in all qualities, I am called the best.

Thus, the Blessed One, having revealed to the Brahmin his own unexcelled state of being the eldest and the best, now says “Brahmin, my energy was stirred,” etc., in order to show the practice (paṭipadā) by which he attained that state, starting from the preliminary stage. Alternatively, having heard of the Blessed One's unexcelled state of being the eldest and the best, the thought arose in the Brahmin's mind: “By what practice did he attain this?” Knowing the Brahmin's mind, the Blessed One spoke thus, wishing to show: “By this practice, I attained this unexcelled state of being the eldest and the best.”

In that passage, “Brahmin, my energy was stirred” means: Brahmin, this unexcelled state of being the eldest and the best was not attained by me while being lazy, unmindful, with an agitated body, or a distracted mind. On the contrary, for the sake of that attainment, my energy was indeed stirred. Seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, I stirred up energy endowed with four factors; it means I exerted energy that was upheld and not lax.

Because it was stirred up, that energy of mine was unshakable. Not only energy, but my mindfulness was also established by being directed toward the object. Because it was established, it was unforgetting. “The body was tranquil, not agitated” means that through the power of the tranquillity of both mind and body, my body was also tranquil. In this regard, since the physical body (rūpa-kāya) is also tranquil when the mental body (nāma-kāya) is tranquil, he said “the body was tranquil” without making a distinction between the mental and physical bodies. “Not agitated” means that because that body was tranquil, it was free from the fever of defilements; it means it was cool from the heat of defilements. “The mind was concentrated” means my mind was well-placed, as if fixed on a single object. Because it was well-placed, it was one-pointed, unshakable, and steady. This should be understood as the detailed meaning.
112:
It is said, "The body is tranquil." "Without distress" means that because the body is tranquil, it is without distress; it means the distress of defilements has been calmed. "The mind is concentrated and one-pointed" means that my mind also was well-placed, as if it had reached absorption (appanā); because it is well-concentrated, it has one-pointedness and is steady and unshakable. By this much, the practice that precedes jhāna has been taught.

## Discussion on the First Jhāna

Now, wishing to show the distinction beginning with the first jhāna attained through this practice and ending with the three true knowledges (vijjā), he said, "That I...", and so forth. Regarding the meaning of the phrases "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states," etc., it has already been taught in the Vibhaṅga in this way: "Therein, what are sensual pleasures? Desire is a sensual pleasure, lust is a sensual pleasure, desire and lust are sensual pleasures, thought (saṅkappa) is a sensual pleasure, lust is a sensual pleasure, thought and lust are sensual pleasures—these are called sensual pleasures. Therein, what are unwholesome states? Sensual desire (kāmacchanda)... doubt (vicikicchā)—these are called unwholesome states." Thus, one is secluded, or particularly secluded, from these sensual pleasures and these unwholesome states; therefore, it is said, "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states." Even though it has been taught thus, because it is not very clear without the method of the Commentary, I shall explain that meaning by the method of the Commentary alone.

To explain: "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" means being secluded, without, or having moved away from sensual pleasures. The word "eva" (quite/only) here should be understood as having a restrictive (niyama) meaning. Because that word "eva" has a restrictive meaning, it shows that although sensual pleasures are not present at the time of dwelling in the attainment of the first jhāna, they are the opposite of that first jhāna, and that the first jhāna is attained only by the abandonment of sensual pleasures. How is it shown? When the restriction is made as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," this meaning becomes clear. Just as a lamp does not shine when there is darkness, this jhāna cannot occur when those sensual pleasures are present; therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed the opposite of this jhāna. Just as one can reach the further shore only by leaving this shore, this jhāna is attained only by abandoning those sensual pleasures; therefore, the restriction is made.

Here, an objection might be raised: "Why is this word 'eva' mentioned only in the first phrase and not in the second? Can one dwell in the attainment of jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states?"
113:
This should not be understood in that way. Because this first jhāna is the escape from those sensual pleasures, this word "eva" is taught only in the first phrase. Because it is the means for completely transcending the sensual realm (kāmadhātu) and because it is the opposite of sensual lust (kāmarāga), this jhāna is the escape from, or the means of escape from, sensual pleasures alone. It is as he said: "This renunciation (nekkhamma), namely the first jhāna, is the escape from sensual pleasures." In the second phrase also, the word "eva" should be understood as being brought over and applied, just as it is said: "Monks, only here is the first ascetic, only here is the second ascetic." This is because it is impossible to dwell in the attainment of jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states called hindrances (nīvaraṇa), other than these sensual pleasures. Therefore, this word "eva" should be understood in both phrases as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, quite secluded from unwholesome states."

Although all kinds of seclusion, such as seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgaviveka) and bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), are included by the general term "vivicca" (secluded) in both phrases, here only three should be understood: bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka), mental seclusion (cittaviveka), and seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka). By the word "kāmehi" (from sensual pleasures), it should be understood that both objective sensual pleasures (vatthukāma), taught in the Mahāniddesa as "delightful forms are objective sensual pleasures," etc., and defilement-based sensual pleasures (kilesakāma), taught in the Vibhaṅga as "desire is sensual pleasure," etc., are all included. When they are thus included, in the phrase "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," the meaning "quite secluded from objective sensual pleasures" is appropriate. By that phrase, bodily seclusion (kāyaviveka) is taught. In the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states," the meaning "secluded from defilement-based sensual pleasures" or "from all unwholesome states" is appropriate. By that phrase, mental seclusion (cittaviveka) is taught.

Between these two phrases, by the first phrase teaching seclusion from objective sensual pleasures, the abandonment of sensual happiness is shown. By the second phrase teaching seclusion from defilement-based sensual pleasures, the acquisition of the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma) is shown. Furthermore, it should be understood that the first phrase clarifies the abandonment of the objects of defilement (saṅkilesavatthu), and the second phrase clarifies the abandonment of defilements (saṅkilesa); the first phrase clarifies the abandonment of the cause of fickleness, and the second phrase clarifies the abandonment of the cause of foolishness; the first phrase clarifies the purity of preliminary effort (payoga), and the second phrase clarifies the nourishment of the inclination (āsaya). This is the method stated regarding objective sensual pleasures in the word "kāmehi." However, regarding defilement-based sensual pleasures, only sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which has many varieties such as desire and lust, is intended as "sensual pleasure." That sensual pleasure...
114:
Even though it is included within unwholesome states, it is taught separately in the Vibhaṅga as an opponent of jhāna, in such ways as: "In that context, what is sensual desire? What is sensuality?" Alternatively, it is taught in the first phrase because it is defilement-sensuality (kilesakāma), and in the second phrase because it is included within unwholesome states. Because of its many varieties, it is not said in the singular as 'kāmato,' but in the plural as 'kāmehi.' Although other states are also unwholesome, only the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are taught in the Vibhaṅga—in such ways as: "In that context, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire..."—to show that they are the opponents of the jhāna factors to be mentioned later. Indeed, the hindrances are the opponents of the jhāna factors; it means that only the jhāna factors are the opponents that destroy those hindrances. Thus it is said in the Peṭakopadesa: "Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire, rapture (pīti) of ill will, applied thought (vitakka) of sloth and torpor, happiness (sukha) of restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought (vicāra) of doubt."

In this way, by the phrase 'vivicceva kāmehi,' the seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka) of sensual desire is stated. By the phrase 'vivicca akusalehi dhammehi,' the seclusion by suppression of all five hindrances is stated. Alternatively, by way of 'taking what has not been taken' (aggahitaggahaṇa), the first phrase states the seclusion by suppression of sensual desire, and the second phrase states that of the remaining hindrances. Similarly, by the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of greed (lobha) regarding the five objects of sensual pleasure among the three unwholesome roots is stated; by the second phrase, that of hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) regarding objects such as the bases of resentment (āghātavatthu). Or, among states such as the floods (ogha), the first phrase states the seclusion by suppression of the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual lust; the second phrase states that of the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. By the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of craving (taṇhā) and its associated states is stated; by the second phrase, that of ignorance (avijjā) and its associated states. Furthermore, it should be understood that the first phrase states the seclusion by suppression of the eight consciousnesses associated with greed, and the second phrase states that of the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses. This is the explanation of the meaning of 'vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi.'

Having thus shown the factors of abandoning (pahānaṅga) of the first jhāna, he now says 'savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ' (with applied thought and sustained thought) to show the factors of association (sampayogaṅga). Therein, vitakka is the act of thinking; it means thinking about the object (ūhana). That vitakka has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object (abhiniropana) and the function of striking and threshing (āhanana-pariyāhanana). Thus it is said: "By that [vitakka], the practitioner makes the object struck by thought and threshed by thought." It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of bringing the mind to the object (ānayana). Vicāra is the act of wandering on the object...
115:
Wandering along and around the object is called 'anusañcaraṇa.' That vicāra has the characteristic of continued pressure on (examining) the object. It has the function (rasa) of connecting the co-nascent (sahajāta) states to that very object. It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of binding the mind [to the object].

Although these two, vitakka and vicāra, are inseparable in certain types of consciousness, vitakka is the first impact of the mind on the object, being gross like the striking of a bell. Vicāra is the continued binding of the mind, being subtle like the reverberation of the bell.

Between these two, vitakka has the state of vibrating the mind and is thus expansive. It is like the flapping of wings of a large bird wishing to fly into the sky, or like a bee diving towards a lotus with its mind following the scent. Vicāra has a peaceful state as it does not have excessive vibration of the mind. It is like the bird gliding with outstretched wings after having flown up into the sky, or like the bee hovering over the lotus after having dived towards it. The distinction between vitakka and vicāra becomes clear in the first and second jhānas. Thus, because it occurs together with this vitakka and this vicāra, like a tree with its flowers and fruits, this jhāna is called 'savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ.' In the Vibhaṅga, however, the teaching is given by way of person-based discourse (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) in such ways as: "He is endowed with, fully endowed with, this vitakka and this vicāra." Nevertheless, the meaning therein should be understood in the same way as stated here.

In the word 'vivekaja,' seclusion from the hindrances is 'viveka.' Alternatively, the collection of states associated with jhāna that is secluded from the hindrances is 'viveka.' Because it is born from that seclusion or born in that seclusion, it is called 'vivekaja' (born of seclusion). In the word 'pītisukha,' it is 'pīti' (rapture) because it creates fondness (in the body and mind). That pīti has the characteristic of endearing; it has the function of refreshing the body and mind, or the function of pervading; it is manifested as elation. Happiness is 'sukha.' Or, it is 'sukha' because it thoroughly removes the affliction of body and mind. It has the characteristic of being pleasant; it has the function of intensifying associated states; it is manifested as assistance (or support).

Although pīti and sukha are inseparable in some places and exist together, the fondness upon obtaining a desired object is pīti, and the experiencing of the taste of the object already obtained is sukha. Where there is pīti, there is always sukha, but where there is sukha, there is not necessarily pīti. Pīti is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and sukha is included in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Pīti is to be understood like the joy of a person exhausted by a journey upon seeing or hearing of a forest and water. Sukha is to be understood like the happiness when entering the forest shade and using the water. It should be understood that this is said because of their prominence at those respective times. Because this pīti and this sukha exist in this jhāna, this jhāna is called 'pītisukha.'

Alternatively, pīti and sukha are combined as 'pītisukha,' like 'Dhamma-Vinaya' etc. Because this jhāna has pītisukha born of seclusion, it is also called 'vivekajapītisukha.'
116:
Just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, in this first jhāna, joy and happiness are also born of seclusion. Since this joy and happiness exist in this jhāna, it is appropriate to describe it with the single term 'vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ' (joy and happiness born of seclusion). In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated as 'this happiness is accompanied by this joy,' etc., but the meaning there should be understood in this same way.

'First' (pathama) means first according to the numerical order, and also first because this jhāna is attained at the beginning. It is called 'jhāna' because it burns up opposing states (hindrances). By means of this, yogis burn up opposing states; or it means they contemplate the object. Alternatively, it is called 'jhāna' because it closely contemplates the object itself. For that reason, jhāna is said to have the characteristic of 'close contemplation' (upanijjhāyana).

That jhāna is of two types: contemplation of the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and contemplation of characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Among them, the eight attainments together with access concentration are called contemplation of the object. Why? Because they closely contemplate objects such as the kasiṇas. Insight, Path, and Fruit are called contemplation of characteristics. Why? Because they closely contemplate characteristics. Here, insight closely contemplates characteristics such as impermanence. Since the task of insight's contemplation of characteristics is completed by the Path, the Path is called contemplation of characteristics. The Fruit is called contemplation of characteristics because it closely contemplates the true characteristic of cessation (Nibbāna). However, in this context, only contemplation of the object is intended as 'jhāna'.

Here, one might ask: 'What is that jhāna which deserves to be designated as being with initial application, sustained application... joy and happiness?' To answer: Just as in the phrases 'a man with wealth' or 'a man with attendants,' if wealth and attendants are set aside, there is no other person to be designated; similarly, if the states such as initial application are set aside, there is no other jhāna to be designated. However, just as when one says 'a chariot' or 'an army,' the term 'army' is a designation for the army's components, so too here, it should be understood that 'jhāna' is a designation for the five factors. Which five factors? They are initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), joy (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā). These very states are stated as factors in the manner of 'with initial application, with sustained application,' etc. If it is argued that 'one-pointedness is not a factor because it is not mentioned (in the Pali text),' that is not so. Why? Because it is indeed mentioned (elsewhere). In the Vibhaṅga, it is stated: 'Jhāna means initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.' Therefore, although 'with one-pointedness of mind' is not mentioned here, it should be understood that one-pointedness of mind is also a factor according to that statement in the Vibhaṅga.
117:
The intention with which the Blessed One made the summary (uddesa) is the same intention he revealed in that Vibhaṅga. 'Upasampajja' means having approached, having reached. Or it means having fulfilled, having accomplished. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is said: 'Upasampajja means the gain, the regaining, the attainment, the arrival, the touching, the repeated touching, the realization, the fulfillment of the first jhāna.' The meaning of that Vibhaṅga Pali should also be understood in this same way. 'Vihāsi' means that by dwelling in the posture of sitting at the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhi-maṇḍa), being endowed with the jhāna of the aforementioned variety, he accomplished the movement, the occurrence, the protection, the maintenance, the sustenance, the range, and the dwelling of the individual existence. For it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Viharati means he moves, he occurs, he protects, he maintains, he sustains, he ranges, he dwells; therefore it is said "he dwells" (viharati).'

What did the Blessed One do to attain and dwell in this jhāna? He did so by developing a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Which meditation subject? It was the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati). What should another person who desires that jhāna do? Another person should also develop either this meditation subject or one of the others such as the earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa). The method of developing those meditation subjects should be understood exactly as stated in the Visuddhimagga. However, if it were discussed here, the introduction to the Vinaya (Vinaya-nidāna) would become too burdensome; therefore, I shall only clarify the meaning of the Pali text.

## The Discussion on the First Jhāna is Finished.

## Discussion on the Second Jhāna
'Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā' means because of the subsiding, because of the surmounting of these two: initial application and sustained application. It means because of their non-appearance at the moment of the second jhāna. In that second jhāna, it is true that all states of the first jhāna are absent; for the contact (phassa) and so forth that arise in the first jhāna are of one kind, while the contact and so forth that arise here in the second jhāna are of another kind. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated as 'vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā' to show that the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth, which are subsequent to the first jhāna, occurs through the surmounting of the gross factors. 'Ajjhattaṃ' (internally) here means the internal relating to oneself. In the Vibhaṅga, it is stated only as 'ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ' (internally, individually). Since the internal relating to oneself is intended, the meaning here is 'arisen within oneself, produced in one's own continuity'.
118:
Sampasādana (internal confidence) refers to faith (saddhā). Just as a cloth is called 'blue' because of its association with a blue color, this jhāna can also be called 'sampasādana' because of its association with the faith known as sampasādana. Alternatively, it is called 'sampasādana' because it is endowed with the faith called sampasādana, and because it clarifies the mind by stilling the agitation of initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra). In this interpretation, the connection of the words should be understood as 'cetaso sampasādanam' (the confidence of the mind). In the previous interpretation, however, the word 'cetaso' (of the mind) should be associated with 'ekodibhāva' (as the unification of the mind).

In that context, the explanation is: it is called 'ekodi' because it arises as single (being noble). The meaning is that it arises as the highest and most excellent because it is not overridden by initial and sustained application. In the world, the most excellent is also commonly called 'eka' (single). Or it can be said that it arises as single and without a companion because it is devoid of initial and sustained application. Alternatively, 'udi' means it causes associated states to arise; it means it uplifts them. Because it is 'eka' in the sense of being most excellent, and 'udi' because it causes associated states to arise, it is called 'ekodi'. This is a designation for concentration (samādhi). Because it develops this concentration called ekodi, this second jhāna is called 'ekodibhāvum' (the state of unification). Since that unification belongs to the mind, and not to a being or a soul, it is said to be 'cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ' (the unification of the mind).

Now, does this faith not also exist in the first jhāna? And does this concentration named ekodi not also exist there? If so, why is only this second jhāna described as 'sampasādana' and 'cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ'? To answer: that first jhāna is not very clear, like water disturbed by waves due to the agitation of initial and sustained application. Therefore, even though faith is present, it is not called 'sampasādana'. And because it is not very clear, concentration is also not very distinct in that first jhāna; therefore, it is not called 'ekodibhāva'. In this second jhāna, however, faith is powerful, having found its opportunity due to the absence of the obstacles of initial and sustained application. Because of obtaining the companion of powerful faith, concentration also becomes distinct. Therefore, it should be understood that only this second jhāna is described in this way. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is taught only this much: 'Sampasādana is that faith, believing, plunging in, full confidence. Cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ is that stability of mind... right concentration.' It should be understood that this commentary is not contradictory to what is taught there, but rather coincides and agrees with it.

'Avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ' (without initial and sustained application) means that because they have been abandoned by development (bhāvanā), there is no initial application in this jhāna or of this jhāna; thus it is 'avitakka'. In the same way, it is 'avicāra' because there is no sustained application. In the Vibhaṅga also, it is stated: 'Thus this initial application and this sustained application are stilled, are quieted...'
119:
...stilled, subsided, terminated, vanished, dissipated, dried up, withered, and done away with; therefore it is called 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ'.

Here, one might ask: 'Is this meaning not already established by the phrase vitakka-vicārānaṃ vūpasamā (with the stilling of initial and sustained application)? Why then is it said again, avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ?' To answer: That is true; the meaning is established. However, that phrase (vitakka-vicārānaṃ vūpasamā) does not only indicate that meaning. Was it not said that 'vitakka-vicārānaṃ vūpasamā' is stated to show that the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, which are subsequent to the first jhāna, occurs by transcending the gross factors?

Furthermore, this second jhāna is called 'sampasādana' (clarifying) because of the stilling of initial and sustained application, not because of the stilling of the turbidity of defilements. It is called 'ekodibhāva' (unification) because of the stilling of initial and sustained application, not because of the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) like access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), nor because of the manifestation of factors like the first jhāna. Thus, this statement points out the cause of sampasādana and ekodibhāva. Similarly, this second jhāna is called 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ' because of the stilling of initial and sustained application, not because of their absence by nature as in the third and fourth jhānas, or as in eye-consciousness and so on. Thus, it points out the cause of the state of being without initial and sustained application, and does not merely point out the absence of initial and sustained application.
