The phrase 'avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ', however, points out merely the absence of initial and sustained application. Therefore, even though the former was said, the latter must also be said.

'Samādhijaṃ' (born of concentration) means born from the concentration of the first jhāna or born from the associated concentration. In this regard, although the first jhāna is also born from associated concentration, only this second jhāna deserves to be called 'concentration' (samādhi) because it is exceedingly unshakable and very clear due to the absence of the agitation of initial and sustained application. Therefore, to praise the quality of this second jhāna, only it is called 'samādhijaṃ'. The term 'pīti-sukhaṃ' (rapture and happiness) should be understood in the same way as already mentioned.

'Dutiyaṃ' (second) means second in numerical order, or second because of the attainment of this second jhāna. Regarding 'jhānaṃ' here, just as the first jhāna is fivefold with initial application and so on, this second jhāna should be understood as 'fourfold' (caturaṅgika) with internal confidence and so on. As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'Jhāna means internal confidence, rapture, happiness, and unification of mind.' This is a figurative (pariyāya) description. But setting aside internal confidence, in the literal sense (nippariyāya), it is only threefold. As it is said in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī: 'What at that time is the threefold jhāna? It is rapture, happiness, and unification of mind.' The rest is as already mentioned.

## The Discussion of the Second Jhāna is Finished.

In the three words 'pītiyā ca virāgā' (and with the fading away of rapture), 'pīti' has the same meaning as mentioned in the discussion of the first jhāna. ...
120:
## Discussion on the Third Jhāna

In the phrase "pītiyā ca virāgā" (with the fading away of rapture), "pīti" (rapture) has the same meaning as previously stated in the First Jhāna. "Virāga" means either disgust for that rapture or the complete transcending of it. The word "ca" (and) between the two terms has a conjunctive meaning. This "ca" connects either the subsiding [of rapture] or the subsiding of initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra). Among these connections, when it connects only the subsiding [of rapture], the construction should be understood as: "due to disgust for rapture, and further, due to the subsiding of rapture." In this construction, the word "virāga" carries the meaning of disgust. Therefore, the meaning should be regarded as: "due to disgust for rapture and due to its subsiding."

However, when it connects the subsiding of initial and sustained thought, the construction should be understood as: "due to the transcending of rapture, and further, due to the subsiding of initial and sustained thought." In this construction, the word "virāga" carries the meaning of transcending. Therefore, the meaning should be regarded as: "due to the transcending of rapture and due to the subsiding of initial and sustained thought."

Although these factors of initial and sustained thought have indeed already subsided in the Second Jhāna, they are mentioned here to indicate the path to attaining this Third Jhāna and to praise its attributes. When it is said, "due to the subsiding of initial and sustained thought," it becomes clear that "the subsiding of initial and sustained thought must be the path to this Third Jhāna." Just as in the case of the third path, the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga), it is said, "due to the abandoning of the five lower fetters (saṃyojana)," even though [some of them like] personality-belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) etc., were not [actually] abandoned [by this specific path but by previous ones]; such a statement is a praise that inspires effort in those striving to attain that path. Similarly, here, although initial and sustained thought have not [just now] subsided, mentioning their subsiding is a form of praise. Therefore, the meaning is stated as: "due to the transcending of rapture and due to the subsiding of initial and sustained thought."

In the phrase "upekkhako ca vihāsi" (he dwells equanimous), it is called "upekkha" (equanimity) because it looks on (ikkhati) properly (upapattito). The meaning is that it looks on evenly, looking on without partiality. Because he is endowed with that equanimity which is clear, abundant, and has reached a state of strength, the person possessed of the Third Jhāna is called "upekkhako" (one who is equanimous). There are ten kinds of equanimity: six-limbed equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkha), equanimity as a divine abiding (brahmavihārupekkha), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgupekkha), equanimity of energy (vīriyupekkha), equanimity about formations (saṅkhārupekkha), equanimity of feeling (vedanupekkha), equanimity of insight (vipassanupekkha), equanimity as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatupekkha), jhāna-equanimity (jhānupekkha), and equanimity of purity (pārisuddhupekkha). These ten types of equanimity should be understood according to the methods mentioned in the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī called the Atthasālinī, in terms of the various scriptural methods, planes (bhūmi), persons, consciousness, objects, the grouping of aggregates, and the summary of the single-moment wholesome triads. However, if they were to be discussed here [in the commentary on the Third Jhāna], it would make the Vinaya introduction (Vinaya-nidāna) excessively burdensome.
121:
It is not mentioned because it would make [the text] too burdensome. However, in terms of characteristics etc., the equanimity intended here in this Third Jhāna has the characteristic of neutrality (majjhatta-lakkhaṇā), the function of non-attention (anābhoga-rasā) [even to sublime pleasure], the manifestation of non-anxiety (abyāpāra-paccupaṭṭhānā), and the fading away of rapture as its proximate cause (pīti-virāga-padaṭṭhānā).

Here, a doubter asks: "Is not this intended jhāna-equanimity, in essence, just specific neutrality (tatra-majjhattatupekkha)? And does that equanimity not also exist in the First and Second Jhānas? Therefore, should it not also be said in those [jhānas] that 'he dwells equanimous' (upekkhako ca vihāsi)? Why is it not said?" [The answer is:] Because its function is not distinct. Indeed, its function there [in the first two jhānas] is unmanifest because it is overwhelmed by initial thought (vitakka) and so on. But in this Third Jhāna, because it is not overwhelmed by initial thought, sustained thought, and rapture, it has become manifest in its function, like a head held high. Therefore, it is mentioned here.

The complete explanation of the meaning of "he dwells equanimous" (upekkhako ca vihāsi) is finished.

Now, in the phrase "sato ca sampajāno" (mindful and clearly comprehending), he is "sato" (mindful) because he remembers (sarati); he is "sampajāno" (clearly comprehending) because he knows distinctly (sampajānāti). Mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) are stated here in terms of the person. Among them, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering (saraṇa-lakkhaṇā), the function of non-forgetting (asammusana-rasā), and the manifestation of guarding (ārakkha-paccupaṭṭhānā). Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion (asammoha-lakkhaṇā), the function of investigating (tīraṇa-rasā), and the manifestation of scrutiny (pavicaya-paccupaṭṭhānā).

Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension certainly exist in the previous jhānas as well—for even access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) cannot be accomplished by one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension, let alone absorption (appanā)—nevertheless, because those [earlier] jhānas are gross (oḷārika), the movement of the mind is easy, like a man walking on the ground. The function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is unmanifest there. But because this [Third] Jhāna is subtle (sukhuma) due to the abandoning of gross factors [like rapture], the movement of the mind must be desired as being gripped by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a man walking on the edge of a razor. Therefore, they are mentioned only here.

What is more? Just as a calf that is accustomed to staying with its mother cow, even if removed from her, will return to the mother cow if not guarded; similarly, this Third Jhāna happiness, even if removed from rapture, would return to rapture if not guarded by mindfulness and clear comprehension, and would become associated with rapture again. Alternatively, beings are prone to be attached to pleasure, and this Third Jhāna happiness is an extremely sweet pleasure because there is no higher happiness than this. However, through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, there is no attachment to this pleasure; it cannot be otherwise. It should be understood that they are mentioned only here to show this special meaning.

Now, in the phrase "sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesi" (and experiences happiness with the body), although one possessed of the Third Jhāna has no active attention to the experience of happiness, nevertheless, because he has happiness associated with the mental body (nāmakāya), or because his physical body (rūpakāya) is suffused with an extremely refined material form produced by that happiness associated with the mental body...
122:
Because of being permeated by that mind-produced matter, one experiences happiness even after emerging from the third jhāna. Therefore, desiring to show this meaning, the Blessed One said: "and he experiences happiness with the body."

Now, in the phrase "whom the Noble Ones describe as: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness,'" it means that the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, describe, teach, make known, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, manifest, and praise the person endowed with that third jhāna because of that jhāna. How? As "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness." The connection here should be understood as: "having attained that third jhāna, he dwells."

Why do those Noble Ones praise him so? Because he is worthy of praise. This person is equanimous even in the third jhāna, which has extremely sweet happiness and has reached the pinnacle of happiness; he is not pulled by the strong attachment to happiness there. He is mindful because his mindfulness is established in such a way that joy (pīti) does not arise. He is worthy of praise because he experiences with the mental body (nāmakāya) that happiness which is loved by the Noble Ones, cultivated by the Noble Ones, and is undefiled. Thus, being worthy of praise, it should be understood that the Noble Ones praise him, manifesting the qualities that are the reasons for such praise, saying: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness."

"Third" means third in numerical order. It is also called "third" because one attains this third jhāna. Regarding the word "jhāna" here, just as the second jhāna has four factors such as internal confidence (sampasāda), this third jhāna has five factors such as equanimity. As the Blessed One said in the Vibhaṅga: "Jhāna means equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind." This is only a figurative (pariyāya) teaching. However, excluding equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, in the literal (nippariyāya) sense, this jhāna has only two factors. As said in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī: "At that time, what is the jhāna of two factors? It is happiness and one-pointedness of mind." The rest is as previously explained.

## The Discussion of the Third Jhāna is Finished.

## The Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna

"With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain" means with the abandoning of physical pleasure and physical pain. "Beforehand" means that such abandoning occurred beforehand, ...
123:
At the moment of the fourth jhāna, "with the disappearance of joy and grief" means with the disappearance and abandoning of these two—mental pleasure (somanassa) and mental pain (domanassa)—beforehand. When are these abandoned? They are abandoned at the moment of access (upacāra) to the four jhānas. Indeed, somanassa is abandoned only at the moment of access to the fourth jhāna, while pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and pleasure (sukha) are abandoned at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas respectively. Although they are not taught in this order of abandonment, the abandonment of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief should be understood here as taught in the order of the enumeration of the faculties in the Indriya Vibhaṅga.

If these are abandoned only at the moment of access to each respective jhāna, then why did He say: "Monks, where does the arisen pain faculty (dukkhindriya) cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna; here the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder. Where does the arisen grief faculty... pleasure faculty... joy faculty cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; here the arisen joy faculty (somanassindriya) ceases without remainder"? Why is the cessation taught only in the jhānas? Because of surpassing cessation (atisayanirodha). Indeed, the cessation of these in the first jhāna and so on is a surpassing cessation, not just mere cessation. At the moment of access, there is mere cessation, not surpassing cessation.

For instance, although the pain faculty has ceased in the access to the first jhāna with various advertings (āvajjanas), it might still arise due to the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, etc., or due to the heat from an uneven seat; but it does not arise within absorption (appanā). Alternatively, although it has ceased in access, it is not well-ceased because it has not been struck down by the opposite state. But within absorption, the entire body is permeated with happiness through the suffusion of joy (pīti). For one whose body is permeated with happiness, the pain faculty is well-ceased because it is struck down by the opposite state.

The grief faculty (domanassindriya), which is abandoned in the access to the second jhāna with various advertings, arises when there is physical exhaustion and mental distress caused by initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra); it does not arise when initial and sustained thought are absent. In whichever consciousness it arises, it arises because of the presence of initial and sustained thought. Since initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in the access to the second jhāna, the grief faculty might still arise there because its cause is not yet abandoned. But it cannot arise in the second jhāna because its cause is abandoned.

Similarly, although the pleasure faculty (sukhindriya) is abandoned in the access to the third jhāna, it might still arise for one whose body is permeated with refined matter produced by joy (pīti); but it cannot arise in the third jhāna. Indeed, in the third jhāna, of pleasure...
124:
The joy (pīti) that serves as a condition has completely ceased. Likewise, although the faculty of mental pleasure (somanassindriya) has been abandoned in the access (upacāra) to the fourth jhāna, its arising is still possible [in the access] because of its proximity [to the fourth jhāna] and because it has not been fully transcended due to the absence of equanimity (upekkhā) that has reached absorption (appanā); however, it does not arise in the fourth jhāna itself. For this very reason, the phrase 'without remainder' is used in various places, such as: 'The faculty of pain that has arisen here (in the fourth jhāna) ceases without remainder.'

In this context, it may be asked: 'If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access to their respective jhānas, why are they gathered and taught together here [in the fourth jhāna]?' [The answer is:] To make it easy to understand. For the neither-painful-nor-pleasant (adukkhamasukha) feeling taught in the phrase 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' is extremely subtle and very difficult to know; it cannot be easily grasped by the intellect. Therefore, as an analogy: when a cowherd is unable to approach and catch a difficult cow by any means, he gathers all the cows into a single pen to catch that cow. Then, as he lets them out one by one, he has the people catch that specific cow when it comes out in order, saying, 'This is the one, catch it!' In the same way, the Blessed One gathered all these feelings and taught them together so that [the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling] could be easily known. Only when they are gathered and shown in this way is it possible to make that feeling understood, saying: 'That feeling which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental pleasure nor mental pain—this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.'

Furthermore, it should be understood that these feelings were also taught to show the causes for the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind (cetovimutti). The abandoning of pleasure and so forth are the causes for that liberation of mind. Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta said: 'Friends, there are four causes for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. These, friends, are the four causes for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind.' Alternatively, just as self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth, though already abandoned in other [lower paths], are said to be abandoned in the third path for the sake of praising the virtues of that [third path]; even so, it should be understood that these feelings are mentioned here for the sake of praising the virtues of this jhāna. Or else, it should be understood that they are mentioned to show how far removed lust (rāga) and hatred (dosa) are in this [fourth jhāna] through the destruction of their causes. For among these feelings, pleasure is a cause for mental pleasure, mental pleasure for lust, pain for mental pain, and mental pain for hatred. By destroying the causes such as pleasure, lust and hatred along with their causes are killed and thus reach a state of being very far removed.

'Neither-painful-nor-pleasant' means 'not painful' due to the absence of pain, and 'not pleasant' due to the absence of pleasure. By this [term], he points out the third feeling which is the opposite of pain and pleasure in this jhāna, not merely the absence of pain and pleasure.
125:
The third feeling is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it is also called equanimity (upekkhā). It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing in a neutral (majjhatta) way that is distinct from both the desirable and the undesirable; its function is neutrality; its manifestation is unmanifest [unlike pleasure and pain]; its proximate cause is the cessation of mental pleasure [which is the access to the fourth jhāna].

'Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity' (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi) refers to the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity (specifically tatramajjhattatā). For in this fourth jhāna, mindfulness is extremely pure. And that purity of mindfulness is produced by equanimity alone, not by any other state. Therefore, this [fourth jhāna] is called 'purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.' It is also stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'This mindfulness is clarified, purified, and cleansed by this equanimity; therefore it is called "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity."' The equanimity that purifies mindfulness in this jhāna should be understood as the mental factor of neutrality (tatramajjhattatā). In this fourth jhāna, not only is mindfulness purified by that equanimity, but all associated (sampayutta) states are also purified; however, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the primary element.

In this regard, although this neutrality (tatramajjhattatā) exists in the lower three jhānas as well, just as the crescent moon, though present during the day, is not pure or bright because it is overcome by the sun's light, and because of its cool nature, it lacks the night which is its natural support; even so, this crescent moon of neutrality, though present in the divisions of the first jhāna and so forth, is not pure because it is overcome by the power of opposing states such as initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra), and because it lacks the night of equanimity-feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) which is its natural support. Because that equanimity is not pure, the co-nascent states such as mindfulness are also not pure, like the light of the impure crescent moon during the day. Therefore, not even one of those [lower jhānas] is called 'purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.'

But in this fourth jhāna, because there is no overcoming by the power of opposing states such as initial application, and because it has gained the night of equanimity-feeling which is its natural support, this crescent moon of neutrality is exceedingly pure. Because that equanimity is pure, the co-nascent states such as mindfulness are also pure and cleansed, like the light of the pure crescent moon. Therefore, it should be understood that this [fourth jhāna] alone is called 'purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.'

'Fourth' means the fourth in the numerical order, and it is called 'fourth' because one attains this fourth jhāna. In this term 'jhāna,' just as the third jhāna is endowed with five factors such as equanimity and so forth, so this fourth jhāna is endowed with three factors such as equanimity and so forth. As the Blessed One said: 'Jhāna means equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā).' This is a figurative (pariyāya) teaching. However, if one sets aside mindfulness and takes only equanimity and one-pointedness, it is directly (nippariyāyena) only two-factored. As the Blessed One said in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī: 'Which jhāna at that time has two factors, equanimity and one-pointedness of mind? What is that jhāna?' The remaining words are just as previously stated. The explanation of the Fourth Jhāna is finished.
126:
At that time, the jhana has two factors: equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind (cittassekaggatā). The rest is exactly as previously explained.

## The discussion on the Fourth Jhana is finished.

## Discussion on Pubbenivāsa (Recollection of Past Lives)

Thus, these four jhanas serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind for some; they are the basis for insight (vipassanā) for some; the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) for some; the basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for some; and for the purpose of entering a new existence (rebirth) for some.

Among them, for Arahants, they serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind. Thinking, 'Having entered these attainments, we shall dwell happily throughout the day with a concentrated mind,' they perform the preliminary work for the kasinas and produce the eight attainments. For trainees (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas), who produce them thinking, 'Having emerged from the attainment, we shall practice insight with a concentrated mind,' they are the basis for insight. For those who, having produced the eight attainments and entered the jhana that is the basis for direct knowledge, emerge from the attainment and produce them while aspiring for direct knowledges—according to the method stated as 'being one, he becomes many'—they are the basis for direct knowledge. For those who produce them thinking, 'Having entered the attainment of cessation and being without mind for seven days, we shall dwell happily having reached cessation, which is Nibbāna, in this very life,' they are the basis for the attainment of cessation. For those who produce them thinking, 'With jhana unimpaired, we shall be reborn in the Brahma world,' they serve the purpose of entering a new existence.

The Blessed One, however, produced this Fourth Jhana at the foot of the Bodhi tree. It should be understood that for the Blessed One, it was the basis for insight, the basis for direct knowledge, the basis for the attainment of cessation, the accomplisher of all tasks, and the giver of all mundane and supramundane qualities. Desiring to show a portion of those qualities which it gives, he said: 'So evaṃ samāhite citte' (He, with the mind thus concentrated), and so forth.

In that passage, 'so' means 'that I'. 'Evaṃ' is an indication of the sequence of reaching the Fourth Jhana. It means 'having obtained the Fourth Jhana in this sequence'. By the word 'samāhite', [it means] by the concentration of this Fourth Jhana...
127:
...concentrated by the concentration of the Fourth Jhana. 'Citte' refers to the fine-material sphere mind (rūpāvacara-citta). Among the terms beginning with 'parisuddhe', it is 'parisuddhe' (purified) when it is purified all around by the state of purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Because it is purified all around, it is 'pariyodāte' (bright/cleansed) when it is exceptionally clean, and 'pabhassare' (radiant) when it emits a brilliant light. It is 'anangaṇe' (unblemished) because blemishes such as lust are removed by the destruction of causes such as [sensual] pleasure. Because it is unblemished, it is 'vigatūpakkilese' (free from impurities), as the mind becomes defiled only by blemishes (angaṇa).

It is 'mudubhūte' (malleable) because it is well-developed; this means it has reached mastery (vasībhāva). A mind that is under one's control is called malleable. Because it is malleable, it is 'kammaniye' (wieldy), which means it is enduring in work and fit for work. Just as well-smelted gold is malleable and can be made into whatever is desired, so too a malleable mind is wieldy in work. Both of these are due only to being well-developed. The Blessed One said: 'Monks, I do not see even one other thing that, when thus developed and cultivated, is so malleable and wieldy as this mind.'

It is 'thite' (steady) because it stands in such states as purity. Because it is steady, it is 'āneñjappatte' (attained to imperturbability), which means it is unshaken and still. Alternatively, it is 'thite' because it stands under one's control due to being malleable and wieldy, and it is 'āneñjappatte' because it is upheld by faith and other qualities. For a mind upheld by faith is not shaken by faithlessness; upheld by energy, it is not shaken by laziness; upheld by mindfulness, it is not shaken by negligence; upheld by concentration, it is not shaken by restlessness; upheld by wisdom, it is not shaken by ignorance; and a mind that has attained light is not shaken by the darkness of defilements. A mind upheld by these six qualities reaches imperturbability (āneñja). A mind thus endowed with eight factors is fit for directing towards the realization through direct knowledge of those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge.

Another method: In the mind concentrated by the concentration of the Fourth Jhana, it is 'parisuddhe' due to the remoteness of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). It is 'pariyodāte' due to the transcending of initial thought (vitakka) and so forth. It is 'anangaṇe' due to the absence of evil unwholesome desires (icchāvacara) which are obstacles to obtaining jhana. It is 'vigatūpakkilese' due to the departure of mental impurities such as covetousness (abhijjhā). These two should be understood in accordance with the Anangaṇa Sutta and Vattha Sutta. It is 'mudubhūte' due to the mastery attained. It is 'kammaniye' due to reaching the state of the bases of power (iddhipāda). It is 'thite' and 'āneñjappatte' due to reaching a sublime state through the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). It means it is steady in such a way that it reaches imperturbability. A mind thus endowed with eight factors is the basis and proximate cause for directing towards the realization of those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge.
128:
"Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya" means for the purpose of the knowledge that arises in the mindfulness that recollects the sequence of aggregates previously lived, when this fourth jhāna mind, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā), has arisen. In that phrase, "Pubbenivāsa" refers to the aggregates lived in previous past lives. "Lived" (nivuttha) means things experienced and felt by having arisen and ceased within one's own continuity, or things that existed as objects known and delimited by one's own consciousness, or in the case of recollecting the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples (sāvakas) who have cut off the cycle of rebirth, things known by another's consciousness. "Pubbenivāsānussati" is the mindfulness by which one recollects past lives; that mindfulness is called pubbenivāsānussati. "Ñāṇa" is the knowledge associated with that mindfulness. Thus, it means for the benefit of this knowledge of recollecting past lives, for the attainment and achievement of that knowledge. "Abhininnāmesiṃ" means I directed or inclined (the mind) forward.

"So" means I, the Buddha. "Anekavihitaṃ" means occurring in various ways or having many forms. "Pubbenivāsaṃ" refers to the continuity of aggregates lived in various lives, starting from the life immediately preceding. "Anussarāmi" means I recollect by following the sequence of births with knowledge, such as 'one birth, two births,' or I recollect immediately upon inclining the mind. For Great Beings (Mahāpurisas) who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no need for preliminary preparation (parikamma); therefore, they can recollect just by inclining the mind. However, for noble sons who are beginners (ādikammika), they can only recollect after performing preliminary preparation; thus, the preparation should be described for them. But if it were described here, it would make the Vinaya Nidāna very heavy (lengthy); therefore, it is not mentioned here. Those who desire it should take it according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, we shall only explain the Pali text.

"Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle used to show the manner in which something is begun. Therefore, wishing to show the various types of past lives that have been started, He said "ekam-pi jātiṃ" and so on. There, "ekam-pi jātiṃ" means one continuity of aggregates included within a single existence, from rebirth to death. This same method applies to "dve-pi jātiyo" and so on. In "anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe" and so on, an aeon that is diminishing and being destroyed is to be known as "saṃvaṭṭakappa" (aeon of dissolution), and an aeon that is increasing and evolving is to be known as "vivaṭṭakappa" (aeon of evolution). In that context, by the term "saṃvaṭṭa," the "saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (the period during which the world remains dissolved) is also included because it is based on it. By the term "vivaṭṭa," the "vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (the period during which the world remains evolved) is also included. When taken this way, all four incalculable periods of an aeon mentioned as "Monks, there are these four incalculables of an aeon. Which four? Saṃvaṭṭa, saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, vivaṭṭa, and vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" are encompassed.
129:
Among those aeons, there are three types of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa): dissolution by fire (tejosaṃvaṭṭa), dissolution by water (āposaṃvaṭṭa), and dissolution by wind (vāyosaṃvaṭṭa). There are three boundaries of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭasīmā): the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. When the aeon is destroyed by fire, the fire burns the realms below the Ābhassara realm. When the aeon is destroyed by water, the water dissolves and destroys the realms below the Subhakiṇha realm. When the aeon is destroyed by wind, the wind blows away and destroys the realms below the Vehapphala realm. In detail, in every instance of destruction, one Buddha-field (Buddhakkhetta) is destroyed.

The Buddha-field is of three kinds: the birth-field (jātikkhetta), the authority-field (āṇākkhetta), and the scope-field (visayakkhetta). Among these three, the birth-field extends to ten thousand world systems, which tremble at the Tathāgata's conception and so on. The authority-field extends to a hundred thousand koṭis of world systems. In this field, the power of these protective chants (parittas) such as the Ratana Sutta, Khandha Sutta, Dhajagga Sutta, Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, and Mora Sutta prevails. The scope-field is infinite and immeasurable; as it is said, "as far as He wishes," He can recollect whatever object He desires. Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, one authority-field is destroyed. When that authority-field is destroyed, the birth-field is also destroyed; they are destroyed together and they are re-established together. The destruction and re-establishment of that field are stated in the Visuddhimagga. Those who desire it should take it from that text.

Among those aeons of dissolution and evolution that have been mentioned, the Blessed One, while sitting at the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhimanda) for the purpose of attaining Supreme Enlightenment, recollected many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of evolution, and many aeons of both dissolution and evolution. How? In the manner beginning with "I was there." In that phrase, "I was there" means "In that aeon of dissolution, I existed in that life, or in that womb (yoni), or in that destination (gati), or in that station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), or in that abode of beings (sattāvāsa), or in that community of beings (sattanikāya)." "Having such a name" means having a name such as Vessantara or Jotipāla. "Having such a clan" means having a clan such as Bhaggava or Gotama. "Having such an appearance" means having a fair appearance or a dark appearance. "Having such food" means having food consisting of rice and meat, or eating wild fruits. "Experiencing such pleasure and pain" means experiencing various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, categorized as carnal (sāmisa) or spiritual (nirāmisa). "Having such a lifespan" means having a lifespan of a hundred years at most, or a lifespan of eighty-four thousand aeons at most.
130:
I, having passed away from that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or category of beings, was reborn again in such an existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or category of beings. 'I was there' means I had existed again in that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or category of beings. The phrases starting with 'having such a name' should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

Alternatively, the phrase 'I was there' refers to the recollection of one who ascends through previous lives in order, as far back as desired. 'Having passed away from there' refers to the retrospective review while returning. Therefore, 'I was reborn here' refers to the birth in this human world, and 'I was reborn there' immediately preceding it should be understood as referring to the Tusita heaven. 'There I had such a name' means that in that Tusita heaven, I was a deity named Setaketu. 'Of such a clan' means being of the same clan as those deities. 'Of such an appearance' means having an appearance like the color of gold. 'With such food' means consuming divine ambrosia (sudhā). 'Experiencing such pleasure and pain' means experiencing such divine pleasure. As for pain, it was merely the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha). 'With such a lifespan' means having a lifespan of fifty-seven crores and sixty hundred thousand years. 'Having passed away from there' means I, having passed away from that Tusita heaven, 'was reborn here' means being conceived in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

'Thus' means in such a manner. 'With aspects and details' means with details in terms of name and clan, and with aspects in terms of appearance and so on. For a being is indicated by name and clan as 'Datta, Tissa, Gotama'; and is known by distinction through appearance as 'fair or dark'. Therefore, name and clan are the 'details' (uddesa), and the others are the 'aspects' (ākāra).

If it is asked whether only Buddhas can recollect their past aggregates, the answer is: not only Buddhas, but also Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and sectarians (titthiyas) can also recollect them. However, they are not all equal without distinction. Sectarians can recollect only forty aeons (kappas) and no further. Why? Because their wisdom is weak. Their wisdom is weak because they lack the discernment of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda). Among the disciples, the eighty Great Disciples can recollect one hundred thousand aeons. The two Chief Disciples can recollect one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas can recollect two incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons. This is the extent of their resolution (abhinīhāra). For Buddhas, however, there is no limit; they can recollect as far back as they desire. Sectarians can only recollect according to the succession of aggregates. They are unable to recollect by skipping the succession through death and rebirth. Like blind people, they cannot leap over to a desired place. Disciples can recollect in both ways, and likewise...
131:
...Paccekabuddhas. Buddhas, however, can recollect everything they desire, whether below or above, through many millions of aeons, either by the succession of aggregates, by way of death and rebirth, or by way of the 'lion's leap' (sīhokkanta).

In the phrases such as 'This, O Brahmin, was my...', 'my' (me) means 'by me'. 'Knowledge' (vijjā) is so called because it makes known what should be known. What does it make known? It makes known the past lives (pubbenivāsa). 'Ignorance' (avijjā) refers to the delusion (moha) that covers that very recollection of past lives, in the sense of making it unknown. 'Darkness' (tamo) is also a name for that same delusion in the sense of covering. 'Light' (āloko) is a name for that same knowledge in the sense of producing radiance. Here, 'knowledge was attained' is the actual meaning; the rest are words of praise. The construction (yojanā) here is: 'This knowledge was attained by me; for me who has attained that knowledge, ignorance was destroyed,' meaning it vanished. Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method applies to the other two pairs of words.

In the phrase 'as that' (yathā taṃ), 'as' (yathā) is used in the sense of a simile. 'That' (taṃ) is a particle. 'For one who is diligent' (appamattassa) means through non-separation from mindfulness. 'For one who is ardent' (ātāpino) means through the heat of energy. 'For one who is resolute' (pahitattassa) means having a mind sent forth without regard for body or life. This is what is meant: Just as for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, ignorance would be destroyed and knowledge would arise, darkness would be destroyed and light would arise; even so, for me, ignorance was destroyed and knowledge has arisen, darkness was destroyed and light has arisen. Thus, I have obtained the fruit corresponding to my application of right effort (sammappadhāna).

'Brahmin, this was my first breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell' means: Brahmin, by the beak of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, I have broken the eggshell of ignorance that covered the aggregates previously lived in; this was my first breaking out, the first emergence, the first noble birth (ariyajāti). It is like a chick breaking the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claws, and by breaking out from that eggshell, it is born again into the category of chickens.

## The Discussion on the Recollection of Past Lives is finished.
132:
## Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

"That person thus... for the sake of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth" means for the purpose of knowing near the time of passing away and near the time of rebirth. It means for the benefit of that knowledge by which the passing away and rebirth of beings are known. "Directs the mind" refers to bringing forth (directing) the mind that performs the preliminary work (parikamma). "That person sees with the divine (eye)..." In this context, for the Great Beings (Mahāsattas) who have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), there is no need to perform preliminary work for the knowledge of the divine eye. These Great Beings can see beings with the divine-like eye (the eye of higher knowledge) just by directing the mind. However, beginners of good family can see only after performing the preliminary work. Therefore, the preliminary work should be described in accordance with those beginners. But if that preliminary work were described, it would make the introduction to the Vinaya too burdensome; therefore, it is not described here. Those who wish to know should take it according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, I will only comment on the Pali text.

"So" means "that I". In the words starting with "dibbeṇa", it is called "dibba" (divine) because it is like that of the devas. For the devas, there is a divine sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) produced by well-performed kamma, which is not oppressed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from defilements, is capable of receiving even distant objects. This eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu) produced by the power of energy and meditation is just like that of the devas; thus, it is called "dibba" because it is like the divine. It is also called "dibba" because it is obtained through the power of the divine abidings (jhanas) and because it itself depends on the divine abiding (the foundation jhana/pādaka-jhāna). It is called "dibba" because it has great radiance by grasping light. It is called "dibba" because it has a great range by seeing forms that have gone beyond walls, etc. All this should be understood according to the science of grammar. It is called "cakkhu" (eye) in the sense of seeing. It is also called "cakkhu" because it performs the function of an eye and is like an eye. It is called "visuddha" (purified) because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing passing away and rebirth. If a person sees only passing away and not rebirth, he holds the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi). If a person sees only rebirth and not passing away, he holds the view that new beings appear. If a person sees both, he can transcend both those views; therefore, that seeing is the cause for the purification of view. The Blessed One saw both. Therefore, it is said: "It is called purified because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing passing away and rebirth."

Alternatively, it is called "purified" because it is free from the eleven defilements. The Blessed One's divine eye is free from the eleven defilements. As he said: "Anuruddha, I, having known that 'doubt is a defilement of the mind', abandoned doubt, the defilement of the mind. Inattention (amanasikāra)... sloth and torpor (thina-middha)... fear (chambhitatta)... elation (uppila)... coarseness (duṭṭhulla)... over-strenuous energy (accāraddha-vīriya)... over-lax energy (atilina-vīriya)... longing (abhijappā)... perception of diversity (nānatta-saññā)..."
133:
"Knowing that 'the state of staring too much at forms is a defilement of the mind', I abandoned that defilement of the mind which is staring too much at forms." "Anuruddha, while I was dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived light but did not see forms. I saw forms but did not perceive light," and so on. Thus, it is purified because it is free from the eleven defilements.

It is called 'atikkanta-mānusaka' (surpassing the human) because it sees forms by surpassing the human range of vision (dassanūpacāra). Or it should be known as 'atikkanta-mānusaka' because it surpasses the human fleshy eye (maṃsa-cakkhu). "With that divine eye, purified, surpassing the human."

"Sees beings" means seeing, looking at, and observing beings just as one sees with the human fleshy eye. In "passing away, being reborn," it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the exact moment of death or the exact moment of rebirth. Those who are near death and are about to pass away are meant by "cavamāna" (passing away). Those who have just taken rebirth or have just been born are meant by "upapajjamāna" (being reborn). It shows that he sees such beings who are passing away and being reborn. "Inferior" (hīna) refers to those who are despised and known as low by way of inferior birth, family, and wealth because of being associated with the result of delusion (moha). "Superior" (paṇīta) refers to those who are the opposite because of being associated with the result of non-delusion (amoha). "Beautiful" (suvaṇṇa) refers to those who have desirable, pleasing, and agreeable complexions because of being associated with the result of non-hatred (adosa). "Ugly" (dubbaṇṇa) refers to those who have undesirable complexions because of being associated with the result of hatred (dosa). It also means beautiful and ugly. "Gone to a good destination" (sugata) refers to those who have gone to a happy state (sugati), or those who are wealthy and have great riches because of the result of non-greed (alobha). "Gone to a miserable destination" (duggata) refers to those who have gone to a woeful state (duggati), or those who are poor and have little food and drink because of the result of greed (lobha). "Passing according to their kamma" (yathākammūpaga) refers to those who arrive at their respective accumulated kamma. Therein, the function of the divine eye is shown by the previous words like "cavamāna", while the function of the knowledge of passing according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) is shown by this word "yathākammūpaga".

The sequence of the arising of that knowledge is: The one who has attained the divine eye extends the light towards the hells below and sees the hell-beings experiencing great suffering. That seeing is the function of the divine eye alone. He then reflects: "By performing what kamma do these beings experience this suffering?" Then, the knowledge taking that kamma as its object arises: "By performing such-and-such kamma." Similarly, extending the light upwards towards the deva worlds, he sees beings experiencing great prosperity in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, etc. That seeing is also the function of the divine eye alone. He reflects thus...
134:
That possessor of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) reflects: "By performing what kind of kamma do these beings experience this prosperity?" Then, the knowledge that takes that performed kamma as its object arises in him: "By performing such and such kamma." This knowledge is called yathākammūpagatāñāṇa (knowledge of beings passing away according to their deeds). For this knowledge, there is no separate preliminary work (parikamma). Just like yathākammūpagatāñāṇa, anāgataṃsañāṇa (knowledge of the future) also has no separate preliminary work. This is because these knowledges are based on the divine eye and are accomplished along with the divine eye itself.

In the terms such as "kāyaduccaritena," it is called duccarita (misconduct) because it is practiced badly, or because it is a bad practice due to the foulness of defilements. It is called kāyaduccarita (bodily misconduct) because it is practiced by the body or because it arises from the body. Verbal misconduct (vacīduccarita) and mental misconduct (manoduccarita) should be understood in the same way.

"Samannāgatā" means those who are endowed with or those who have a state similar to that kamma. "Ariyānaṃ upavādakā" refers to those who, desiring harm, revile the Noble Ones—the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, including even lay stream-enterers (sotāpanna)—either by accusing them of an ultimate offense (antimavatthu, i.e., Pārājika) or by disparaging their virtues (guṇa). It means those who abuse or blame. Among them, one who says, "These people have no ascetic qualities, they are not true ascetics," is one who reviles by accusing of an ultimate offense. One who says, "These people have no jhāna, liberation (vimokkha), path (magga), or fruition (phala)," is one who reviles by disparaging their virtues. Whether the reviler knows they are Noble Ones or not, in both cases, it is ariyūpavāda (insulting Noble Ones). This kamma is very heavy and obstructs heaven and the path and fruition. However, it is an offense that can be remedied. To clarify this offense, the following story is cited as an example:

In a certain village, an elder monk and a young monk were wandering for alms. At the very first house, they received about a ladleful of hot gruel (yāgu). The elder monk had a wind ailment in his stomach and thought, "This gruel is suitable for me; I will drink it before it gets cold." He sat on a log brought by people to be used as a threshold and drank it. Seeing this, the young monk felt disgusted, thinking, "This old monk is truly very hungry; he has made us feel ashamed." After wandering through the village and returning to the monastery, the elder monk asked the young monk, "Friend, do you have a footing (special attainment) in this Dispensation?" The young monk replied, "Yes, Bhante, I am a stream-enterer (sotāpanna)." Then the elder said, "Friend, in that case, do not strive for the higher paths; you have reviled an Arahant." Then the young monk apologized to the elder. Because of that apology, his kamma returned to its normal state.

Therefore, if anyone else reviles a Noble One, they should go to that person and, if the person is senior to them, apologize by saying, "Bhante, I said such and such to you; please forgive me for that fault." If the person is junior, one should pay homage, sit in a crouching position, and with joined palms...
135:
...apologize by saying, "Bhante, I said such and such to you; please forgive me." If that person does not forgive, or has departed to another region, one should go to the monks residing in that monastery and, if senior to them, while standing, or if junior, by sitting in a crouching position with joined palms, apologize by saying, "Bhante, I said such and such to the venerable one named so-and-so; may that venerable one forgive me." If that person has attained parinibbāna (passed away), one should go to the place where the deathbed was located or even as far as the cemetery to apologize. When this is done, there is no obstruction to heaven or the path; it returns to its normal state.

Micchādiṭṭhikā means those with perverted views. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā means those who have various kammas undertaken by the power of wrong view, and those who cause others to undertake bodily kamma and so on which have wrong view as their root. In those (misconducts), although insulting Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is already included by taking verbal misconduct, and wrong view is included by taking mental misconduct, it should be understood that these two are mentioned again to show their great blameworthiness. Indeed, insulting Noble Ones is a great fault similar to ānantariya kamma. As it was said: "Sāriputta, just as a monk endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain Arahantship in this very life; so too, Sāriputta, I say that if one does not give up that speech, does not give up that mind, and does not relinquish that view, one will be cast into hell as if carried and dropped there."

There is no other thing more blameworthy than wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). As it was said: "Monks, I do not see any other single thing so blameworthy as this, namely, wrong view. Monks, wrong view is the greatest of faults."

Kāyassa bhedā means because of the discarding of the grasped aggregates (upādinnakhandha). Paraṃ maraṇā means in the taking up of new aggregates immediately after death. Alternatively, kāyassa bhedā means because of the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and paraṃ maraṇā means after the death-consciousness (cuticitta). All these words such as "apāya" are synonyms for hell (niraya). Indeed, hell is called "apāya" because it is devoid of happiness (aya) which is known as merit, the cause of heaven and liberation, or because of the absence of the arising of happiness. It is called "duggati" because it is the resort of suffering, or because it is a destination produced by kamma full of hatred (dosa). It is called "vinipāta" because those who do evil fall into it against their will, or because they fall into it while their limbs and organs are being destroyed. It is called "niraya" because there is no happiness known as enjoyment there.
136:
Alternatively, by the word *apāya*, the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*) is shown. The animal realm is called *apāya* because it is departed from the happy destination (*sugati*). It is not a *duggati* (bad destination) because great powerful beings like serpent kings (*nāgarājā*) and others can be born there. By the word *duggati*, the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is shown. That realm is called both *apāya* and *duggati* because it is departed from the happy destination and is a place of suffering. However, it is not *vinipāta* (perdition) because it is not a falling down without choice like the *asuras*. For powerful *petas*, celestial mansions (*vimāna*) also arise. By the word *vinipāta*, the host of *asuras* is shown. That host is called both *apāya* and *duggati* for the reasons mentioned, and it is called *vinipāta* because they fall away from all prosperity. By the word *niraya*, only hell with its many varieties such as *Avīci* and others is shown. *Upapannā* means those who have reached or been born in those realms. The bright side (*sukkapakkha*) should be understood as the opposite of what was said.

The distinction here is: by the word *sugati*, the human realm is also included. By the word *sagga*, only the deva realm is included. In that context, it is called *sugati* because it is a good destination. It is called *sagga* because it is exceedingly excellent due to sense objects like forms and so on. All these, *sugati* and *sagga*, are called *loka* (world) in the sense of being subject to crumbling and destruction; this is the meaning of the term. *Vijjā* refers to the knowledge of the divine eye. *Avijjā* is the ignorance that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings. The rest is as previously explained. There is only this distinction here: just as in the discussion on *pubbenivāsa*, it was said, "having broken the eggshell of ignorance that covers the aggregates lived in the past with the beak of the knowledge of recollection of past lives," so here in this discussion on the knowledge of the divine eye, it should be said, "having broken the eggshell of ignorance that covers passing away and rebirth with the beak of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth."

## The Discussion on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints

In the phrase "when the mind was thus concentrated," the fourth jhāna mind, which is the basis for insight (*vipassanā*), should be understood. "For the knowledge of the destruction of taints" means for the sake of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (*arahattamaggañāṇa*). The path of Arahantship is called the destruction of taints (*āsavakkhaya*) because it destroys the taints. This knowledge is also called so because it is included within that path. "I directed my mind" means I brought forth and directed the mind of insight. In the words "this is suffering" and so on, "this much is suffering, there is nothing beyond this," I knew and realized the entire truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) as it really is by penetrating its individual essence (*sarasalakkhaṇa*) with higher knowledge. Regarding the craving that produces that suffering, "this is..."
137:
"...the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*), which is this craving." And regarding that *Nibbāna* where both suffering and its origin reach and cease, that non-occurrence of those two, "this is the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*)." And regarding the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) that leads to that *Nibbāna*, "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*)." It should be understood that I knew and realized these as they really are by penetrating their individual essence without confusion (*asammoha*).

Having thus shown the truths in their own nature, now wishing to show them by way of the taints (*āsava*) through a figurative method (*pariyāya*), he said the words beginning with "these are the taints." By the words "to me who thus knew, thus saw," he speaks of the path of Arahantship that has reached its peak along with insight for me who thus knew and thus saw. "*Kāmāsavā*" means (liberated) from the taint of sensual desire. By the word "*vimuccittha*," he shows the moment of the fruition of Arahantship (*arahattaphala*). This is because at the moment of the path, the mind is being liberated from the taints, and at the moment of fruition, it has been liberated. By the words "when liberated, there was the knowledge that it is liberated," he shows the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). By the words "birth is destroyed" and so on, he shows its object. For when the Blessed One was reviewing with that reviewing knowledge, he knew "birth is destroyed" and so on.

If it is asked, "What kind of birth of the Blessed One is destroyed, and how did he know it?" The answer is: the past birth of the Blessed One was not destroyed by the path, for it had already ended. The future birth was also not destroyed by the path, for there is no effort to be made in the future. The present birth is also not destroyed, for it is currently existing. However, that birth which would have arisen in the realms of one, four, or five aggregates because the path of Arahantship had not yet been developed—that birth is destroyed by reaching the state of non-arising because the path has been developed. The Blessed One, having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the path, knew and realized, "When defilements are absent, even existing kamma does not cause rebirth in the future."

"*Vusitaṃ*" means used, completely used, done, practiced, or reached completion. "*Brahmacariyaṃ*" means the holy life of the path. This is because the seven types of noble learners (*sekha*), along with the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇa puthujjana*), are said to be living the holy life, while the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is one who has lived the life. Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own living of the holy life, knew, "The holy life has been lived." "What had to be done has been done" (*kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ*) means that the sixteen-fold task—by way of full understanding (*pariññā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*) through the four paths regarding the four truths—has been completed. For the virtuous worldling and others are still doing this task, while the one whose taints are destroyed has done what had to be done. Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own task, knew, "What had to be done has been done." "There is no more for this state" means I knew that "now there is no more task for me to develop the path for the sake of such sixteen-fold tasks or for the destruction of defilements in this manner again."
138:
Now, wishing to show the Brahmin the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, which is grasped through reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), as a conclusion, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa." In those words, vijjā refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa). Avijjā refers to the ignorance that covers the Four Noble Truths. The rest is as previously explained.

To state the distinction: in the words "Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa tatiyā abhinibbhidā ahosi," it should be understood as: "Brahmin, this breaking of the eggshell of ignorance that covers the Four Noble Truths, by the beak of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, was my third breaking out, my third emergence, my third noble birth." It is just like a young chick breaking the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claws and emerging from that eggshell, being born into the species of fowl.

What is shown by this sequence of words? Brahmin, that young chick, having broken the eggshell and emerged, is born only once. I, however, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that covers the aggregates of past lives, was first born through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa-vijjā). After that, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings, I was born for the second time through the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa-vijjā). Again, having broken the eggshell of ignorance that covers the Four Noble Truths, I was born for the third time through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa-vijjā). Thus, through the three knowledges, I was born three times. And that birth of mine is noble and perfectly pure—this is the meaning shown. In showing this, through the knowledge of past lives, He showed knowledge of the past; through the divine eye, He showed knowledge of the present and the future; and through the destruction of the taints, He showed all mundane and supramundane qualities. Thus, by revealing all the qualities of omniscience through these three knowledges, He showed the Brahmin His state of being the eldest and the foremost by virtue of His noble birth.

## The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints is Finished.

## Discourse on Rejoicing in the Teaching

"Evaṃ vutte verañjo brāhmaṇo" means that when the Blessed One, who has compassion for the world, out of compassion for the Brahmin, spoke this Dhamma teaching revealing the three knowledges—showing His state of being the eldest and the foremost by virtue of His noble birth, which should otherwise be kept hidden—the Brahmin Verañja, with his body and mind filled with the pervading of joy, [addressed] the Blessed One...
139:
Knowing the state of being the eldest and the foremost by virtue of the noble birth, he thought: "I have said of such an Omniscient One, who is the eldest and the foremost in the whole world, endowed with the three knowledges and all qualities, that 'He does not perform acts such as saluting others.' My ignorance (aññāṇa) is indeed truly blameworthy!" Having thus reproached himself, he reached a conclusion: "This Venerable Gotama is now the eldest in the world because He was born first through the noble birth, and He is the foremost because He is peerless in all qualities." He then addressed the Blessed One: "The Venerable Gotama is the eldest; the Venerable Gotama is the foremost." Having said this, and again greatly rejoicing in that Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, he spoke the words beginning with: "Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!"

In those words, the word "abhikkanta" is found in the senses of exhaustion (khaya), excellence (sundara), beauty (abhirūpa), and great rejoicing (abbhanumodana). In passages such as "Venerable Sir, the night is exhausted (abhikkantā); the first watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time," it is found in the sense of exhaustion (khaya). In passages such as "I like this person; among these four persons, this one is more excellent (abhikkantatara) and more sublime," it is found in the sense of excellence (sundara).

"Who is it that bows at my feet,
Shining with psychic power and fame,
Illuminating all directions
With a beautiful (abhikkanta) complexion?"

In verses such as these, it is found in the sense of beauty (abhirūpa). In passages such as "Venerable Sir, it is most wonderful (abhikkanta)," it is found in the sense of great rejoicing (abbhanumodana). Here too, it is used in the sense of great rejoicing. Since it is in the sense of great rejoicing, it should be understood as meaning "Sadhu, Sadhu, Master Gotama!"

"In fear, anger, praise, haste,
Wonder, joy, sorrow, and faith,
A wise person should repeat the word twice."

According to this rule, it should be understood that here, the word "abhikkanta" is spoken twice by virtue of faith and praise.

Alternatively, "abhikkanta" means that which is highly desirable, highly pleasing, and highly excellent. Of the two instances, with one "abhikkanta" he praises the teaching, and with the other, he praises his own faith. The meaning here is: "Master Gotama, this Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama is most excellent. My faith, which has arisen depending on the Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama, is also most excellent." Or, he praises the words of the Blessed One themselves, intending two meanings for each—that the words of Master Gotama are [excellent] because they destroy (defilements), because they cause the attainment of (qualities), because they inspire faith, because they produce wisdom, because they are endowed with meaning, because they are endowed with phrasing, and because they consist of easily understood terms...
140:
Venerable Gotama, [the words of Venerable Gotama] are excellent because they destroy faults, because they enable the attainment of virtues such as morality, because they inspire faith, because they produce wisdom, because they are rich in meaning, because they are rich in phrasing, because they have clear words, because they have deep meaning, because they are pleasant to the ear, because they reach the heart, because they do not involve self-exaltation, because they do not involve disparaging others, because they are cool with compassion, because they are pure with wisdom, because they are delightful just by hearing, because they can withstand investigation, because they bring happiness while being heard, and because they bring welfare when reflected upon. Thus, it should be understood in connection with these and other such reasons.

After praising in this way, he further praises the teaching itself with four metaphors. Among those four metaphors, 'nikkujjita' refers to a pot or similar object placed face down or naturally overturned. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to set it upright so it faces upwards. 'Paṭicchanna' means covered with grass, leaves, and so forth. 'Vivareyya' means to open or reveal it. 'Mūḷha' refers to one who is confused about the directions. 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means to take one by the hand and say, "This is the path." 'Andhakāra' refers to the darkness consisting of four factors: the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest, and a mass of clouds. This is the meaning of the words that were not clear.

As for the application of the meaning: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, in the same way, [the Blessed One] has raised me up from wrong teachings, I who was standing in wrong teachings and turned away from the true Dhamma. Just as one might reveal what was hidden, in the same way, [the Blessed One] has revealed the Dispensation which had been hidden by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. Just as one might show the way to one who is lost, in the same way, [the Blessed One] has shown the right path to heaven and liberation to me who had entered upon the wrong path of false views. Just as one might bring an oil lamp into the darkness, in the same way, [the Blessed One] has held forth the lamp of the teaching which destroys the darkness of delusion that covered me, who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the forms of the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha. Thus, he means: "The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Venerable Gotama, being revealed through these various methods."

## The Discussion on Rejoicing in the Teaching is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Manner of Devotion

Having praised the teaching in this way, with a mind full of faith in the Triple Gem due to this teaching, and wishing to show the manner of one who is devoted, he said the words beginning with "Esāhaṃ." In that context, "Esāhaṃ" means "I here." "Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi" means "I go to the Venerable Gotama for refuge." It means: "I approach, I resort to, I serve, and I attend upon the Venerable Gotama with the intention that 'The Venerable Gotama is my refuge, my resort, the dispeller of my suffering, and the provider of my welfare.'" Alternatively, it means "I know thus, I understand thus." Indeed, roots that have the meaning of 'going' (gati) also have the meaning of 'knowing' (buddhi). Therefore, in this word "gacchāmi," this meaning of "I know, I understand" also...
141:
The meaning has been stated. In these words 'Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca', the meaning of the components should be understood as follows: It is called 'Dhamma' (the Law/Truth) because it sustains those established in the Fruit who have attained the Path and realized the Truth of Cessation, as well as those established in the Path who are practicing in accordance with the instructions and noble worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), preventing them from falling into the four woeful states. In the ultimate sense, that Dhamma is indeed the Noble Path and Nibbāna.

It has also been said: 'Monks, as far as conditioned things (saṅkhata) extend, the Noble Eightfold Path is said to be the foremost among them,' and so on, the detail of which should be understood. This Dhamma is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna; indeed, it also includes the Noble Fruits along with the Scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma). It has also been said in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna:

'Go for refuge to this Dhamma, which is the fading of lust, free from craving and sorrow, unconditioned, not repulsive, sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed.'

In this verse, the word 'rāgavirāga' (fading of lust) refers to the Path. The words 'anejamasoka' (free from craving and sorrow) refer to the Fruit. The words 'dhamma-masaṅkhata' (unconditioned Dhamma) refer to Nibbāna. The words 'appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ' (not repulsive, sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed) refer to all the masses of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) as categorized in the Three Piṭakas.

It is called 'Saṅgha' (the Community) because it is joined together by the union of view and virtue. In the ultimate sense, that Saṅgha is the assembly of the eight noble persons. In that very same Vimāna, it is said:

'The Buddhas say that an offering given to these four pairs of pure men bears great fruit; these four pairs are the eight noble persons; go for refuge to this Saṅgha.'

The assembly of monks is called the 'Bhikkhu-saṅgha'. With this sequence of words, the Brahmin declared his three goings for refuge to the Blessed One.

## The Discussion on the Manner of Devotion is finished.

## Discussion on Going for Refuge

Now, for the sake of skill regarding these three goings for refuge, one should understand the following procedure: the refuge (saraṇa), the going for refuge (saraṇagamana), the one who goes for refuge, the divisions of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, the defilement, and the breach. If it were spoken here, it would make the Vinaya-nidāna (Introduction to the Vinaya) too burdensome, so it is not mentioned. Those who desire it should take it from the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, in the explanation of the Bhayabherava Sutta, or from the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, in the explanation of the Refuges.

## Discussion on Going for Refuge is finished.

## Discussion on the Declaration of Being a Lay Follower

'May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower' means 'May Master Gotama record me thus: This person is a lay follower.' For the sake of skill in the procedure of being a lay follower...
142:
In this context, who is a lay follower (upāsaka)? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his virtue (sīla)? What is his livelihood (ājīva)? What is his failure (vipatti)? What is his success (sampatti)? These miscellaneous points should be understood. Because these points are very burdensome [to explain here], they are not analyzed in detail here. Those who wish to know should understand them according to the method already stated in the Majjhima Commentary named Papañcasūdanī.

In the word 'ajjatagge', the term 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning, tip, portion, and best. In phrases such as 'Friend gatekeeper, from today onwards (ajjatagge), I close the door to the Nigaṇṭha men and Nigaṇṭha women,' it is seen in the sense of 'beginning'. In phrases such as 'With that very fingertip (aṅgulagga), one should touch that fingertip,' and 'the tip of a sugarcane, the tip of a bamboo,' it is seen in the sense of 'tip'. In phrases such as 'I allow a sour portion (ambilagga), or a sweet portion, or a bitter portion,' and 'Monks, I allow [you] to distribute by the portion of a monastery (vihāragga) or the portion of a precinct (pariveṇagga),' it is seen in the sense of 'portion'. In phrases such as 'Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed... the Tathāgata is said to be the best (agga) among those beings,' it is seen in the sense of 'best'.

In this context, however, this word 'agga' should be understood in the sense of 'beginning'. Therefore, 'ajjatagge' means 'starting from today'; this is how the meaning should be understood here. 'Ajjataṃ' means 'the state of today'. There is also a reading 'ajjadagge', where the letter 'da' is a euphonic sandhi consonant; it means 'starting from today'.

'Pāṇupetaṃ' means endowed with life, endowed with life for as long as my life lasts. It means: 'May the Venerable Gotama recognize and know me as one who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, having no other teacher.' For even if they were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' or of the Dhamma, 'It is not the Dhamma,' or of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha.' In this context, it should be understood that the Brahmin, by stating his taking of refuge again with the words 'gone for refuge for as long as life lasts,' manifests his self-dedication (attasanniyyātana).

Having thus dedicated himself, wishing to serve the Blessed One together with his retinue, he said: 'May the Venerable Gotama together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus consent to spend the rains retreat (vassāvāsa) in Verañjā.' What is meant is: 'May the Venerable Gotama recognize me as a lay follower, and may he consent to spend the rains retreat in Verañjā for my benefit, accepting to stay for three months depending on Verañjā.' The Blessed One consented by silence. This means that upon hearing the Brahmin's words, the Blessed One, without moving any part of his body or speech, and having internal endurance, consented by silence; he accepted in his mind for the sake of favoring the Brahmin.
143:
Then the Verañja Brahmin, knowing the Blessed One's acceptance—this means: Then the Verañja Brahmin, [thinking] 'If the ascetic Gotama did not accept my invitation, he would have rejected it by body or speech. But since he did not reject it and maintained internal endurance, he has accepted it for me by mind alone,' thus knowing the Blessed One's acceptance through his skill in observing signs, he rose from his seat, respectfully saluted the Blessed One from the four directions, and circumambulated him three times. Although he had previously criticized [the Buddha] by saying that since the time he arrived, he did not perform salutations and so on to Brahmins who were elderly by birth, now, having understood the Buddha's qualities, even though he saluted many times with body, speech, and mind, he was still not satisfied. He raised his joined palms, which were brilliant with the combination of his ten fingernails, placed them on his head, and as long as he was within sight, he departed while facing the Blessed One. At the point where he was leaving the range of vision, he saluted and went away.

## The Discussion on the Declaration of Lay Followership is finished.

## Discussion on Famine

At that time, Verañjā was afflicted by famine—this means: At the time when the Verañja Brahmin requested the Blessed One to spend the rains retreat depending on Verañjā, Verañjā was afflicted by famine. Famine (dubbhikkhā) means that alms are difficult to obtain. This difficulty in obtaining alms can occur even when crops are good and prices are very cheap in a place where people have no faith and no devotion. In Verañjā, however, it was not like that; it occurred because of the fault of hunger due to bad crops. Therefore, wishing to show that reason, [the Buddha] said 'dvīhitikā' and so on. Therein, 'dvīhitikā' means having two kinds of anxiety (īhita). 'Īhita' means a state of mind. It refers to the occurrence of two kinds of mental states or anxieties, such as: 'Will we get anything or not when we wander for alms here?' and 'Will we be able to survive or not?'

Alternatively, 'dvīhitikā' means difficulty in livelihood (dujjīvikā). The terms īhita, īhā, iriyana, pavattana, and jīvita have the same meaning. Therefore, it is called 'dvīhitikā' because one lives with difficulty and effort. 'Setaṭṭhikā' means having white bones. It means that the bones of poor people, who died without receiving anything even after begging all day, are scattered here and there, white like mushrooms. Alternatively, there is a reading 'setaṭṭhikā' [with a different nuance]. The meaning of that reading is as follows: In this Verañjā, there is a crop disease called 'seta-aṭṭhi'. Therefore, it is called 'setaṭṭhikā'. 'Aṭṭhi' refers to a distressing disease or affliction. In Verañjā, at the time when the crops were just beginning to ear, a disease caused by white insects (setaka) destroyed them, causing the milky sap to dry up so that the grains did not form, and only white ears of hill rice, barley, and wild rice appeared. Because of having such a crop disease, Verañjā is called 'setaṭṭhikā'.
144:
Regarding the term "setaṭṭhikā," there is also a variant reading "setaṭṭhikā." The meaning of this term is: it is called "setaṭṭhikā" because there is white blight (aṭṭi) in this place. "Aṭṭi" means an oppressive affliction or disease. In that city of Verañjā, when the crops are about to form ears and are in the stage of taking in the embryo, they are destroyed by a white disease (mildew/blight). Consequently, the milky sap is cut off, the grain does not form, and the heads of the Sāli rice, barley, or wheat emerge as pure white. Therefore, it is called "setaṭṭhikā."

Even if the crops are well-prepared and sown during the planting season, in that place, the crops only grow to the size of a stalk (salākā); hence they are called "salākāvuttā." Alternatively, they are called "salākāvuttā" because people subsist by means of tickets (salākā). What does this mean? In that place, when buyers go to the grain sellers, the strong people overpower the weak and buy up the grain. The weak, unable to get grain, cry out. Then the grain sellers, thinking, "We will support everyone," station a grain measurer at the measuring site and a ticket-issuer on one side. Those desiring grain must go to that clerk. That clerk takes the price according to the order of arrival and writes a ticket saying, "Give this much to such-and-such a person." They take that ticket, go to the grain measurer, and receive grain according to the given order. Thus, because they subsist by means of tickets, it is called "salākāvuttā."

When it is said that it is not easy to subsist by alms-gathering with a bowl held in the hand, it means it is not easy for the Noble Ones (ariyas) to subsist by wandering for alms while holding a bowl.
