At that time, even after wandering through seven or eight villages in that region, they did not receive even enough alms for a single day's sustenance.

At that time, horse merchants from the northern region (Uttarāpatha)... (and so on). "The Blessed One heard the sound of the mortars" means: this occurred at the time when the Blessed One was observing the rains-retreat depending on the city of Verañjā. The horse merchants, called "Uttarāpathaka" because they lived in the northern region or came from the northern region, took five hundred horses from the breeding grounds in the northern region. Seeking double or triple profit, they were traveling to another region and arrived at Verañjā to observe the rains-retreat. Why? Because in that region, it is impossible to travel long distances during the four months of the rainy season. Those merchants built houses for themselves and stables for the horses in a place outside the city that was not flooded by water, and they enclosed them with fences. The places where those merchants lived were known as "horse circles" (assamaṇḍalikā).
145:
Because they could not travel long distances during the four months of the rainy season, those merchants had houses for themselves and horse stables built in a place outside the city that was not flooded by water, enclosed them with fences, and lived there. The places where they lived were called "assamaṇḍalikā" (horse circles). Therefore, (the Venerable Upāli) said: "Those merchants designated a pattha measure of steamed barley for each of the monks in the horse circles."

"Patthapatthapulaka" means a pattha measure of steamed barley for each monk. A pattha is about the size of a nāḷi (measure), which is sufficient for one person's sustenance. Thus, it has been said (in the Jātaka): "Rice cooked from one pattha is not enough for two." "Pulaka" refers to barley grain that has been husked and steamed. If it were with the husks, insects would infest it, and it would not last for a long journey. Therefore, those merchants took barley grain prepared to last for a long journey, thinking, "In places where grass for the horses to eat is scarce, this barley will be fodder for the horses."

Why did those merchants designate that barley to be offered to the monks? To answer: Those merchants were not like the people of the southern region (Dakkhiṇāpatha) who lack faith and devotion. They were faithful and devoted, having great affection for the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. While entering the city for some business in the morning, those merchants saw seven or eight monks, well-dressed, well-robed, and possessed of graceful deportment, wandering for alms throughout the entire city for two or three days without receiving anything. Seeing this, the thought occurred to those merchants: "The venerable ones have entered the rains-retreat depending on this city, but because there is a famine, they receive nothing and are suffering greatly."

"We are also visitors, so we are unable to prepare and offer gruel and rice to the venerable ones every day. However, our horses receive fodder twice, in the evening and in the morning. It would be good if we were to give a pattha measure of barley from the morning meal of each horse to each monk. In this way, the venerable ones will not suffer, and the horses will also subsist." (Thus they thought). Those merchants went to the monks, informed them of this matter, and requested, "Venerable sirs, please accept this pattha measure of barley and consume it however you can," and they designated a pattha measure of barley to be offered daily. Therefore, it is said: "Those merchants designated a pattha measure of steamed barley for each of the monks in the horse circles."
146:
"Paññatta" means established in the form of a regular meal. In the current context of the phrase "bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā" and so forth, "pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" means in the forenoon or morning time. Alternatively, it refers to the entire duration of the morning. The accusative case (upayogavacana) is used here in the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). "Nivāsetvā" means adjusting and wearing the inner robe. This should be understood as readjusting the inner robe already worn in the monastery. This is because those monks were not without inner robes before that adjustment. "Pattacīvaramādāya" means taking the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, or receiving and carrying them. This is because monks who take them in any manner are simply said to be "taking" (ādāya), as in the teaching "Having undertaken (samādāya), he departs." "Piṇḍaṃ alabhamānā" means that although they wandered through the whole of Verañjā, they did not receive alms-food, and they did not even receive the words "Please move on" (aticchatha).

"Patthapatthapulakaṃ ārāmaṃ āharitvā" means taking a measure (pattha) of steamed grain (pulaka) obtained from wherever they went and bringing it to the monastery. "Udukkhale koṭṭetvā koṭṭetvā paribhuñjanti" (they eat after pounding it in a mortar) is because there was no lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) for the elders who would take that grain and cook gruel or rice for them. Cooking for oneself is neither suitable nor allowable for monks. Those elders, thinking, "In this way, we will have a light livelihood and be free from the fault of self-cooking," gathered in groups of eight or ten, pounded the grain in a mortar, moistened their respective portions with water, and ate. Having eaten in this way, they practiced the Dhamma of a recluse without anxiety. For the Blessed One, however, those horse traders offered a measure of steamed grain along with suitable ghee, honey, and sugar. The Venerable Ānanda brought that grain and ground it on a stone slab. The work done by a person endowed with merit and wisdom is indeed pleasing. Then, having ground it and mixed it well with ghee and other ingredients, he offered it to the Blessed One. At that time, the deities infused divine essence (dibboja) into that grain. The Blessed One partook of it. Having eaten, he spent the time in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). From that time on, he did not wander for alms.

If it is asked, "Was the Venerable Ānanda the attendant of the Blessed One at that time?" The answer is: He was, but he had not yet received the official position of attendant. For during the first twenty years after the Blessed One's Enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi), there was no permanent attendant. Sometimes the Venerable Nāgasamāla attended the Blessed One, sometimes the Venerable Nāgita, sometimes the Venerable Meghiya, sometimes the Venerable Upavāṇa, sometimes the Venerable Sāgata, and sometimes Sunakkhatta.
147:
The Licchavi prince (Sunakkhatta) also used to attend the Blessed One. Those attendants, such as Nāgasamāla, would attend according to their own desire and depart when they wished. The Venerable Ānanda would remain indifferent while those various elders were attending, and only when they had departed would he himself perform the major and minor duties. The Blessed One also reflected, "Although my noble kinsman (Ānanda) has not yet received the official position of attendant, in such a situation (where alms are scarce), he alone is suitable," and thus he consented. Therefore, it is said: "The Venerable Ānanda, having ground the horse-grain (or dried grain) on a stone slab, offered it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One partook of it."

Do not people strive greatly to perform meritorious deeds when a famine occurs? Do they not think that even if they do not eat themselves, they should give to the bhikkhus? Why, then, did they not give even a spoonful of alms at that time? And this Brahmin of Verañjā, who had invited the Blessed One to spend the rains with great effort—why did he not even know of the Blessed One's presence? It is said: because of the interference of Māra (mārāvaṭṭana). As soon as the Brahmin of Verañjā had departed from the presence of the Blessed One, Māra confused the entire city and the surrounding area within a league—wherever one could go for alms and return before the meal—making everyone forgetful, and then he departed. Therefore, not a single person remembered to perform even the slightest act of respect.

Did the Blessed One enter the rains-retreat there without knowing about Māra's interference? He did not enter without knowing. If so, why did he not go to one of the cities such as Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha? Let alone Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha; even if the Blessed One had gone to Uttarakuru or the city of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa) to spend the rains that year, Māra would have interfered there as well. For in that year, Māra's mind was overwhelmed by an extreme grudge. However, the Blessed One saw this special reason here: "The horse traders will support the bhikkhus." Therefore, he spent the rains in Verañjā itself.

Could Māra not interfere with the traders? It is not that he could not, but those traders arrived after the interference had ended. Why did he not interfere when they returned? Because he did not dare. Māra does not dare to obstruct the alms-food brought for the Tathāgata, the regular offerings, or the requisites brought to the monastery. In fact, no one can obstruct four things. Which four? 1. No one can obstruct the alms-food brought for the Tathāgata or the four requisites that have already been dedicated as regular offerings. 2. No one can obstruct the life of the Buddhas. 3. No one can obstruct the eighty minor marks and the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabhā). (The light of the moon, sun, devas, and Brahmas vanishes in the presence of the Buddha's radiance). 4. No one can obstruct the Omniscient Wisdom (sabbaññutaññāṇa) of the Buddhas. Since no one can obstruct these four things, Māra also could not, and the Blessed One and the community of monks received alms-food.
148:
No one is able to cause harm to the life of the Buddhas. No one is able to cause harm to the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana) or to the fathom-wide aura (byāmappabhā). Indeed, even the radiance of the moon, the sun, the devas, and the Brahmas loses its power upon reaching the vicinity of the Tathāgata's minor marks and fathom-wide aura. No one is able to cause harm to the omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) of the Buddhas. Thus, no one can cause harm to these four things. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, then partook of the alms-food that Māra could not interfere with.

While partaking in this way, one day the Blessed One heard the sound of mortars (udukkhalasadda). The Blessed One heard the sound of mortars produced by the striking of pestles by monks who were pounding portions of grain. Thereafter, the statement beginning with 'The Tathāgatas ask even though they know' was spoken (by the Elders of the Council) to show the answer to the question asked later: 'Ānanda, what is that sound of mortars?' In this regard, this is the summary explanation: The Tathāgatas, even though they know, ask if there is a reason for such a question. If there is no such reason, they do not ask even though they know. Since there is no such thing as 'not knowing' for the Buddhas, it is not said 'even though they do not know.' They ask knowing the proper time: if it is the right time for that question, they ask knowing that time; if it is not, they do not ask, also knowing the time. In asking thus, the Tathāgatas ask only what is connected with benefit (atthasaṃhita); they ask only what is based on benefit and based on reason, not what is not connected with benefit. Why? Because the Tathāgatas have completely destroyed what is not connected with benefit by means of the bridge-destruction (setughāta). The 'bridge' (setu) refers to the Path (magga); it means the destruction and uprooting of such speech by the Path itself.

Now, in this phrase 'connected with benefit' (atthasaṃhitaṃ), to show what kind of speech connected with benefit the Tathāgatas ask about, he said 'for two reasons' (dvīhākārehi), etc. There, 'reasons' (ākārehi) means causes. 'We shall teach the Dhamma' means we shall speak a Sutta connected with a present occasion or a Jātaka connected with past conduct. 'We shall prescribe a training rule (sikkhāpada) for the disciples' means we shall make the transgression manifest to the disciples through that question and prescribe a heavy or light training rule, establishing the authority.

In the passage 'Then the Blessed One... pe... reported this matter,' there is nothing special to be said. It is said 'reported this matter' referring to the reporting of what was mentioned before: the monks obtaining portions of grain, their simple living, and their release from cooking for themselves.
149:
The Blessed One said 'Excellent, excellent, Ānanda' (Sādhu sādhu, Ānanda) wishing to greatly gladden the Venerable Ānanda. Having given the approval (sādhukāra), and choosing one of the two reasons—teaching the Dhamma—he said: 'Ānanda, by you good men, victory has been won; the future generation will look down upon even rice and meat (sālimaṃsodana).'

The meaning therein is: Ānanda, by you good men, in this time of famine when alms-food is hard to get, victory has been won through this simple living and this practice of effacement (sallekha). What victory has been won? Victory over famine has been won, victory over greed (lobha) has been won, victory over evil desire (icchācāra) has been won.

How was victory over famine won? 'This city of Verañjā is short of food, but the nearby villages and market towns all around are abundant with food and easy to get alms, with crops bending under the weight of fruit. Even so, the Blessed One stays here, restraining us.' Not even a single monk had such a thought or mental distress. Thus, famine was conquered, overcome, and brought under control.

How was victory over greed won? 'This city of Verañjā is short of food, but the nearby villages are abundant. Come, let us go there and eat.' Not even a single monk, through the power of greed, cut short the night or cut short the Vassa saying 'Let us spend the latter Vassa there.' Thus, greed was conquered.

How was victory over evil desire won? 'This city of Verañjā is short of food, and these people do not care for us even though we have lived here for two or three months. What if we engage in trading virtues (guṇavāṇijja), making it known to people that "this monk has attained the first jhāna... this monk has the six higher powers (abhiññā)," and after supporting our bellies, we later undertake the precepts?' Not even a single monk gave rise to such a desire. Thus, evil desire was conquered, overcome, and brought under control.

In the future, the later generation of monks, while staying in the monastery and obtaining food without difficulty, will look down upon even rice and meat, saying: 'What is this? The rice is too hard, or too soft; it lacks salt, or is too salty; it is not sour, or too sour; what is the use of this food?' and so on. They will discriminate between low and high quality.

Alternatively, a region is not always famished; sometimes it is famished, sometimes it is abundant. When that region becomes abundant, people who are inspired by this practice of effacement of you good men will think: 'They offer various kinds of delicacies, rice, and meat to the monks.' The future generations, your fellow practitioners, will live among you and enjoy those gains and offerings (lābhasakkāra) that arose because of you, and they will think too much of it. Because of those gains and offerings, they will become arrogant and dismissive. They will say to one another: 'Why do you cook so much food? Put your own property in the pot!'
150:
People will think: 'Various kinds of fine rice and meat-curry should be offered to the monks.' Relying on you, the future generations of your fellow practitioners will sit among you and enjoy the offerings that have arisen, and they will become conceited. Because of enjoying those offerings, they will act with pride and contempt. How? (They will say:) 'Why is so much food cooked? Do you not have pots to put your own property in?' (thus showing contempt).

## The Discussion on Famine is Finished.

## The Section on the Lion’s Roar of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna

In the words beginning with "Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno," the word "Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. It is also a designation expressing respect, reverence, and deference towards those worthy of honor. "Mahāmoggallāna" means he is "Mahā" (Great) due to the greatness of his virtues, and "Moggallāna" by lineage; thus, he is called "Mahāmoggallāna." "Etadavoca" means he spoke these words. Now, the words spoken such as "Venerable Sir, at this time" are shown. Why did he speak? It is heard that the Elder reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa) on the seventh day after his ordination. The Teacher also placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) for having great psychic power. Relying on his great psychic power, that Elder thought: "This city of Verañjā is very famine-stricken, and the monks are exhausted. What if I were to overturn the earth and let the monks eat the essence of the earth (papphaṭakoja)?"

After thinking thus, the thought occurred to the Elder again: "While I am living in the presence of the Blessed One, if I were to do this without requesting the Blessed One, it would not be proper for me; it would be as if I were competing with the Blessed One." Therefore, desiring to request, he came and spoke these words to the Blessed One.

The phrase "heṭṭhimatalaṃ sampannaṃ" means that there is soil-essence, earth-nutriment, and an earth-layer on the lower surface of the earth; he spoke referring to that earth-essence. In that phrase, "sampannaṃ" means sweet and having a delicious taste. Just as in the phrase "There the tree has sweet fruit (sampannaphala) and abundant fruit," where "sampannaphala" means having sweet fruit, so too here "sampannaṃ" should be understood as sweet and having a delicious taste. The phrase "seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ anīḷakaṃ" is said to illustrate the sweetness of that earth-essence by way of a simile. "Khuddamadhu" is honey made by small bees. "Anīḷakaṃ" means pure honey that is without bees and without larvae. That honey is [superior] to all other honeys...
151:
...is supreme, excellent, tasty, and nutritious. Therefore, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said: "Just as, for example, pure honey made by small bees, without bees or larvae, has such a taste."

"Sādhāhaṃ bhante" means "Venerable Sir, I request well." Here, the word "Sādhu" is a word expressing a request. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, desiring to request to overturn the earth, spoke thus to the Blessed One. "Parivatteyyaṃ" means "I would overturn [the earth]," "I would make the lower surface the upper surface." Why did he wish to do so? Because if it were done thus, the monks would easily enjoy the earth-essence, the layer of the earth's surface.

Then the Blessed One, although not wishing to grant permission, asked the Elder in order to let him utter a lion's roar: "Moggallāna, what will you do with the beings that depend on the earth?" This means: the beings in the villages, market towns, etc., who depend on the earth, will not be able to stay in the sky when the earth is being overturned; what will you do with them, and where will you place them?

Then the Elder, wishing to manifest his psychic power in accordance with the foremost position (etadagga) bestowed upon him by the Blessed One, said: "Venerable Sir, I [will make] one hand..." and so on. The meaning is: "Venerable Sir, I will create one hand to be like this great earth; I will make it similar to the earth. Having done so, I will transfer the beings depending on the earth onto that created hand, just as one transfers beings from one palm to the second palm."

Then the Blessed One, wishing to reject his request, said: "Enough, Moggallāna," and so on. There, "Alaṃ" is a word of rejection. Beings might also fall into confusion (vippallāsa). How? "Is this the earth, or is it not?" Or, "Is this our village, or is it someone else's?" Thus, they might reach a perverted view regarding market towns, districts, fields, parks, and so on.

Alternatively, this kind of confusion is not [necessarily] "vippallāsa," for the range of psychic power of one with psychic power is unthinkable. However, they might obtain this kind of confusion: "This famine does not occur only now; it will also occur in the future. At that time, where will the monks find such a fellow practitioner possessed of psychic power?" At that time, even though there may be monks who are Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, dry-insight practitioners, attainers of jhānas, or Arahants who have reached the analytical knowledges, they will approach other families for alms because they lack the strength of psychic power.

Then, people will have this thought: "In the time of the Buddha, monks were fulfillers of the training rules. Having produced virtues, they overturned the earth and enjoyed the earth-essence during times of famine. Now, however, there are no fulfillers of the training rules. If there were, they would do the same. For us, any..."
152:
“They might think, ‘One should not give anything, whether cooked or raw, to be eaten.’ In this way, they would acquire this perversion of view (vipallāsa) even regarding those manifest Noble Ones (Ariyas), thinking, ‘There are no Noble Ones.’ By the power of that perversion of view, they would revile and slander the Noble Ones to their faces and behind their backs, and thus they would go to the states of deprivation (apāya). Therefore, Moggallāna, do not favor the overturning of the earth.”

Then the Elder, not obtaining this request to overturn the earth and wishing to make another request, said, “Very well, Bhante,” and so on. The Blessed One, wishing to reject that request as well, said, “Enough, Moggallāna,” and so on. In those words, “Enough, Moggallāna,” even if it was not explicitly said that “beings would acquire a perversion of view,” it should be understood according to the method previously mentioned; the meaning of those words should be known as being similar to what was already stated. If the Blessed One had given permission, what would the Elder have done? He would have resolved that the Great Ocean be like a small trench that could be crossed in a single stride, and having brought forth the path from the Naḷerupucimanda tree towards the island of Uttarakuru, he would have placed Uttarakuru in a position accessible for coming and going. If he had shown it thus, the monks would have entered and exited for alms as easily as if they were entering a village for fodder.

## The account of Mahā Moggallāna’s Lion’s Roar is finished.

## Commentary on the Request for the Promulgation of the Vinaya

Now, the Venerable Upāli, wishing to show the origin and the starting point of the promulgation of the Vinaya, and to show the arising of the reflection concerning the training rules (sikkhāpada) of the Elder Sāriputta, said, “Atha kho āyasmato Sāriputtassa,” and so on. Therein, “rahogatassa” means of one who has gone into seclusion. “Paṭisallīnassa” means of one who is well-withdrawn, who has attained the state of being alone. “Katamesānaṃ” means of which of the past Buddhas, such as Vipassī and others. “Ciraṭṭhitikaṃ” means that which has a long endurance, or because of its long-lasting nature, it is called ciraṭṭhitika. The remaining words here have meanings that are plain and clear.

Was the Elder unable to decide this reflection of his by himself? It is said: He was both able and unable. He was able to distinguish and decide this much: “The Dispensation (Sāsana) of Buddhas with such names did not last long; the Dispensation of Buddhas with such names lasted long.” However, he was unable to personally distinguish and decide the root cause: “For this reason it did not last long; for this reason it lasted long.” But the Elder Mahā Paduma said: “Even this matter...”
153:
“For a Chief Disciple who has reached the pinnacle of the sixteen kinds of knowledge, it would not be a burden (to know that reason). However, while living in the same place as the Fully Enlightened One, making a decision by oneself would be like discarding a scale and weighing with one's hand; therefore, he approached the Blessed One and asked. Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer him, said, ‘Sāriputta, of the Blessed One Vipassī...’ and so on. The meaning of that speech is plain and clear.

Again, the Elder, wishing to ask for the cause, said, ‘Bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition?’ and so on. Therein, ‘Bhante, what is it?’ is an inquiry into the cause, and its meaning is ‘Bhante, which one is it?’ Both terms ‘hetu’ (cause) and ‘paccaya’ (condition) are designations for a cause. Because the result is produced from it, it is called ‘hetu.’ Because the result arises depending on it, it is called ‘paccaya.’ Thus, although they are one in meaning, both are used in various places for the sake of conventional usage and for the smoothness of speech. The remaining words here have meanings that are plain and clear.

Now, to show that cause and condition, He said, ‘Sāriputta, the Blessed One Vipassī...’ and so on. Therein, ‘kilāsuno’ (weary/indolent) does not mean being weary due to laziness; for Buddhas have no laziness or slackening of energy. When Buddhas teach the Dhamma to one person, to two, or to the beings of the entire universe, they teach the Dhamma with equal effort. They do not slacken their energy upon seeing a small audience, nor do they increase their energy upon seeing a large one. For example, a lion, the king of beasts, when going out for food after seven days, runs with the same speed whether the prey is small or large. Why is that? Thinking, ‘Let my speed not diminish.’ Similarly, the Buddhas teach the Dhamma with equal effort whether the audience is small or large. Why is that? Thinking, ‘Let our reverence for the Dhamma (dhamma-garutā) not diminish.’ This is because Buddhas are those who revere the Dhamma.

Although our Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail, as if filling the Great Ocean, those Buddhas did not teach in such detail. Why? Because beings had little dust in their eyes (defilements). It is said that in the time of those Buddhas, beings were long-lived and had little dust in their eyes. They could penetrate the Dhamma even by hearing a single verse related to the Four Noble Truths; therefore, they did not teach the Dhamma in detail. For that very reason, their Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—the nine factors—were few. The differences among these Suttas and so on have already been stated in the commentary on the First Council.”
154:
Because the disciples were faultless, [the Buddha] did not yet prescribe the disciplinary rules (Sikkhāpada) of authority, which are prescribed according to the nature of the fault through the power of the seven groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha). The Pātimokkha shown by authority (Āṇā-pātimokkha) was also not recited every fortnight.

Those Buddhas recited only the Ovāda-pātimokkha (Pātimokkha of exhortation). Even that Ovāda-pātimokkha was not recited every fortnight. How was it then? The Blessed One Vipassī recited the Ovāda-pātimokkha only once every six years. In doing so, he recited it himself. His disciples did not recite the Pātimokkha in their respective places of residence. In the whole of Jambudīpa, in only one place—the royal capital of Bandhumatī, in the Khema Deer Park, where the Blessed One Vipassī resided—the entire Saṅgha of monks performed the Uposatha together. That Uposatha was only the Saṅgha-uposatha; it was not Gaṇa-uposatha, Puggala-uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha, or Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha.

At that time, it is said there were eighty-four thousand monasteries in Jambudīpa. In each monastery, ten thousand, twenty thousand, or even more monks resided. Deities who announce the Uposatha day would go to those various monasteries and say: "Sirs, one year, two, three, four, five years have passed. This is now the sixth year. You should go to see the Buddha and perform the Uposatha on the coming full moon day. The time for your assembly has arrived."

Upon hearing this, the monks with psychic power went by their own power; others went by the power of the deities. How? It is said that those monks, whether they were at the edge of the eastern, western, northern, or southern oceans, would fulfill their minor and major duties before traveling, take their bowls and robes, and as soon as the thought "Let us go" arose, they would arrive at the place of the Uposatha. Those monks would pay homage to the Fully Enlightened One Vipassī and sit down. The Blessed One would then recite this Ovāda-pātimokkha to the assembled company:

"Patience is the highest austerity, forbearance;
The Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme;
One who harms others is not a renunciant;
One who oppresses others is not a recluse (samaṇa).

Not doing any evil,
The fulfillment of what is wholesome,
Purifying one's own mind—
This is the teaching of the Buddhas."
155:
"Not reviling, not harming,
Restraint in the Pātimokkha,
Moderation in eating,
Secluded lodging,
Devotion to higher mind—
This is the teaching of the Buddhas." (D. ii. 90; Dhp. 183-185)

In this same way, the recitation of the Pātimokkha of other Buddhas should also be understood. Indeed, for all Buddhas, there are only these three verses of the Ovāda-pātimokkha. For long-lived Buddhas, these come to be recited [as the Pātimokkha] until the end of the Dispensation (Sāsana). For short-lived Buddhas, it is only during the early period of Enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi). From the time the training rules (Sikkhāpada) are prescribed, however, only the Āṇā-pātimokkha (Pātimokkha of authority) is recited. And that Āṇā-pātimokkha is recited only by the monks, not by the Buddhas. Therefore, our Blessed One also recited this Ovāda-pātimokkha only for about twenty years during the early period of Enlightenment. Then one day, while sitting at the Migāramātu Palace in Pubbārāma, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, from now on, I will no longer perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha. Monks, from now on, you yourselves shall perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha. It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a Tathāgata should perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly." (Cv. 386). From that time onwards, the monks have recited the Āṇā-pātimokkha. This Āဏာ-pātimokkha was not recited during the time of those [three] Buddhas [beginning with Vipassī]. Therefore, it is said, "the Pātimokkha was not recited."

"Of those Buddhas" refers to the three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī. "By disappearance" means by the disappearance of the aggregates, which is to say, by attaining Parinibbāna. "Of the disciples who knew after the Buddhas" refers to the disappearance of the aggregates of the direct disciples who realized the Dhamma in the presence of those Buddhas. "Those later disciples" refers to the later disciples who went forth in the presence of those direct disciples. "Of various names" means those with diverse names such as Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, etc. "Of various clans" means those of diverse clans such as Gotama, Moggallāna, etc. "Of various castes" means those of diverse castes such as Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, etc. "Those who went forth from various families" means those who left their homes and went forth from diverse families, whether by way of the warrior-noble family and so on, or by way of high, low, or very wealthy families.
156:
That holy life means that the later disciples, being of the same name, same lineage, same birth, and same family, went forth and, taking it as their own burden, thinking 'This is the lineage and tradition of our Dispensation,' protected the holy life and maintained the scriptural Dhamma for a long time. However, these disciples were not of such a nature. Therefore, by disputing with one another, taking opposing views, and acting negligently, thinking 'This elder will know, that elder will know,' they caused that holy life to disappear quickly; they did not protect it by rehearsing it in a council. The word 'seyyathāpi' is an illustration of that meaning. 'Vikirati' means scattering in various ways. 'Vidhamati' means carrying to another place. 'Viddhaṃseti' means removing from its place. 'Yathā taṃ suttena asangahitattā' means just as the wind scatters flowers because they are not strung or tied together with a thread, so too it causes them to be scattered. 'Evameva kho' is the completion of the simile. 'Antaradhāpesuṃ' means that without collecting them according to Vaggas or Paṇṇāsas, they took only what they liked and destroyed the rest, leading them to disappearance. 

Those Blessed Ones were not weary in teaching the disciples, discerning their minds with their own. Sāriputta, those Buddhas did not regard teaching as a burden or as a proliferation after knowing the minds of others. The words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ Sāriputta' were spoken to show the tireless effort of those Buddhas. 'Bhiṃsanake' means in a place that is terrifying and causes fear. 'Think in this way' means to think the three kinds of wholesome thoughts, such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka). 'Do not think in this way' means not to think the three kinds of unwholesome thoughts, such as the thought of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka). 'Attend in this way' means to attend as 'impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.' 'Do not attend in this way' means not to attend as 'permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful.' 'Abandon this' means to abandon the unwholesome. 'Having attained this, dwell in it' means to dwell after attaining and accomplishing the wholesome. 

'The minds were liberated from the taints without clinging' means they were liberated without grasping the taints. Indeed, their minds were liberated from the taints, but they did not liberate them by grasping those taints. Rather, they were liberated without clinging because the taints ceased through non-arising. Therefore, it is said, 'The minds were liberated from the taints without clinging.' All those monks, having reached the fruition of Arahantship...
157:
(Those monks, having reached the fruition of Arahantship,) had blossoming minds like a lotus grove touched by the sun's rays. In the phrase 'Tatra sudaṃ sāriputta bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti,' 'tatra' refers to the previously mentioned 'in a certain terrifying forest grove.' 'Sudaṃ' is a particle used merely to complete the word, and 'Sāriputta' is a vocative. The connection of meaning here is: 'tatra' means in that terrifying forest grove spoken of by the Buddha, it occurs because of the terrifying behavior (or state) of that forest grove. What occurs? This occurs: when anyone who is not free from lust (enters that forest), generally their hairs stand on end; this horripilation occurs. 

Alternatively, 'tatra' should be taken as a locative case in the sense of possession (sāmī). 'Su' is a particle, and 'idaṃ' is a word showing the intended meaning as if it were present. In the phonetic combination of 'su-idaṃ,' it should be known that the letter 'i' is dropped to become 'sudaṃ.' The connection of meaning is: Sāriputta, because of the terrifying nature of that terrifying forest grove, this (horripilation) occurs intensely. 'Bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ' means because of the terrifying nature, and it should be noted that one 'ta' is omitted (the original might be bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ). Or, instead of using the feminine form 'bhiṃsanakatāya,' the neuter form is used. This locative case is in the sense of cause (nimittattha); therefore, the connection should be understood as: this occurs because of the terrifying nature, due to that cause, depending on that nature, and by reason of that nature. 

When one who is not free from lust enters that forest grove, 'generally the hairs stand on end' means that many hairs stand up, facing upwards like needles or thorns; a few hairs do not stand up. Or it means horripilation occurs to many beings, but it does not occur to a few very brave men. 

Now, the words beginning with 'Ayaṃ kho sāriputta hetu' are the conclusion. The words left unexplained in between should be understood according to the order of the Pali text, as their meanings are already clear. The phrase 'na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ahosi' (it did not last long) should be understood as being spoken in terms of the generations (succession) of men. In terms of the number of years, the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī was eighty thousand years, and the lifespan of his contemporary disciples was the same. Thus, calculating together with the very last disciple, the Dispensation lasted for one hundred and sixty thousand years. However, in terms of the succession of generations of men...
158:
(By way of pairs of men), when coming down through the succession, only two pairs of men remained. Therefore, it was said, "It is not long-lasting." The lifespan of the Blessed One Sikhī was seventy thousand years. The lifespan of his direct disciples was also the same. The lifespan of the Blessed One Vessabhū was sixty thousand years. The lifespan of his direct disciples was also the same. Thus, the dispensation of those Blessed Ones, in connection with all the final disciples, lasted for forty thousand and twenty thousand years beyond one hundred thousand. However, when coming down through the succession by way of pairs of men, only two pairs of men each remained. Therefore, it was said, "It is not long-lasting."

Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, having heard the reason for the short duration of the dispensations of the three Buddhas, and desiring to hear the reason for the long duration of the dispensations of the other three Buddhas, asked the Blessed One again in this manner: "Venerable Sir, what is the cause?" and so forth. The Blessed One also answered the Venerable Sāriputta. All of that should be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated. In this context of being long-lasting, it should be understood that the dispensations of those Buddhas were long-lasting in two ways: by way of the extent of their lifespan and by way of the pairs of men. The lifespan of the Blessed One Kakusandha was forty thousand years; the lifespan of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was thirty thousand years; and the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa was twenty thousand years. The lifespan of their direct disciples was also the same. Many successions of their pairs of disciples continued the dispensation. Thus, the dispensations of those Buddhas were long-lasting in two ways: by way of the extent of their lifespan and by way of the pairs of disciples.

As for our Blessed One, he should have appeared during the time when the human lifespan was ten thousand years, which is half the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa. Failing to reach that time, he should have appeared when the lifespan was five thousand years, one thousand years, or even five hundred years. However, while our Blessed One was seeking the qualities that make one a Buddha (pāramīs), maturing his knowledge, and conceiving the "womb" of omniscience, his knowledge reached maturity during the time when the lifespan was one hundred years. Therefore, he appeared during a time of very short lifespan. Because of this, although his dispensation is long-lasting by way of the succession of disciples, it is appropriate to say it is "not long-lasting" in terms of the number of years by way of the extent of the lifespan.

What is the connection (anusandhi) of the words "Atha kho āyasmā Sāriputto"? Having heard the reason for the long duration of the dispensations of the three Buddhas, and having reached the conclusion that the prescription of training rules is the only cause for the long duration of the dispensation, and for the long duration of the Blessed One's dispensation...
159:
Having reached the conclusion that the prescription of training rules is the only cause for the long-lasting nature of the dispensation, and desiring the long-lasting nature of the Blessed One's dispensation, the Venerable Sāriputta requested the Blessed One to prescribe training rules. To show the manner of that request, it was said: "Then the Venerable Sāriputta, rising from his seat... may it last for a long time." In that passage, "addhaniya" means capable of enduring a long journey, meaning lasting for a long time. The remaining words have clear meanings.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to make it clear that "this is not yet the time for prescribing training rules," said: "Wait, Sāriputta," and so forth. In that phrase, "āgamehi tvaṃ" means "you stay for a while, you endure for a while." It was said twice here only for the sake of showing respect. By this, the Blessed One rejected the idea that prescribing training rules is within the domain of the disciples, and making it clear that "the prescription of training rules is only the domain of the Buddhas," he said: "The Tathāgata alone (will know the time)," and so forth. Here, the word "tattha" is a locative case word referring to the request for prescribing training rules. The connection of the sentence is as follows: regarding that prescription of training rules which was requested as "may he prescribe training rules," the Tathāgata alone will know the time for that prescription. Having spoken thus, to show that it was not yet the time, he said: "Not yet, Sāriputta," and so forth.

In that passage, those things in which taints (āsava) reside are called "bases for taints" (āsavaṭṭhāniya). This means that in those acts of transgression, there reside the taints of suffering and the taints of defilements pertaining to this life and the next, as well as the taints consisting of others' blame, remorse, killing, imprisonment, and so forth, and the taints that are the specific sufferings of the four lower realms; because those acts of transgression are the cause of those taints. The connection of the sentence here is: as long as those acts of transgression, which are the bases for taints, do not manifest in the Sangha, the Teacher does not yet prescribe training rules for the disciples. For if he were to prescribe them, he would not be free from the faults of others' blame, interference, and criticism.

How so? If he were to prescribe training rules, he would have to prescribe everything, such as: "Whatever monk should engage in sexual intercourse," and so forth. Without seeing the fault of transgression, and knowing only this prescription, others would bring about blame, interference, and criticism in this way: "How is it that the ascetic Gotama binds and entangles us with training rules and prescribes Pārājika offenses just because 'the Sangha of monks follows my will and obeys my words'? Have these noble sons not renounced a great mass of wealth, a great circle of relatives, and even kingdoms already in their hands to go forth? They are content with mere food and clothing, and in training..."
160:
They are content (having great effort in food and clothing). They have a strong sense of reverence for the training. They live without regard for their bodies or their lives. Among those sons of good family, who would indulge in sexual intercourse, which is a worldly bait of defilement? Who would steal another's property? Who would take the life of another, which is desired, beloved, and exceedingly sweet? Or who would make a living by speaking of non-existent qualities? Even though the Pārājika rules have not yet been prescribed, is it not already clear through the very form of monkhood that one should abstain from such things as sexual intercourse?

Beings would not be able to know the power of the Tathāgata in prescribing training rules, nor the strength of His knowledge that penetrates all things. The prescribed training rule would also be corrupted and would not remain in its proper place.

For example, an unskilled physician might call a man who does not yet have a boil and say, "Come, good man, a great boil will arise in this part of your body and bring you to ruin and destruction; let it be treated beforehand." The man says, "Very well, teacher, you yourself treat it." The physician then cuts the healthy part of the body, draws blood, and after applying ointment, bandaging, and washing, makes the flesh grow back. He then says to the man, "I have treated a great disease for you; give me a gift."

That man would accuse, rebuke, and disparage the physician, saying, "What is this foolish physician saying? What disease of mine has he treated? He only caused me pain and made me lose blood." He would not recognize the physician's service.

In the same way, if the Teacher were to prescribe training rules for His disciples before an offense of transgression had occurred, He would not be free from the disparagement of others. Beings would not know the Teacher's power or strength. The prescribed training rule would be corrupted and would not remain in its proper place. Therefore, it was said: "Sāriputta, the Teacher does not [prescribe training rules for His disciples]... until [certain conditions] manifest."

Having thus shown the time that is not suitable for prescribing training rules, He spoke the words beginning with "But when, Sāriputta..." to show the suitable time. In that passage, "yato" means "yadā" (when/at which time). The rest should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

Alternatively, the summary of the meaning is this: At the time when the offenses of transgression, known as "things that are the basis for taints" (āsavaṭṭhāniyā dhammā), manifest in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher prescribes training rules for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha. Why? To ward off those very offenses of transgression known as things that are the basis for taints.

Prescribing in this way is like a skilled physician who treats an existing boil by lancing, applying ointment, bandaging, and washing, thereby calming the disease and making the flesh grow back. He is not subject to disparagement and gains honor as one with recognized power in his craft. Similarly, [the Teacher] is not subject to disparagement, and in the scope of His omniscience...
161:
When [the Blessed One] prescribes a training rule, such prescription is like a physician skilled in treatment who heals a developed abscess by lancing, applying ointment, bandaging, and washing, thereby curing the wound and promoting the growth of new skin. Such a physician is not blamed or criticized but receives honor and respect for being clearly proficient in his teacher's art. Similarly, the Blessed One is not blamed or criticized but attains honor and respect, being clearly proficient in His own domain of Omniscience. That prescribed training rule also remains established in its original state without perishing. This is the summary of the meaning.

In this way, having stated that the non-arising of the states that are the basis for taints (āsavas) is not the time for prescribing training rules, and their arising is the time for prescribing them, He now spoke the words beginning with, "Sāriputta, as long as certain [states that are the basis for taints] have not appeared in this Dispensation..." to show the time of their non-arising and the time of their arising. In that passage, the words with clear meanings should be understood according to the Pāli text itself. This is the explanation of the words that are not clear: They are called 'Rattaññū' because they know the nights. It means they have known many nights since the day of their own renunciation; they have been ordained for a long time. 'Rattaññu-mahattaṃ' means the state of the Saṅgha being great with long-standing monks.

It should be understood that when the Saṅgha reached greatness in terms of long-standing members, the training rule was prescribed on account of the Venerable Upasena Vangantaputta. Seeing monks with less than ten years of seniority conferring ordination, that venerable one, though having only one year of seniority himself, conferred ordination on a co-resident (saddhivihārika). Then the Blessed One prescribed the training rule: "Monks, one with less than ten years of seniority should not confer ordination. Whoever should confer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." After the training rule was thus prescribed, again, foolish and incompetent monks, saying "We have ten years, we have ten years," conferred ordination. Then the Blessed One prescribed another training rule: "Monks, a foolish and incompetent monk should not confer ordination. Whoever should confer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow a competent and capable monk with ten years or more than ten years of seniority to confer ordination." Thus, two training rules were prescribed when the Saṅgha reached greatness in terms of long-standing members.

'Vepulla-mahattaṃ' means greatness by way of abundance and expansion. As long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness in terms of abundance through the presence of elders (thera), newly ordained (nava), and those of middle standing (majjhima), the lodgings remain sufficient. Certain states that are the basis for taints do not yet arise in the Dispensation. Only when greatness in terms of abundance is reached do those states arise. Then the Teacher prescribes training rules for the disciples. In that regard, the training rules prescribed when the Saṅgha reached greatness in terms of abundance should be understood in this manner: "If a monk should lie down for more than two or three nights in the same place with one who is not ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"; "If a bhikkhunī should confer ordination [on a probationer] every year, it is an offense of expiation"; "If a bhikkhunī should confer ordination on two [probationers] within one year, it is an offense of expiation."

'Lābhagga-mahattaṃ' means reaching the pinnacle of gains, meaning the state of having reached the highest and greatest abundance of gains. Or, by way of gains...
162:
Aggamahatta means reaching the state of being noble and great in terms of gains. As long as the Saṅgha has not reached the peak of greatness in gains, things that are the basis for taints (āsavaṭṭhāniyā dhammā) do not arise on account of gains. However, when that state is reached, they do arise. Then the Teacher prescribes a training rule for his disciples: 'If any monk should give with his own hand food or edibles to an unclothed ascetic, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is an offense of Pācittiya.' This training rule was prescribed when the Saṅgha reached the peak of greatness in gains.

Bāhusuccamahatta means the abundance of the state of being very learned. As long as the Saṅgha has not reached the peak of greatness in learning, things that are the basis for taints do not arise. However, when the peak of greatness in learning is reached, individuals who have learned one Nikāya, two... or five Nikāyas, but who reflect improperly, mix the essence of sense-objects with the essence of women and so on, and demonstrate the Teacher's Dispensation in a way that is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya. Then the Teacher prescribes a training rule in this manner: 'If any monk should say thus: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One..." and if a novice should also say thus,' and so on.

In this way, the Blessed One, having shown the time when things that are the basis for taints have not yet arisen and the time when they arise, and wishing to show their total absence at that time, said: 'Sāriputta, the Saṅgha is free from thieves (nirabbuda),' and so on. In that passage, 'nirabbuda' means being free from 'abbuda'; 'abbuda' refers to thieves, thus it means 'without thieves.' In this context, 'thieves' refers specifically to immoral persons. This is because they are not true recluses but, by claiming to be recluses, they steal the requisites of others. Therefore, 'nirabbuda' means free from thieves, which means free from immoral persons. 'Nirādīnava' means free from danger and free from misfortune; it means being free from the fault of immorality. 'Apagatakāḷaka' means 'kāḷaka' refers to immoral persons; even if they have a golden complexion, they should be known as 'black' (kāḷaka) because they are associated with dark, unwholesome states. Because of their absence, it is called 'apagatakāḷaka.' There is also a variant reading 'apahatakāḷaka.' 'Suddha' (pure) means pure, completely clean, and radiant precisely because of being free from stains. 'Sāre patiṭṭhita' (established in the essence) means the qualities of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) are called the 'essence' (sāra); because of being established in that essence, it is called 'sāre patiṭṭhita.'

Having thus spoken of the state of being established in the essence, he again said, 'Sāriputta, to these [monks],' and so on, wishing to show how that state of being established in the essence should be understood.
163:
In that passage, this is the summary explanation: Among those five hundred monks who entered the rains retreat in Verañjā, the monk who is the lowest in terms of qualities, possessing the least qualities, is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). A Stream-enterer is one who has entered the stream (of the Path). 'Sota' (stream) is a designation for the Path. 'Sotāpanna' refers to the person endowed with that Path. As it was said: 'Sāriputta, it is said, "The stream, the stream." What, Sāriputta, is the stream?' 'Venerable sir, this Noble Eightfold Path is the stream; that is, Right View... Right Concentration.' 'Sāriputta, it is said, "A stream-enterer, a stream-enterer." What, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?' 'Venerable sir, the person who is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer; such a venerable one of such a name and such a clan.' In this context, however, the name of the Path is given to the Fruit (phala). Therefore, one who stands in the Fruit should be understood as a 'Stream-enterer.'

'Avinipātadhamma' means one who does not have the nature of falling into the lower realms. Why? Because the states that lead to the lower realms have been exhausted. Or, 'vinipāta' means falling, and 'avinipātadhamma' means one who does not have the nature of falling; it means the nature of falling into the lower realms does not exist for him. He is 'niyata' (assured) because he is fixed by the path which is the law of rightness (sammatta-niyāma). He is 'sambodhiparāyaṇa' (destined for enlightenment) because enlightenment is his ultimate destination and goal. It means he will certainly reach the three higher paths. Why? Because he has attained the first path.

## The Discussion on Requesting the Prescription of Vinaya is Finished.

## Discussion on the Custom of the Buddhas

Having thus convinced the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta), and having spent the rains retreat in Verañjā, the Blessed One, after completing the vassa and performing the Pavāraṇā with the Mahāpavarāṇā, addressed the Venerable Ānanda. 'Addressed' means he spoke to him, conversed with him, and informed him. How? 'Ānanda, this is indeed the custom,' and so on. 'Āciṇṇa' means a practiced habit, a duty, or a tradition. That custom is of two kinds: the custom of the Buddhas (Buddhāciṇṇa) and the custom of the disciples (Sāvakāciṇṇa). What is the custom of the Buddhas? This is one such custom: they do not depart for a walking tour in the countryside without first informing and taking leave of those who invited them to spend the rains retreat.
164:
They depart. As for the disciples, they depart as they please, whether having informed those who invited them or not.

Another custom of the Buddhas is that after completing the rains retreat and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they set out on a walking tour (cārika) through the countryside for the welfare of the people. While wandering on such a tour, they travel within one of these three circles: the Great Circle (Mahāmaṇḍala), the Middle Circle (Majjhimamaṇḍala), or the Final Circle (Antimamaṇḍala). Among these, the Great Circle is nine hundred yojanas in extent, the Middle Circle is six hundred yojanas, and the Final Circle is three hundred yojanas.

When they wish to wander in the Great Circle, they perform the Pavāraṇā on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā (the full moon of Assayuja). On the first day of the waning moon, they set out surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus. Favoring the people in villages and market towns by accepting material offerings and increasing their wholesome merits rooted in liberation through the gift of Dhamma (dhammadāna), they conclude the tour of the countryside in nine months.

However, if the monks' tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) are still immature during the rains retreat, they do not perform the Pavāraṇā on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā but postpone it. They then perform the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Kattika and set out on the first day of Māgasira, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus. Following the aforementioned method, they conclude the tour in the Middle Circle in eight months.

If, at the end of the rains retreat, the spiritual faculties (indriya) of the beings to be tamed (veneyya) are not yet mature, the Buddhas wait for the maturation of their faculties. They remain in that same residence throughout the month of Māgasira and set out on the first day of Phussa, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus. Following the aforementioned method, they conclude the tour in the Final Circle in seven months. While wandering anywhere within these circles, they liberate various beings from defilements and establish them in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so forth, wandering like one who gathers flowers of various colors according to the needs of the beings to be tamed.

Another custom of the Buddhas is to daily enter the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) at dawn, taking the peaceful bliss of Nibbāna as the object; to emerge from the attainment of fruition and daily enter the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti); and after emerging from that, to survey the ten thousand world systems for beings capable of enlightenment.

Another custom of the Buddhas is to be the first to greet visitors with friendly and welcoming speech, to preach the Dhamma according to the occasion, and to prescribe training rules (sikkhāpada) when a fault has been committed. This is the custom of the Buddhas (buddhāciṇṇa).
165:
What is the custom of the disciples (sāvakāciṇṇa)? During the time of the Blessed Buddha, they assembled twice: once before the commencement of the rains retreat to receive meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and once after completing the rains retreat to report the spiritual qualities they had attained and to receive further meditation subjects for higher attainments. This is the custom of the disciples. Here, however, to show the custom of the Buddhas, it was said: "Ananda, this is the custom of the Tathāgatas."

"Āyāma" means "Come, let us go." "Apalokessāma" means "We shall take leave [of the residents] for the purpose of wandering on a tour." The particle "Evaṃ" is used in the sense of consent. "Bhante" is a term of respect; it can also be said to be the response given to the Teacher. "Bhagavato paccassosi" means he listened to the words of the Blessed Buddha, faced him, and accepted them. It means he consented with the word "Evaṃ."

In the phrase "Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā" (Then the Blessed One, having dressed), it is not explicitly stated whether it was morning or evening. Nevertheless, after the Blessed One had finished his meal and let the midday pass, he took the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk and, starting from the city gate, proceeded toward the residence of the Brahmin Verañja, illuminating the city streets with rays as golden as liquid gold. As soon as they saw the Blessed One standing at the door of the house, the attendants informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin, regaining his mindfulness and being moved by a sense of urgency (saṃvega), rose suddenly, prepared a costly seat, and went out to meet the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, please come this way." The Blessed One approached and sat on the prepared seat. Then the Brahmin Verañja, wishing to sit near the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One from where he was standing. The meaning of the words following this is clear.

Regarding what the Brahmin said: "Moreover, though there were gifts to be given (deyyadhamma), they were not given," the intention is as follows: "To you who were invited by me and have completed the rains retreat, I should have given gifts such as gruel and snacks every morning for three months, food and meals at midday, and various drinks, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in the evening; however, these were not given." In the phrase "Tañca kho no asantaṃ," a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa) should be understood. The meaning here is: "It is not that those gifts were not with us." Or, it should be understood as: "That gift-object which we would have given to you was not absent from us."
166:
It is not that we lack the intention to give. It is not as if we lack the desire to give, as is the case with miserly people who possess many riches and resources (that is to say, we always have the intention to give).

In the statement, "Where can such an offering be found in this world? Those who lead the household life have many duties," the explanation is as follows: Because those who lead the household life have many duties, even though there are things to be given and the desire to give exists in this world, where can we find such an offering that we should give to you? How can it be obtained? Thus, he spoke disparagingly of the household life. It is said that he did not know he had been turned away by Māra, but thought, "I have become forgetful due to the preoccupations of household life"; therefore, he spoke thus. Alternatively, "Where can such an offering be found in this world?" means: Where can I find that offering which I should have given to you during these three months? For household life is full of many duties. Thus should the explanation be understood.

Then the Brahmin, thinking, "It would be good if I could give in a single day all the things to be given that should have been offered over the three months," said, "May the Venerable Gotama accept my offering," and so on. In those words, "for the sake of tomorrow" means: for the sake of the merit and the joy and happiness that will arise tomorrow for me who performs a grand honor to you. Then the Blessed One thought, "If I do not accept, the Brahmin and the residents of Verañjā might think, 'This Venerable Gotama seems to be angry because he received nothing for three months; therefore, even though I entreat him, he does not accept even a single meal; there is no patience (khanti) in this Venerable Gotama; he is not all-knowing (Sabbaññū),' and thus they might disparage me and produce much demerit. Let that not happen to them." Out of compassion for them, the Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.

Having accepted, the Blessed One then informed the Brahmin of Verañja, "There is no benefit in worrying about the preoccupations of household life," and showed him the benefits of the present life and the life to come with a Dhamma talk suitable for that moment. Having established him in wholesome states, encouraged him in those wholesome deeds, gladdened him with that encouragement and other existing virtues, and showered the rain of the Dhamma-treasure, he rose from his seat and departed. When the Blessed One had departed, the Brahmin of Verañja addressed his wife and children: "Friends, although we invited the Blessed One for three months, we have not given even a single meal for one day. Come now, prepare the offering in such a way that the gifts for three months can be given tomorrow in a single day." Then, having had an excellent offering prepared, when the night of the day the Blessed One was invited had passed, he had the dwelling place decorated and costly seats prepared...
167:
...and having prepared a great offering diverse with perfumes, incense, and flowers, he had the time for the meal announced to the Blessed One. Regarding this, the Elder Upāli said: "Then the Brahmin of Verañja, at the end of that night... the meal is ready."

The Blessed One, surrounded by the Community of Monks, went to the Brahmin's house. Regarding this, it was said: "Then the Blessed One... sat down together with the Community of Monks." Then the Brahmin of Verañja [served] "the Community of Monks with the Buddha at its head" (buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ). "With the Buddha at its head" means with the Buddha as the leader, having seated the Buddha as the Elder of the Sangha. "With excellent" (paṇītena) means with the best (food). "With his own hand" (sahatthā) means by his own hand. "Having satisfied" (santappetvā) means having well-satisfied, making them full and satiated as much as they desired. "Having refused" (sampavāretvā) means having well-refused, causing them to decline by a sign of the hand, a sign of the face, or by speech, saying "Enough." "One who has eaten" (bhuttāviṃ) means one who has finished the meal. "One who has removed his hand from the bowl" (onītapattapāṇiṃ) means one who has taken his hand away from the bowl; it means the hand is removed. "Clothed him with a set of three robes" (ticīvarena acchādesi) means he gave the three robes to the Blessed One. This expression "clothed him with a set of three robes" is merely a conventional way of speaking. In that set of three robes, each single cloth was worth a thousand (kahāpaṇas). Thus, the Brahmin gave the Blessed One a set of three robes worth three thousand, which were excellent like Kāsian cloth. To each monk, he gave a pair of cloths. In those pairs, each single cloth was worth five hundred. Thus, he gave cloths worth five hundred thousand to the five hundred monks. Even after giving this much, the Brahmin was not satisfied and again gave many red blankets worth seven or eight thousand, and cloths from the Patta and Paṭṭa regions, cutting them up for the purpose of meditation straps (āyoga), shoulder straps (aṃsakūṭa), waistbands (kāyabandhana), water filters (parissāvana), and so on. Furthermore, having filled pots of medicinal oils cooked a hundred or a thousand times, he gave oil worth a thousand to each monk for anointing their feet. What more need be said? Among the four requisites, there was no equipment used by recluses that was not given. However, in the Pali text, only the robes are mentioned.

Having thus performed a great sacrifice, and sitting down after paying homage together with his wife and children, the Blessed One showered the rain of the Deathless Dhamma in a single day upon the Brahmin of Verañja—who had been deprived of the flavor of the Deathless Dhamma for three months due to the interference of Māra—fulfilling his aspirations and well-demonstrating with a Dhamma talk... he rose from his seat and departed. The Brahmin, too, together with his wife and children, paid homage to the Blessed One and the Community of Monks, saying, "Venerable Sir, please favor us again in the future," and followed them for a distance, returning with tears flowing. Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Verañja as long as he liked, set out and while wandering on tour in the Great Region (Mahāmaṇḍala), wishing to lead the Community of Monks—who were exhausted due to the famine—by a straight path, avoiding the usual route of the Buddhas, he did not go to the cities of Soreyya, Sahassa, and Kaṇṇakujja, but headed towards the Payāga landing...
168:
"May you favor us once again," saying such words as these, he followed the Buddha, shedding tears, and then returned.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Verañjā as long as he wished, departed from Verañjā. When wandering through the great regions, he set aside the usual route taken by the Buddhas. Wishing to lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, who were exhausted by the affliction of famine, by a direct route, he did not go to Soreyya and other places but went to the landing place at Payāga. Having crossed the river Ganges there, he arrived at Vārāṇasī. Having stayed in Vārāṇasī as long as he wished, he proceeded to Vesālī. Regarding this journey, [the Elder Upāli] said: "Without going to Soreyya... he stayed at the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood in Vesālī."

## The discussion on the habits of the Buddhas is concluded.
## In the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,
## the explanation of the Verañjakaṇḍa is concluded.
## Regarding the state of being entirely pleasing of this Samantapāsādikā commentary, it is said:

Through the lineage of teachers, and by illustrating the various origins and stories,
By avoiding the doctrines of others, and by purifying our own doctrine;
By refining the phrasing, by the meanings of words, and by the sequence of connecting the Pali text,
By the determination of training rules, and by showing the various methods of the Vibhaṅga;
Since nothing unpleasing is seen here by the wise who examine it,
Therefore, for the wise, this is called "Samantapāsādikā" (The Entirely Pleasing).
This commentary on the Vinaya, spoken by the Lord of the World out of compassion for the world,
Has been set forth by the one skilled in disciplining those who are to be disciplined.
